source: hand-written: the extension, code-of-practice and plan literature the journal sources do not index

papers.title: Corrals for Handling Beef Cattle (Agdex 420/723-1)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture, Food and Rural Development
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta (free low-resolution PDF)
papers.abstract: The most directly applicable Canadian source. Covers cattle behaviour, flight zone, handling technique, corral geometry and components with full dimension tables: collection alley 10-16 ft, crowding pen 8-10 head, funnel pen with one straight side and one at 30 degrees, working chute 18/22/28 in by weight class and 28-32 in general, tapered chute options, chute length 20-50 ft, 'maximum curve is a 15 degree angle, meaning a 16 ft or greater radius', single-chute capacity table by radius, catwalk 18 in wide and 36-42 in below the top of the chute fence, one-way gate 12 ft ahead of the squeeze, man gates 18 in spring-loaded opening inward, fence 5-6 ft with 6 in top-diameter posts 8 ft on centre, loading chute 30-35 in wide with 20 degree fixed / 25 degree adjustable maximum slope, and holding pen areas by weight. Notably honest on evidence: states that circular chutes and crowding pens can cut handling time by up to 50 percent for queued cattle but that 'for cattle running freely through the chute it makes no difference, curved or straight'.

papers.title: Code of Practice for the Care and Handling of Beef Cattle
papers.authors: National Farm Animal Care Council (NFACC) / Canadian Cattlemen's Association
papers.licence: Free download from NFACC
papers.abstract: Canada's national welfare code and the only quasi-regulatory document that applies to this ranch. Still the current version as of November 2026; a revision is under way with public comment 13 April to 12 June 2026 and completion projected for Q2 2027. IMPORTANT FINDING: the Code contains NO facility dimensions whatsoever. Its handling-facility Requirements are only that all beef operations must have access to equipment or facilities for safe handling, restraint, treatment, segregation, loading and unloading; that facilities provide well-drained comfortable resting areas; and that traction be provided in handling areas to minimise slips and falls. Section 4.1 lists outcome-based handling measures to watch (falling, stumbling after release, running or jumping when leaving the chute) and says increasing levels may indicate a need to change lighting, noise, equipment, handling methods or environment. Recommended Practice 1.2(e) notes high-pitched sounds are especially disturbing to cattle.

papers.title: Designing a Bud Box for Cattle Handling (MF3349)
papers.authors: Kansas State University Research and Extension; dimension table by Raymond L. Huhnke and Sam Harp
papers.source: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
papers.licence: Free K-State Research and Extension publication
papers.abstract: The best free source of Bud Box geometry, with eleven scaled layout templates. Minimum box 12 ft wide by 20 ft deep processing 5-6 mature cows; 24 ft box works 6-8 head; load-out box for semis commonly 14 ft wide by 30 ft deep. Alleyway minimum 28 in wide; allow 5-6 ft of alleyway per mature cow; the box must always be big enough to fill the alley it leads into and must never be used as a holding pen. Drive alleys 12 ft minimum on foot, 16 ft if horses are used. Explicit corner guidance: the purpose of angled fences is to eliminate as many 90-degree turns as possible; a 45-degree angled fence section aids turning cattle around; a single-file alley at 60 degrees from the box improves flow over the common 90 degrees. Curved alleys must be long enough for the lead animal to stay visible, at minimum fitting two head. Converted round tubs: limit a 12 ft diameter half-tub to 4-5 head, a 10 ft diameter to 3-4 head. Loading ramp steps 12 in wide and 4 in high. Reprints the Midwest Plan Service corral dimension table.

papers.title: The Visual, Auditory, and Physical Environment of Livestock Handling Facilities and Its Effect on Ease of Movement of Cattle, Pigs, and Sheep
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0 (open access)
papers.abstract: Grandin's most recent facility-environment review and the single most useful source for automated fault flagging, because it names the two worst layout mistakes explicitly: a single-file race that is too wide ('if it is one and a half animals wide, there will be constant jamming') and a crowd pen with a funnel that is too gradual ('cattle will constantly jam in the gradual funnel'). Also gives cleat spacing 20 cm for cattle with the rule that a hoof must fit easily between cleats, 20 degree maximum ramp angle for cattle, the finding from Willson et al. 2021 that sharp high-contrast shadows caused more balking than no shadow or a soft shadow, and outcome-based numeric thresholds: falling should be 1 percent or less across three audit surveys; mean electric prod use at large feedlots 3.8 percent with the best at 0 and worst at 45 percent; adding a light at a stun box entrance cut prod-driven vocalisation from 8 to 0 percent; reducing neck stanchion pressure cut vocalisation from 23 to 0 percent. Argues that rebuilding is usually unnecessary and that lighting and flooring fixes are often enough.

papers.title: Behavioral Principles of Livestock Handling (with 1999 and 2002 updates on vision, hearing, and handling methods in cattle and pigs)
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.source: The Professional Animal Scientist, December 1989, pp. 1-11 (American Registry of Professional Animal Scientists)
papers.licence: Author-hosted copy; Semantic Scholar open PDF
papers.abstract: Grandin's core design review with a full bibliography, which is what makes the numbers traceable. Curved race inner radius 3.5-5 m (12-16 ft); if bends smaller than 3.5 m are used there must be a 3 m (10 ft) straight single-file section at the crowd-pen junction; short 1.5 m bends are possible per Grandin 1984b. Round crowd pen radius 3.5 m cattle, 1.83 m pigs, 2.4 m sheep, attributed explicitly to 'practical experience'. Straight crowd pen: one fence straight, the other at 30 degrees, cited to the UK Meat and Livestock Commission. Maximum stationary ramp steepness 20 degrees for market-weight animals. Flight zone 2-8 m for feedlot cattle and up to 50 m for extensively raised cows. Crucially, attributes the 'circular crowd pen and curved race reduced time moving cattle by up to 50 percent' claim to Vowles and Hollier 1982, a one-page Australian conference abstract, letting the reader see how thin the evidence base is.

papers.title: Cattle Behavior and Cattle Handling
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.source: American Association of Bovine Practitioners Conference Proceedings
papers.licence: Open access AABP Proceedings
papers.abstract: Practitioner-facing summary of why a curved chute works, with figures for a curved cattle handling facility and a curved loading ramp. States that circular crowd pens and curved chutes can reduce handling time, that curved chutes must have a straight section where they join the crowd pen and must be built as a smooth continuous curve, and that if the curve is too sharp the chute looks like a dead end. Confirms solid sides for single-file chute, loading chute and crowding pen; recommends the catwalk along the inner radius; and notes that for unloading only a wide straight chute of 6 to 10 ft is appropriate. Useful because it states the design rules in the same voice a vet would use with a producer.

papers.title: Engineering and design of holding yards, loading ramps and handling facilities for land and sea transport of livestock
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Free full text from Istituto Zooprofilattico Sperimentale dell'Abruzzo e del Molise
papers.abstract: The citation behind Grandin's flooring and cleat numbers, which later papers (including Grandin 2021) point to. Argues that stair steps beat grooves because 'steps are more effective than grooves and provide non-slip footing even when old and worn. Grooves wear down quickly and become slick.' Concrete stair step dimensions for a cattle truck loading ramp: 10 cm rise with a 30 cm or longer tread, plus two grooves at least 2.5 cm deep in each step. Cleats 5 cm by 5 cm hardwood for cattle and other large livestock, 2.5 cm by 2.5 cm for smaller species, with concrete reinforcing rod suitable for steel ramps, and the governing rule that cleats must be spaced so a hoof fits between them. Also distinguishes facilities for intensively raised halter-trained animals from those for extensively raised cattle - directly relevant to a range cow herd.

papers.title: Corral and Working Facilities for Beef Cattle (BAE-1219)
papers.authors: Raymond L. Huhnke
papers.licence: Free Oklahoma Cooperative Extension Service fact sheet
papers.abstract: The canonical North American dimension table (Table 1, Corral and Working Facilities Dimensions), derived from the Midwest Plan Service Beef Housing and Equipment Handbook: holding area 14/17/20 sq ft per head and crowding pen 6/10/12 sq ft per head for to-600 lb, 600-1200 lb and over-1200 lb; working chute with vertical sides 18/24/28 in wide and 20 ft minimum length; sloping sides 13/15/16 in bottom and 20/24/26 in top; working chute fence 45/50/60 in minimum height with posts 30 in deep; corral fence 60 in; loading chute 26 in wide, 12 ft minimum, 3.5 in rise per foot, with ramp heights of 15 in stock trailer, 28 in pickup, 40 in stock truck, 48 in tractor-trailer and 100 in double-deck. Adds two rules not in the table: add width for exotic breeds over 1200 lb, and the maximum width for a common alleyway used to SORT cattle is 12 ft. A quarter-circle crowding area with a 12 ft crowding gate handles up to eight mature cows. Note: this table is reprinted by Kentucky, Tennessee, Mississippi and Kansas, so those are not independent confirmations.

papers.title: Cattle Handling and Working Facilities Design (Beef Cattle Manual, Chapter 40)
papers.authors: Ray Huhnke, Bob LeValley and Brian Freking
papers.source: Oklahoma State University Master Cattleman Program, Beef Cattle Manual
papers.licence: Free Oklahoma State University Extension chapter
papers.abstract: Teaching chapter version of the Oklahoma design guidance, organised around the components a corral designer must place: holding pens, crowding area, working chute, working area, headgate or squeeze, loading chute, scales and hospital area. Repeats the Midwest Plan Service dimension table and adds discussion of why a circular crowding pen with solid sides and a solid crowding gate works (the only escape route the animal can see is the chute) and why the working chute should be curved with solid sides (cattle cannot see the handlers or the squeeze until a few feet from the end). Useful as a plain-language cross-check on the Oklahoma fact sheet.

papers.title: Beef Cattle Handling Facilities (SP690)
papers.authors: University of Tennessee Extension
papers.source: University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture Extension
papers.licence: Free University of Tennessee Extension publication
papers.abstract: Gives dimensions split by British versus exotic breeds, which is the split that matters for a Red Angus herd. Table 1: holding chute height 60 in British and 66-72 in exotic, width 22-26 in, length 5 ft with service gate or 7 ft without; working chute with vertical sides 22-26 in wide and 20 ft minimum; sloping sides 16 in bottom and 28 in top, with the useful detail that a CURVED chute is allowed 28-29 in top inside width rather than 28 in; chute fence 60 in British and 66-72 in exotic with post spacing 6 ft and post depth 36 in; crowding pen 10 sq ft per head British and 12 exotic; holding pen 20 sq ft per head with 60 in fence, 8 ft post spacing and 30 in post depth. States a straight working chute should be a maximum of 26 in wide and that the loading chute should be 26-30 in wide, at least 12 ft long, with a maximum 30 percent incline and located directly off the crowding pen.

papers.title: Designing or Reworking Your Cattle-handling Facilities: A Checklist for Success (AEN-145)
papers.authors: Morgan Hayes and Josh Jackson
papers.source: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension Service, Biosystems and Agricultural Engineering
papers.licence: Free University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension publication
papers.abstract: A planning checklist rather than a dimension table, which makes it the closest published analogue to what a software corral designer should walk a user through: site selection, access from all pastures, drainage, group sizes used to size the holding and crowding pens, which components are needed for which operation type (cow-calf versus seedstock), and sequencing of a build or rework. Valuable for structuring the designer's prompts and warnings rather than for numeric thresholds.

papers.title: Cattle Behavior During Handling and Corral Design for Beef Cow Herds (Extension Bulletin E-2296)
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.source: Michigan State University Cooperative Extension Service, Michigan Beef Production
papers.licence: Free MSU Extension Publication Archive (archive copy; not current recommendations)
papers.abstract: Grandin writing specifically for beef COW herds rather than feedlots or packing plants, which is the right audience for a cow-calf corral designer. Covers cattle behaviour during handling, flight zone, point of balance, and corral design for cow-calf operations with layout drawings. Archived by MSU with the caveat that it is not current recommendations, so it should be used as a historical statement of Grandin's cow-herd guidance and cross-checked against her 1997 and 2021 papers rather than cited as current.

papers.title: Illinois Grazing Manual Fact Sheet: Livestock Handling Facilities Designs
papers.authors: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Illinois
papers.source: USDA NRCS, Illinois Grazing Manual Part 4
papers.licence: US Government work, public domain
papers.abstract: A USDA fact sheet that summarises the Midwest Plan Service MWPS-6 handling designs and is therefore a free route to numbers otherwise locked in that handbook. Gives several thresholds not found elsewhere: slope working facilities at less than 3 percent to reduce gate swing problems; taper the crowding or funnel pen from 12 ft to about 2 ft at the chute entrance; a minimum curve radius of 15 ft is recommended for a working chute; provide at least a 20 ft long chute to hold 3 or 4 head; chute sides should be about 4 in above the ground for manure removal and insect control; one crowding pen is sufficient for operations up to 250 cattle; conditioning pens for newly arrived stressed cattle at 100 sq ft per head; hospital area concrete roughened and sloped a quarter inch per foot. Also reproduces several complete corral layout plans.

papers.title: Livestock Handling Facilities Designs
papers.authors: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
papers.licence: US Government work, public domain
papers.abstract: The standalone NRCS handling-facility design sheet, same content family as the Illinois Grazing Manual fact sheet, carrying the full set of component specifications (conditioning, holding, sorting and crowding pens; working and loading chutes; headgates; hospital area) plus the dimensional rules: 15 ft minimum curve radius, 20 ft minimum chute, 12 ft to 2 ft funnel taper, under 3 percent site slope, 4 in gap under the chute sides, and sloped chute sides that restrict the animal's feet to a narrow path and prevent turning around. Includes reference layouts with circular crowding pen and curved working chute.

papers.title: Conservation Practice Standard 382: Fence
papers.authors: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
papers.licence: US Government work, public domain
papers.abstract: Included because it is the closest thing to an engineering standard for corral fencing that is freely available, and because it demonstrates that no structural DESIGN LOAD is published. The standard is prescriptive, not load-based: wood fences in a corral situation must have a minimum of four nominal 2 by 6 boards, placed on the livestock side of the posts; steel post spacing is capped at 8 ft on centre; post material options and bracing requirements are specified. If the corral designer needs a load check it must refer the user to MWPS-6 and a licensed engineer rather than cite a number, because figures circulating online (1,500 lb impact, 1,200-2,000 lb from a leaning animal) are vendor marketing with no engineering basis.

papers.title: Feedlot Design and Construction, Section 23: Cattle processing facility
papers.authors: Rod Davis and Scott Janke
papers.source: Meat & Livestock Australia (MLA), Feedlot Design and Construction manual
papers.licence: Free MLA publication
papers.abstract: The most engineering-literate free source, and the only one giving the Bud Box dimension table in metric alongside an explicit safety critique. Race clear width 660-760 mm with the trade-off stated (too wide lets small cattle turn around or all cattle put their heads down beside the animal in front; too narrow constrains large cattle); race length 1.6-2.4 m per adult beast; the race must be straight for at least two animal lengths at the start because an immediate curve would look like a dead end; drafting race 4000-4800 mm long at 760-820 mm single-animal width. Circular forcing yard sweep 180 to 270 degrees, with a funnel alternative of one straight side and the other entering the race at approximately 30 degrees. Catwalk minimum 600 mm wide with handrails required above 300 mm elevation. Bud Box Table 1: 3.7 m wide by 6 m minimum deep for a handler always on foot, 4.3 m by 6-9 m afoot and horseback, 4.9 m maximum by 9 m maximum always horseback; the race entry must be a SQUARE opening not V-shaped; the far end must not be enclosed so cattle see light; cattle must never be held in the box; 90-degree corners in a Bud Box are intentional and make construction simpler. Notably contradicts part of Grandin's circling rationale: 'this circling can raise the arousal level of the cattle making them more difficult and dangerous to handle'.

papers.title: Handling Facilities
papers.authors: Tom Ryan (Teagasc, Kildalton)
papers.source: Teagasc (Irish Agriculture and Food Development Authority) / Irish Farmers Journal
papers.licence: Free Teagasc publication
papers.abstract: Short but contains the clearest published statement anywhere of the funnel angle that causes two cattle to wedge abreast: 'The angle of the funnel is critical and should not exceed 30 degrees. If the angles are wider, cattle may block or turn at the mouth of the race or two cattle may become jammed at the race entrance.' One side of the funnel must be straight; widest point 3-4 m. Race length minimum 3.6 m and preferably over 5 m, with 9 m holding 5-6 cattle and long races above 12 cattle discouraged. Race internal width 650-700 mm adult, up to 900 mm for exceptionally large pedigree stock, about 500 mm for young stock; race height 1.4-1.5 m; uprights about 2 m apart; side bars 350-400 mm apart. Catwalk 300-450 mm high and 375-450 mm wide with a working area not less than 1.2 m. Safety passes 300-350 mm clear, at least one per pen and one every 7.5-8 m in handling passageways, with the warning not to place a pass where animal flow lines up with it because excited animals try to escape through it and become trapped. Collecting pen areas 0.9-1.1 sq m young, 1.4-1.7 finishing, 2.3-2.75 suckler cows with calves.

papers.title: New Zealand Stockyard Loading Facility Guidelines, Version 1.0
papers.authors: National Livestock Transport and Safety Council (New Zealand)
papers.source: National Livestock Transport and Safety Council / Transporting New Zealand
papers.licence: Free industry guideline
papers.abstract: The most recent (2025) codified loading-facility specification found, useful because it independently reproduces several of Grandin's numbers from a completely different tradition and adds truck-access requirements. Cattle yard fencing must be at least 1.7 m high with a backrub indicator cross bar above, with extra height for cattle over 1.4 m at the hip. Ramp height 1.1-1.2 m with slope not exceeding 20 degrees; maximum slope must not exceed 20 degrees for all animals except young animals, for which ramps are discouraged and the maximum should be no greater than 12 degrees. Ramp flooring must be solid and non-slip. Personnel gates at the top of ramps must be self-closing and open onto a flat unobstructed area. Independently recommends aligning ramps north-south to avoid sun, matching Alberta's advice. Access-road clearance 4.5 m high by 4 m wide, with a level firm truck pad and a marked no-go zone between reversing trucks and ramps.

papers.title: Livestock Control: Non-Electric Fence Designs (Order No. 307.260-1)
papers.authors: British Columbia Ministry of Agriculture
papers.source: Government of British Columbia, Ministry of Agriculture
papers.licence: Province of British Columbia, free download
papers.abstract: A Canadian government fence-construction reference covering post sizing, embedment, bracing, rail arrangements and corner and gate construction for livestock containment. Included for the fence and gate construction side of the corral designer, and because it confirms the pattern seen across the whole literature: Canadian and US agencies publish prescriptive material and spacing requirements rather than structural design loads for handling-yard fences.

papers.title: Planning and Building Fences on the Farm (PB1541)
papers.authors: University of Tennessee Extension
papers.source: University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture Extension
papers.licence: Free University of Tennessee Extension publication
papers.abstract: Comprehensive farm fence handbook covering post types and sizes, embedment depth, brace assemblies, wire and board fences, gate hanging and corner construction. Checked specifically for a published structural design load for a handling-yard fence and it does not give one, which supports flagging the absence as a genuine gap rather than a search failure. Useful to the corral designer for post and brace selection once a layout is fixed.

papers.title: Planning and Constructing Fences (Handling Beef Cattle, Section 3)
papers.authors: University of Kentucky / Eden Shale Farm
papers.source: Kentucky Beef Network, Eden Shale Farm
papers.licence: Free Kentucky Beef Network / Eden Shale Farm publication
papers.abstract: Section 3 of a beef-cattle handling manual, dealing with fence planning and construction around handling facilities, drawing on Midwest Plan Service MWPS-6 for its high-tensile fence data. Included for the fence-construction detail the designer will need once pen and alley geometry is settled, and as a further confirmation that design loads are not published in the extension literature.

papers.title: Cattle Handling Pointers: Stockmanship and Low-Stress Handling
papers.authors: Ron Gill and Rick Machen
papers.source: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension (hosted by Utah State University BEHAVE)
papers.licence: Free Texas A&M AgriLife Extension publication
papers.abstract: Gill and Machen are the authors of the Bud Box dimension table that MLA and Kansas State both reproduce, so this is the closest free document to the primary Bud Box source. Covers stockmanship fundamentals that the geometry depends on: working the point of balance, pressure and release, positioning relative to the direction of travel, and the principle that cattle want to go back the way they came, which is the mechanism behind both the Bud Box and the round tub. Important for the designer because the Bud Box's published advantage is conditional on handler skill, and this is the document that defines that skill.

papers.title: Bud Box Bonanza: A rancher's simple handling layout cuts costs and decreases stress
papers.authors: Boyd Kidwell
papers.licence: Free Angus Journal article PDF
papers.abstract: Trade-press account of a working Bud Box on a commercial Angus operation, included because this ranch runs Red Angus and because the published Bud Box literature is thin. Describes the layout, build cost and the operator's experience of cattle flow and reduced stress. It is journalism, not evidence, and should be tagged as such in the library - but it is one of the few free accounts of a Bud Box in an Angus cow-calf setting rather than a feedlot.

papers.title: Bovine Behavior: Key to Handling Cattle
papers.authors: Stanley E. Curtis
papers.source: American Association of Bovine Practitioners Conference Proceedings
papers.licence: Open access AABP Proceedings
papers.abstract: An independent behavioural-science treatment of cattle handling, written by a Penn State animal environment scientist rather than by Grandin, which makes it a useful check on whether the behavioural premises underlying the design rules (flight zone, following behaviour, vision, response to novelty) are accepted outside Grandin's own body of work. Covers bovine sensory capabilities and behavioural responses relevant to facility design.

papers.title: Corrals for Working and Handling Beef Cattle
papers.authors: University of Idaho Cooperative Extension Service
papers.licence: Free University of Idaho Extension archive
papers.abstract: A 1971 bulletin with complete bills of materials and construction drawings for working corrals, retained because it documents the pre-Grandin design tradition and gives construction detail modern sheets omit: post depth varying from two and a half feet in heavy gravelly soil to four feet in light clay, posts with at least five-inch tops treated to 12 in above ground line, post spacing no more than six feet (extendable to ten with heavier rails), catwalk 36-40 in above ground, alleys always at least 12 ft wide, gates 10-12 ft long for crowding areas, crowding pens sloped about 2 percent (half an inch per foot) for drainage, and loading chutes up to 16 ft long. The scanned text is OCR-degraded, so individual figures should be confirmed against the page images before being coded into the designer.

papers.title: The design and construction of facilities for handling cattle
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Paywalled at Elsevier; full text posted by the author at grandin.com
papers.abstract: THE single most important citation for the corral designer, and the source of nearly every number in the geometry rules. Race width 66-71 cm adult cows and 51 cm calves with only 2 cm clearance per side of the largest cow; V race 41-45 cm at the bottom and 81 cm at the 152 cm level; minimum race length 9 m; curved race inner radius 3.5-6 m with 6 m preferred for rapid in-race vaccination; a 3 m straight section required at the crowd-pen junction if the inner radius is under 3 m; crowd gate 3.5 m ideal and 3 m for smaller operations; funnel crowd pen one side straight and one at 30 degrees; fence height 152 cm English and tame breeds, 167-183 cm Brahman cross and excitable Continental lines; post spacing 1.2 m on wood or concrete curved races; walkway platform 100 cm below the top of the race fence; man gates 45 cm; ramp 76 cm single file for adult cows, 2.5-3 m for unloading only; stair steps 30 cm tread and 10 cm rise; floor grooves 2.5-5 cm deep in a 20 cm square or diamond pattern; belly rail 30-60 cm wide at cow eye height. Crucially for honest software, it reports the contrary evidence: 'Experiments with continuously moving livestock indicated no significant difference between straight and curved races for run-through time (Vowles et al., 1984a)'. It also states the corner rule qualitatively - curved lanes and diagonal pens 'eliminate square corners', round pens have 'no square corners for cattle to bunch up in', and diagonal gates 4.2 m on a 3.5 m lane work 'because gates opening on an angle eliminate sharp corners'. No maximum corner angle is given anywhere in it.

papers.title: Observations of cattle behavior applied to the design of cattle handling facilities
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Paywalled at Elsevier
papers.abstract: Grandin's first paper and the origin of the curved-race rationale, the solid-sides recommendation, and the circling and light-seeking behaviours that the whole design tradition rests on. Cited as the source for the 3.5-6 m curved race radius and for the tendency of cattle to move back in the direction from which they came, which is the mechanism behind both the Bud Box and the tub. It is an OBSERVATIONAL study, not a controlled comparison, which matters for how confidently the software can assert its derived rules. No free PDF located.

papers.title: Race system for cattle slaughter plants with 1.5 m radius curves
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Paywalled at Elsevier
papers.abstract: The ONE peer-reviewed measured result behind the tight-radius and straight-entry rules, and therefore the highest-confidence geometry citation in the whole literature. Shows that a race with an inner radius as small as 1.5 m works IF it is built as a continuous smooth curve and IF there is a straight single-file section of at least 3 m joining the race to the crowd pen - without which the entrance looks like a dead end. Grandin 1997 adds the corollary that 'cattle will get stuck if it is built in a series of straight sections'. The work was done in slaughter plants, so transfer to a ranch corral is an assumption, but it is the only number in the corner-and-radius family with a methods section behind it.

papers.title: The influence of cattle yard design on the movement of animals
papers.authors: W. J. Vowles and T. J. Hollier
papers.source: Proceedings of the Australian Society of Animal Production 14:597
papers.licence: Conference proceedings, not online
papers.abstract: THE source of the single most-quoted number in cattle handling - that a circular crowd pen and curved race can cut the time spent moving cattle by up to 50 percent. Presented at the 14th Biennial Conference of the Australian Society of Animal Production, Brisbane, 15 May 1982, by authors at the Victorian Department of Agriculture and its Animal Research Institute. It is a ONE-PAGE ABSTRACT. The 50 percent figure is repeated by Grandin (1989, 1997), the Alberta Agdex and dozens of extension sheets, but the sample size, cattle class and methods cannot be checked by anyone citing it. The software must not present this as an established effect size. Also cited as a source for the 3.5-6 m race radius.

papers.title: The behaviour and movement of cattle through single file handling races
papers.authors: W. J. Vowles, G. A. Eldridge and T. J. Hollier
papers.source: Proceedings of the Australian Society of Animal Production 15:767
papers.licence: Conference proceedings, not online
papers.abstract: THE CONTRARY EVIDENCE, and the reason the corral designer must not warn that a straight race is a design fault. Grandin (1997) reports it as follows: 'Experiments with continuously moving livestock indicated no significant difference between straight and curved races for run-through time (Vowles et al., 1984a).' In other words the curved race advantage, as measured, applies only when cattle queue for a procedure - exactly the Vowles and Hollier 1982 condition - and vanishes when cattle move through continuously. Like the 1982 paper this is a one-page abstract and no replication of it was found. Together the two abstracts are the entire measured basis for the curved-race convention.

papers.title: The behaviour and movement of cattle through forcing yards
papers.authors: W. J. Vowles, G. A. Eldridge and T. J. Hollier
papers.source: Proceedings of the Australian Society of Animal Production 15:766
papers.licence: Conference proceedings, not online
papers.abstract: The measured basis for SOLID crowd pen sides - arguably better supported than the curve itself. Grandin (1997) reports: 'Cattle moved faster through a crowd pen with solid fences compared to one with a pipe fence or partially open-board fence (Vowles et al., 1984b)', and separately that 'some types of cattle move more slowly when they walk straight through the crowd pen into the single-file race', which is the measured argument for a round rather than straight-through forcing pen. A one-page conference abstract, so the same caveat applies, but this is the one crowd-pen recommendation with a measurement behind it rather than practical experience.

papers.title: An observational field study on the effects of changes in shadow contrasts and noise on cattle movement in a small abattoir
papers.authors: Erika Willson, Fabiola Baier and Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Paywalled at Elsevier
papers.abstract: One of the very few MEASURED facility-environment findings relevant to the designer, and recent. In an outdoor facility, sharp high-contrast shadows were associated with more cattle balking and stopping than no shadows or shadows with soft, faint contrast. A noisy truck near the facility also made cattle harder to move. This is the evidence behind treating shadow geometry as a real design fault - which means a corral designer that models sun angle and casts shadows across the race and crowd pen entrance has firmer ground than one that insists on a curve. Reported in full in Grandin 2021 (Frontiers in Animal Science), which is open access, so the finding is usable without the paywalled original.

papers.title: Cattle vocalizations are associated with handling and equipment problems at beef slaughter plants
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Paywalled at Elsevier
papers.abstract: The before-and-after study behind the outcome-based numbers the designer can use to validate a built facility rather than a drawing. Collected data before and after facility modifications and showed simple changes reduced both vocalisation and electric prod use: adding a light at a stun box entrance cut prod-driven vocalisation from 8 percent of cattle to 0, and reducing the pressure a neck stanchion applied cut vocalisation from 23 percent to 0. Establishes vocalisation and prod use as practical, cheap, repeatable measures of whether a handling facility actually works - which is what the corral designer should encourage users to record after a build.

papers.title: Compliance of large feedlots with the Beef Quality Assurance cattle care and handling guidelines
papers.authors: R. Woiwode, Temple Grandin, B. Kirch and J. Paterson
papers.licence: Paywalled
papers.abstract: The audit study behind the numeric outcome thresholds a corral designer can hold a finished facility to. Across large North American feedlots the average percentage of cattle moved with an electric prod was 3.8 percent, with many feedlots at 0 percent and the worst moving 45 percent of cattle with a prod. Together with Grandin 1998, Simon et al. 2015 and Barnhardt et al. 2016, it supports the threshold Grandin 2021 reports from all three surveys: FALLING SHOULD BE 1 PERCENT OR LESS. These are the only numbers in the whole handling literature that are both well replicated and directly checkable on this ranch, which makes them the right thing for the software to ask the user to record.

papers.title: Design of loading facilities and holding pens
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Paywalled at Elsevier; full text posted by the author at grandin.com
papers.abstract: The source behind the loading-ramp and holding-pen numbers, with each one attributed so the reader can see which are measured and which are not. Ramp slope maximum 25 degrees adjustable and 20 degrees fixed for cattle and sheep, both attributed to Grandin 1979 - a single recommendation, not a trial. Level dock at the ramp top a minimum of one animal body length (Stevens and Lyons 1977; Grandin 1979; Agriculture Canada 1984). Stair steps 30 cm minimum tread and 10 cm rise for cattle (USDA 1967; Grandin 1980c, 1982). Cleat spacing 20 cm start to start for large cattle (Mayes 1978). Ramp width 76 cm single file cattle, 2.5-3 m for unloading only. Curved ramp inside radius 5 m. Round crowd pen radius 3.5 m cattle. Cattle alley 3 m on foot, 3.5 m foot and horseback, 4.2 m horseback; cattle pen width 3.5-4.2 m driven on foot; maximum pen length 25 m without block gates; holding pen 1.6 sq m per hornless and 1.85 sq m per horned feedlot steer under 24 hours.

papers.title: Behavioural Principles of Handling Beef Cattle and the Design of Corrals, Lairages, Races and Loading Ramps (in Livestock Handling and Transport, 6th edition)
papers.authors: Temple Grandin (chapter); Temple Grandin (ed.)
papers.source: CAB International (CABI), Livestock Handling and Transport
papers.licence: Paywalled book chapter (CABI)
papers.abstract: The current, most recent consolidated statement of Grandin's beef corral, race and loading ramp design rules, superseding the 1997 Livestock Production Science paper as the citation of record. This is the chapter the corral designer should cite as the authoritative modern source for the geometry, and it carries the Vowles and Hollier 1982 and Vowles et al. 1984 citations forward, including the related 1984 follow-up on cattle movement through single-file races. Paywalled, so the free Grandin 1997 full text at grandin.com and the open-access Grandin 2021 Frontiers paper are the practical substitutes - but the library should record this as the current edition so the ranch knows the 2024 version exists.

papers.title: Beef Housing and Equipment Handbook (MWPS-6), 4th edition
papers.authors: Midwest Plan Service
papers.source: Midwest Plan Service, Iowa State University
papers.licence: Commercial publication, for sale
papers.abstract: THE ORIGIN of essentially every North American corral dimension table. The Corral and Working Facilities Dimensions table reproduced by Kentucky ID-13 (which credits MWPS explicitly), Oklahoma BAE-1219, Kansas MF3349, Mississippi P2787 and Tennessee SP690 all descend from this handbook, as do the NRCS fact sheets, which cite MWPS-6 fourth edition by name. This matters enormously for how the software reports confidence: five or six extension sheets agreeing on 18/24/28 in chute widths is NOT five independent confirmations, it is one source quoted five times, and no study is cited behind the original table. Recorded here as a citation so the library shows where the lineage terminates. Must be purchased from Midwest Plan Service; no free PDF.

papers.title: Beef Cattle Corrals and Handling Facilities (ID-13)
papers.authors: Roy Burris, Charles Absher, Sam McNeill and Larry Turner
papers.source: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension Service
papers.licence: Free HTML from University of Kentucky; PDF no longer served
papers.abstract: The cleanest surviving rendering of the Midwest Plan Service dimension table, and the version that credits MWPS as the source, which is why it is worth recording even though only the HTML survives. Holding area 14/17/20 sq ft and crowding pen 6/10/12 sq ft per head by weight class; working chute vertical 18/22/26 in, sloping 15/15/16 in bottom and 20/24/26 in top, 20 ft minimum length, fence 45/50/50 in, posts 30 in deep; add 2 in for exotic breeds; corral fence 60 in to 1200 lb and 60-66 in over, posts no more than 8 ft apart and at least 30 in deep; holding pen fence 5 ft British and at least 5.5 ft Brahman-cross and exotic; catwalk about 18 in above ground; circular crowding pen with a 12 ft swinging gate, a quarter-circle handling up to 8 mature cows; gates should swing in the direction of cattle movement and may need to swing up to 270 degrees; loading chute 26-30 in wide, 12 ft minimum, maximum slope 30 percent or 3.5 in rise per foot, stepped ramps with steps at least 18 in wide and risers no more than 4 in, cleats 1 by 3 hardwood nailed 6 in on centre. Also states that a curved chute, or one with at least a 15 degree bend, reduces backing up - while giving no radius. Note its working-chute fence height for over 1200 lb is 50 in where Oklahoma gives 60 in: a genuine discrepancy within one table lineage.

papers.title: Designing a Bud Box
papers.authors: Ron Gill and Rick Machen
papers.licence: Free Texas A&M AgriLife Extension publication; original PDF URL now dead
papers.abstract: THE PRIMARY SOURCE for Bud Box dimensions, and the correction to a widely mis-quoted figure. Its table sets box size by handler type, not by head count: handler ALWAYS ON FOOT 12 ft minimum width by 20 ft depth; AFOOT AND HORSEBACK 14 ft by 20-30 ft; ALWAYS HORSEBACK 16 ft maximum width by 30 ft maximum depth, with depth 'dictated by size of groups handled'. MLA reproduces exactly this table in metric (3.7 by 6 m, 4.3 by 6-9 m, 4.9 by 9 m) in its 2016 feedlot manual, and Kansas MF3349 cites Gill as its source. This means the commonly quoted range of 'about 14 by 20 ft to 20 by 30 ft' is WRONG ON WIDTH: the published widths are 12-16 ft, never 20. The original agrilifecdn.tamu.edu PDF now 404s; the table is recoverable from the MLA manual and from Cornell's hosted copy.

papers.title: Laying out curved handling facilities for ranches and feedlots
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Free on the author's website; HTML only
papers.abstract: The most directly actionable layout page Grandin publishes, and the one a corral designer should encode first. Round crowd pen ideal radius 12 ft, with the reasoning spelled out: a crowd gate longer than 12 ft makes the pen too big and an 8 ft gate makes it too small. Cattle should make a 180 degree turn through a round crowd pen, and where that is not possible a turn of 90 degrees or more. Keep the crowd pen under half full, because cattle need room to turn. An animal standing in the crowd pen must be able to see a minimum of two body lengths up the chute before it turns, and the article elsewhere recommends two to three. The fix for a chute that bends too sharply at the crowd pen - and therefore looks like a dead end - is to add a 10 ft straight section of single-file chute. If a building does not cover the entire crowd pen and chute, at least two body lengths of chute should extend outside it. No PDF; HTML only.

papers.title: Non-slip flooring for livestock handling
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.licence: Free on the author's website; HTML only
papers.abstract: The only source giving flooring groove patterns at a dimension a designer could draw. For BEEF CATTLE, a deep square pattern of 20 by 20 cm (8 by 8 in) squares with V-grooves at least 2.5 cm (1 in) deep and 2.5 cm wide. For high-traffic beef areas, metal grating in 30 by 30 cm (12 by 12 in) squares with rod at least 2.5 cm diameter. Concrete stair steps for cattle at 10 cm rise and 30-45 cm run with 2.5 cm groove depth. Non-adjustable loading ramps 20 degrees or less. Cleats must be spaced to fit the animal's stride so a hoof cannot slip between them, with no numeric spacing given on this page (the 20 cm figure comes from Grandin 2008). Separate, smaller patterns are given for pigs and dairy cows and must not be applied to beef. No studies are cited on the page, so this is the author's engineering judgement.

papers.title: Understanding Flight Zone and Point of Balance for Low Stress Handling of Cattle, Sheep, and Pigs
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.source: grandin.com (author's own behaviour pages, updated July 2022)
papers.licence: Free on the author's website; HTML only
papers.abstract: The reference for the two behavioural quantities a corral designer needs in order to place catwalks, man gates and handler positions. The point of balance is at the SHOULDER for cattle confined in a single-file race, but may move forward to just behind the eye for cattle at liberty on pasture or in large pens - so the same diagram does not apply in both places. Behind the point of balance the animal moves forward; ahead of it, it backs up, and standing ahead of it while trying to drive an animal forward in a race is named as a common handler mistake. Groups in a race often move forward without prodding when the handler walks past each animal's point of balance in the OPPOSITE direction of travel, which is the behavioural justification for a catwalk on the inner radius. Flight zone size varies with tameness, excitement and angle of approach, is larger on a head-on approach, and is zero in completely tame animals; Grandin's published ranges elsewhere are 2-8 m for feedlot cattle and up to 50 m for extensively raised cows.

papers.title: Bud Box vs. Round Tub Systems
papers.authors: South Dakota State University Extension
papers.licence: Free SDSU Extension web article; HTML only
papers.abstract: A recent northern-plains extension comparison, recorded because it is one of the few published side-by-side treatments and because it independently confirms the Bud Box size most often built: 'a rectangular pen (usually 12x20 or 14x20 ft.)'. Its comparison table scores cost (box lower), handler skill required (box higher), cattle flow (box more natural if done right, tub guided by structure) and space required (box smaller footprint, tub larger). IMPORTANT: there is NO controlled trial behind any of these comparisons. I searched for a Journal of Animal Science or Applied Animal Behaviour Science head-to-head study of Bud Box versus tub and found none. Every published comparison, including this one, is qualitative extension opinion, so the corral designer must not score one layout above the other.

papers.title: Beef Cattle Facilities: Handling Systems
papers.authors: Penn State Extension
papers.licence: Free Penn State Extension web article; HTML only
papers.abstract: Recorded for one sentence that captures the real difference between the two crowding-pen options better than any dimension does: Bud Box systems 'rely more on the handler's relationship with, and ability to read, the cattle' while tub-style systems 'rely more on the cattle's instincts to avoid humans'. This is the correct framing for a corral designer, because it means the choice is a function of who will be working the cattle rather than of geometry, and it aligns with the one engineering authority (MLA 2016) that flags the Bud Box's handler-safety disadvantage - the handler must be inside the box with the cattle with no easy escape route.

papers.title: Flight distance in Merino sheep
papers.authors: G. D. Hutson
papers.licence: Paywalled at Cambridge University Press
papers.abstract: Included because it is one of the few MEASURED flight-zone results in the handling literature, and because the finding has a direct geometric consequence a designer can use: animals confined in a NARROW alley had a SMALLER flight zone than animals confined in a wider alley (cited by Grandin 1997). That supports the otherwise unsupported rule that an alley should be narrow enough that cattle cannot circle the handler. The work is in Merino sheep, so transfer to beef cattle is an assumption and should be flagged as such wherever the software leans on it.

papers.title: Welfare requirements of handling facilities
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.source: In: S. H. Baxter, M. R. Baxter and J. A. C. McCormack (eds), Farm Animal Housing and Welfare, Martinus Nijhoff
papers.licence: Paywalled book chapter
papers.abstract: The citation Grandin gives for two rules a corral designer must enforce geometrically. First, the maximum recommended steepness for a stationary cattle ramp of 20 degrees for market-weight animals. Second, and less widely known, that a CROWD PEN MUST NEVER BE BUILT ON A RAMP - 'a sloped crowd pen will cause livestock to pile up against the crowd gate' - with 10 degrees named as a slope to avoid. The crowd pen must be level except for a slight drainage slope. Both are design recommendations rather than measured results, but the crowd-pen-level rule is one of the few that is easy for software to check and expensive for a rancher to get wrong.

papers.title: Effect of the angle of slope on the ease with which pigs negotiate loading ramps
papers.authors: P. A. Phillips, B. K. Thompson and D. Fraser
papers.source: Canadian Agricultural Engineering / Applied Animal Behaviour Science
papers.licence: Paywalled
papers.abstract: Recorded as the honest counterweight to the 20-degree cattle ramp rule. The only CONTROLLED ramp-angle work in livestock is in pigs, not cattle: this study and Fraser et al. 1986 found pigs preferred 20-24 degrees over 28-32 degrees, Warriss et al. 1991 found steep ramps stressful, and Garcia et al. 2019 found heart rate rises on steeper ramps, with ascent time increasing linearly above about 20 degrees. The cattle figures of 20 degrees fixed and 25 degrees adjustable trace to a single Grandin 1979 recommendation repeated for over forty years, with NO cattle trial behind them. The corral designer should state the 20-degree limit and say plainly that it is a convention supported by pig data, not by a cattle experiment.

papers.title: The behavioural response of cattle (Bos taurus) to artificial weaning in two stages
papers.authors: Haley, D.B.
papers.source: PhD thesis, University of Saskatchewan (Large Animal Clinical Sciences)
papers.licence: Open access in the University of Saskatchewan HARVEST repository; author retains copyright
papers.abstract: The foundational Canadian work on two-stage weaning and the single most useful document in this literature, because it contains the full data behind Haley, Bailey & Stookey (2005) plus three more experiments that were never published separately. Chapter 5: 392 cow-calf pairs over 4 trials. After separation, two-stage calves vocalised 96.6% less (P=0.001), spent 78.9% less time walking (P=0.001), 23.0% more time eating (P=0.001) and 24.1% more time resting (P=0.001) than abruptly weaned controls. Pedometers (Trial 4) showed two-stage calves walked 1.3 km/d MORE while the flap was in and 5.8 km/d LESS in the 4 days after separation; day 1 after separation two-stage calves walked 5.2 +/- 0.5 km/d vs controls 16.7 +/- 3.1 km/d. ADG was lower during stage 1 and greater in the 7 days after separation, but similar over the whole study period (P>0.10); Trial 3 alone showed a 7-week growth advantage (P=0.05). Chapter 4: abruptly weaned cows called at 90 calls/h and calves at 56 calls/h; two-stage cows called 83% less and calves 88% less, walking down 60% and 61%, calves ate 30% more, cows ate 43.3 more min/d; 8 days of flap gave no benefit over 4 days. Chapter 6 is the only published head-to-head of two-stage vs fenceline: two-stage calves (n=36) vocalised 81.2% less than fenceline calves (n=30), whose rate of 14.9 calls/calf/h was more than 6x the two-stage rate; two-stage calves lay 23.1% more and stood 60.3% less. Chapter 7 repeats the effect in 5-week-old dairy calves. Practical detail found nowhere else: flaps cost about a dollar and a half Canadian, are reusable after disinfection, can be placed or removed in seconds in a squeeze chute, retention was 95% or better in the trials that worked (one trial was abandoned because devices would not stay in), and Haley explicitly recommends limiting flap wear to 4 or 5 days.

papers.title: The effects of weaning beef calves in two stages on their behavior and growth rate
papers.authors: Haley, D.B.; Bailey, D.W.; Stookey, J.M.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Society of Animal Science / Oxford University Press)
papers.abstract: The canonical two-stage weaning paper and the source of the numbers quoted everywhere: 392 cow-calf pairs, four trials, nose flaps worn before separation. Calves weaned in two stages vocalised 96.6% less, walked 78.9% less, ate 23.0% more and rested 24.1% more than abruptly weaned calves after separation; walking was 5.8 km/d lower over the first 4 days. ADG fell while the flap was in and rose in the week after separation, with no net difference over the whole period. Paywalled, but the complete dataset and methods are in Haley's freely downloadable 2006 University of Saskatchewan thesis, which should be used instead.

papers.title: Fenceline contact of beef calves with their dams at weaning reduces the negative effects of separation on behavior and growth rate
papers.authors: Price, E.O.; Harris, J.E.; Borgwardt, R.E.; Sween, M.L.; Connor, J.M.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Society of Animal Science / Oxford University Press)
papers.abstract: The study that made fenceline weaning mainstream and still the only one to show a lasting production advantage. Three years, about 100 Angus/Hereford-cross calves, five treatments with 7 days of treatment each year and weekly weights for 10 weeks: fenceline separation on pasture, total separation on pasture, total separation in drylot with or without hay preconditioning, and non-weaned controls. Over the first 3 days, fenceline calves spent 37.3% of observations eating vs 23.7% (separated on pasture) and 21.5% (drylot, no hay), walked 10.1% vs 28.1%, and lay down 23.3% vs 16.0%; vocalisation was 216.7 vs 434.6-518.2 calls per 10-calf group, against 0.1 for unweaned controls. Cumulative gain: fenceline 47 lb at 2 weeks and 110 lb at 10 weeks vs 20-30 lb and 79-91 lb for the fully separated groups. In kg, fenceline vs remotely separated was 21.4 vs 11.0 kg at week 2 and 50.0 vs 38.2 kg at week 10, i.e. about 95% more gain in the first fortnight and a 22-24 lb advantage still present at 10 weeks. Except for vocalisation, fenceline calves behaved like unweaned controls. Design note that matters: the cows were moved and the calves stayed in their original pasture. Fence was barbed wire overlaid with woven wire. No free PDF; the behaviour table is reproduced in University of Tennessee Extension AS-B 312 and the growth table in Virginia Cooperative Extension's Cow-Calf Manager, both of which are free.

papers.title: Comparison of effects of four weaning methods on health and performance of beef calves
papers.authors: Taylor, J.D.; Gilliam, J.N.; Mourer, G.; Stansberry, C.
papers.licence: Open access (Cambridge University Press; DOAJ-listed)
papers.abstract: The largest four-way comparison with real production numbers, and the study that shows shipping date matters more than weaning method. About 290 calves aged 7-8 months at two Oklahoma State herds, blocked by sex and weight: abrupt (AW), fenceline 7 d (FL), nose flap in at D-6 and out at D0 (NF), and two 24-h separations at D-13 and D-6 with drylot supplement then 7 d fenceline (SEP); each split between shipping early (D0/D7) and holding to D28, transport about 240 miles. Stage-1 cost of flaps: pre-weaning ADG 0.25 vs 0.64 kg/d for controls at Location 1 (P<0.0001). ADG D13-D28 for calves kept on the ranch: Location 1 FL 0.45 > SEP 0.31 = NF 0.26 > AW-delayed 0.17 > AW-immediate 0.07 kg/d (P<0.0001); Location 2 FL 0.90, SEP 0.87, NF 0.76, AW-delayed 0.70, AW-immediate 0.01 kg/d (P=0.006). The shipping effect dwarfed the method effect: at Location 2, held vs shipped on D7 gave FL 1.1 vs -0.6, SEP 1.0 vs -0.4 and NF 0.7 vs -0.5 kg/d (all P<0.0001) - calves shipped a week after weaning lost weight. Health: no mortality and only 11 calves treated for presumptive BRD (AW 4, FL 3, NF 3, SEP 1), so the authors state the morbidity analyses were inconclusive. This paper must not be cited as health evidence. Authors recommend fenceline weaning with delayed shipment.

papers.title: The Impact of Abrupt and Fenceline-Weaning Methods on Cattle Stress Response, Live Weight Gain, and Behaviour
papers.authors: Mac, S.E.; Lomax, S.; Doughty, A.K.; Thomson, P.C.; Clark, C.E.F.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: The best-instrumented fenceline study and the source of the 3-day recommendation. 32 Angus cow-calf pairs in Australia with ear-tag accelerometers recording behaviour minute by minute for 21 days, plus CCTV ethogram scoring, salivary cortisol and body weights at d0/7/14. Fenceline calves rested and ruminated more with less high activity across the first 3 days (ruminating 13% and 10% more on days 1-2); abrupt calves tripled baseline high activity on day 1 vs fenceline doubling it. Pacing was rare (<1% of time) but higher overall in abrupt calves (P<0.001). Vocalisation only trended higher in abrupt calves (P=0.052). Salivary cortisol did not differ between treatments at any timepoint. Fenceline calf ADG in week 1 was nearly 3x that of abrupt calves (P<0.001) yet body weight never differed at any weigh date; fenceline COWS gained less overall than abrupt cows (P<0.05) because their eating time fell on days 4-7. Fenceline calves were close to the barrier twice as often as abrupt calves on days 2-3 and then PEAKED on day 8 when the cows were finally trucked away (P<0.001) - the clearest evidence in the literature of a second stress spike from a long fenceline period. Fenceline calves made 37 suckling attempts through the fence over 7 days and 91 social contacts (47 calf-initiated, 44 cow-initiated). Authors recommend fenceline weaning for three days then total separation.

papers.title: Minimising the stress of weaning of beef calves: a review
papers.authors: Enriquez, D.; Hotzel, M.J.; Ungerfeld, R.
papers.licence: CC BY 2.0
papers.abstract: The sceptical review every producer-facing summary of this topic leaves out, and the best single bibliography on cow-calf bonding and weaning stress. Covers formation and breaking of the maternal-filial bond, the separate stressors bundled into weaning (loss of milk, loss of the udder, loss of the dam, new environment, social reorganisation), and then assesses the alternative methods critically. Key findings reported: nose-flap calves at 6-7 months, over 5 or 14 days, vocalised and walked less with more eating and lying; but in some studies they also had lower ADG, and after flap fitting they make repeated nursing attempts and stay closer to the cow, suggesting frustration. Fenceline results are described as contradictory - one study found higher stress behaviour during fenceline separation than in calves with no contact, another found no gain or oxidative-stress benefit after 7 days of fenceline, and calves weaned after 14 days of fenceline separation GREW LESS than abruptly weaned calves and vocalised more over more days. In two studies calves spent more than half their time near the dividing fence. The review's central argument is that these methods may REDISTRIBUTE the stress response into two episodes rather than reduce it, and it asks directly whether the benefit justifies the extra management of fitting and checking flaps. It also notes that remaining in the same place after weaning reduces stress in deer, foals and piglets but that no equivalent beef-cattle study exists, and that separating a cow-calf group from the main herd five days before weaning was by itself enough to raise calf cortisol. Flags habituation to handling before weaning as an unexplored question.

papers.title: Case study: effects of low-stress weaning on calf growth performance and carcass characteristics
papers.authors: Gubbels, E.R.; Jaeger, J.R.; Salverson, R.R.; Cammack, K.M.; Grubbs, J.K.; Underwood, K.R.; Olson, K.C.; Blair, A.D.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0 (publisher PDF asset not downloadable without a browser session)
papers.abstract: The clearest Northern Plains null result and the best counterweight to the fenceline literature. 89 single-sourced steers stratified by weight and dam age into ABRUPT, FENCE (7 d) and NOSE (7 d flap), 29-30 per treatment, moved to a commercial feedlot at D+7 and followed to harvest with step-up and finishing rations typical for a Northern Plains yard. Weaning method interacted with time period for ADG and BW (P<0.01), but the differences cancelled: NOSE had greater ADG pre-treatment to weaning than ABRUPT or FENCE (P<0.01); FENCE had greater ADG weaning to post-wean than the others (P<0.01), holding weight while they were negative; ABRUPT then had greater ADG post-wean to receiving (P<0.04), i.e. compensatory gain. ADG was similar for the rest of the feeding period and body weight never differed at any weigh date (P>0.05). No carcass measurement differed (P>0.05). Haptoglobin was undetectable in every sample but two taken on d-7, so there was no measurable acute-phase response for a treatment effect to appear in. Authors conclude that low-stress weaning methods do not significantly improve post-weaning growth performance or carcass characteristics compared with conventional methods despite minor short-term alterations in ADG. SDSU Extension's summary of the same work reports fenceline calves holding weight over the first 7 days while abruptly weaned calves lost about 2.4 lb/day.

papers.title: Calf health and performance during receiving is not changed by fence-line preconditioning on Flint Hills range vs. drylot preconditioning
papers.authors: Bailey, E.A.; Jaeger, J.R.; Waggoner, J.W.; Preedy, G.W.; Pacheco, L.A.; Olson, K.C.
papers.source: Kansas Agricultural Experiment Station Research Reports (Cattlemen's Day), Kansas State University
papers.licence: Free and open access (New Prairie Press); may be freely reproduced for educational purposes
papers.abstract: The most important study for a prairie ranch, because it is the one that shows fenceline weaning onto fall native range can lose weight for a month. 460 Angus x Hereford calves, initial BW 496 +/- 77 lb, weaned at about 180 days, assigned to three 28-day ranch-of-origin programmes: drylot with full dam separation (earth pen, minimum 215 sq ft/calf, 18 in bunk space/calf, diet formulated for 2.2 lb ADG at 2.5% BW DMI); pasture with 7 days of fenceline contact; or pasture plus fenceline plus supplement in portable bunks at 1% BW three times a week. Fenceline specification is given in full: minimum pasture area 118 acres, minimum shared frontage 656 feet (200 m), four-strand barbed wire with the bottom two wires electrified, cows moved out of visual and auditory range after 7 days. 28-day preconditioning ADG was +0.68 lb/d for drylot vs -0.62 (pasture+supplement) and -0.75 lb/d (pasture) (P=0.08). All calves then shipped 4 h to a feedlot: drylot calves had greater ADG day 0-60 (3.13 vs 2.93 and 2.82 lb/d, P<0.01), greater day-60 BW (697 vs 655 and 644 lb, P<0.01), higher DMI and better feed:gain (5.49 vs 6.04), and a greater proportion came to the bunk at feeding during the first 4-5 days (P<0.05). Fever incidence did not differ during preconditioning (P=0.22) and was 0.9% overall during receiving, too low to test. The authors conclude that previous experience eating a concentrate diet from a bunk paid greater dividends during receiving than reducing maternal-separation stress through fenceline contact. The peer-reviewed version is Bailey et al. 2016, Professional Animal Scientist 32:220-228.

papers.title: Effect of fence-line or drylot weaning on the health and performance of beef calves during weaning, receiving, and finishing
papers.authors: Bailey, E.A.; Jaeger, J.R.; Waggoner, J.W.; Preedy, G.W.; Pacheco, L.A.; Olson, K.C.
papers.licence: Subscription (Elsevier)
papers.abstract: The peer-reviewed version of the Kansas State fence-line versus drylot preconditioning work, carried through finishing. Drylot calves were heavier at the end of the 28-day weaning period and gained faster than pasture-weaned calves through day 60 in the feedlot, with no health difference. Carcass traits including yield grade, marbling score and the percentage grading USDA Choice or higher did not differ among treatments. This is the paper that reports the fenceline specification cited throughout: minimum frontage 200 m, four-strand barbed-wire fence with the bottom two wires electrified. The free Cattlemen's Day report (Bailey et al. 2013) carries the same data for the weaning and receiving phases.

papers.title: Influence of weaning strategy on behavior, humoral indicators of stress, growth, and carcass characteristics
papers.authors: Freeman, S.; Poore, M.; Pickworth, C.; Alley, M.
papers.licence: CC BY-NC 4.0 (publisher PDF asset not downloadable without a browser session)
papers.abstract: A four-year North Carolina State trial that concludes against nose flaps on both welfare and performance grounds - the strongest published dissent. Angus and Angus x Senepol steers stratified by dam parity, hair coat and weight: abrupt at 7 months (A, n=39), weaning after a 7-day nose flap (N, n=40), or weaning delayed 49 days (D, n=39); weaned at 237 +/- 3 d of age at 254 +/- 6.7 kg, with accelerometer collars on a subsample and blood for cortisol and haptoglobin in the last two years. ADG over the 42 days after weaning was 0.69, 0.54 and 0.37 kg/d for D, A and N respectively (P<0.01) - the nose-flap arm was the worst. A and D calves were more active and more vocal than N for the first 2-3 days but settled to similar levels by day 4. Cortisol and haptoglobin remained within normal reference ranges in all groups. Twelve of 38 nose-flap steers (32%) had sores in their nostrils when the flaps were removed, and 2, 1, 2 and 7 non-observed steers lost flaps prematurely in 2013-2016. All groups graded Low Choice with similar efficiency of gain through finishing (P>0.2). The authors recommend delaying weaning where pasture and cow condition allow, and state that otherwise abrupt weaning may be the next viable option based on animal welfare concerns and increased handling to place and remove the flaps, adding that abrupt weaning under their conditions was less stressful than it is perceived to be.

papers.title: Development and application of a scoring system for septum injuries in beef calves with and without a nose flap
papers.authors: Kirk, A.A.; Tucker, C.B.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: The properly controlled study of nose-flap injury, and the reason a 2026 operation should not treat two-stage weaning as automatically low-stress. 82 Angus and Angus-Hereford crossbred calves at the UC Davis Sierra Foothill Research and Extension Center, 205 +/- 19 days old and 247 +/- 29 kg, randomly assigned to Flap (n=41, QuietWean plastic flaps from JDA Livestock Innovations, Saskatoon) or No Flap (n=41) and balanced for weight and sex. Critically, ALL calves were fenceline-weaned under identical rangeland conditions so that environmental injury risk was equalised - something earlier injury studies lacked. Nostrils were photographed before insertion, at removal after 7 days, and 6 days after removal, and scored for damage, impression and blood with 97%, 91% and 100% intra-observer agreement. Results: 32% of Flap calves lost the flap before day 7; no No-Flap calf was injured; every calf that kept a flap for 7 days had damage and impressions in at least one nostril and 86% had blood present immediately at removal (P<=0.001 vs No Flap); six days after removal 100% still had visible damage, 64% impressions and 29% blood. Measured septum width was 39 +/- 2 mm. The paper also tabulates flap loss across the literature: under 5% in Haley 2005 and Taylor 2020 versus 24% in Lambertz 2015 and 27% in Valente 2022.

papers.title: Nose-Flap Devices Used for Two-Stage Weaning Produce Wounds in the Nostrils of Beef Calves: Case Report
papers.authors: Valente, T.S.; Ruiz, L.R.B.; Macitelli, F.; Paranhos da Costa, M.J.R.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: The case report that opened the nose-flap injury question, from Brazil with University of Alberta co-authorship. 41 calves (21 purebred Nellore, 20 F1 Angus-Nellore) weaned at 236 +/- 4 days, fitted with commercial WalMur plastic nose flaps measuring 13.5 x 10 cm on d0 and separated on d5. Nose-flap retention was 73.2% (11 of 41 lost the device). Every calf, including every calf that had already lost its flap, had open wounds of the nasal septum at d5, where all 41 had scored 1 (no lesions) on d0; three of the eleven flap-losers reached the purulent-discharge grade. Almost half (46%, 19/41) lost body weight over the five days, with overall mean ADG -0.17 +/- 1.29 kg/d (range -4.0 to +2.6); flap-losers averaged -0.33 kg/d against +0.29 kg/d for keepers. One Angus-Nellore bull had a perforated septum and the worst weight loss. The authors note that flap wounds can progress to traumatic bacterial rhinitis and in severe cases pituitary abscess syndrome, with first clinical signs 12 to 60 days after fitting, and conclude that the method should not be referred to as a low-stress weaning practice. Caveat for an Alberta reader: Nellore cattle and a non-North-American flap design.

papers.title: Effects of two-stage weaning with nose flap devices applied to calves on cow body condition, calf performance, and calf humoral immune response
papers.authors: Lippolis, K.D.; Ahola, J.K.; Mayo, C.E.; Fischer, M.C.; Callan, R.J.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Society of Animal Science / Oxford University Press)
papers.abstract: The study that established the immune cost of long nose-flap periods, and the reason flap wear should not overlap the pre-weaning vaccination window. Cow-calf pairs randomly assigned to a nose flap for 21 days before separation or no flap, with cow body condition scored at the start and day 56 and calves vaccinated and challenged with ovalbumin. Flaps did not change feed intake, feed efficiency or morbidity in the initial post-separation period, but pre-weaning ADG, serum BVDV-1 and BHV-1 titres and the humoral response to ovalbumin were all DECREASED in flapped calves. Control calves had higher BHV-1 titres on days 1 and 28 (P<0.05) and greater ovalbumin-specific IgM on day 28. Twenty-one days is roughly three times the longest flap period any behavioural study has shown a benefit for.

papers.title: Two-step weaning in beef calves: permanence of nose flaps for 7 or 21 days does not influence the behaviour response
papers.authors: Alvez, P.; Quintans, G.; Hotzel, M.J.; Ungerfeld, R.
papers.licence: Subscription (CSIRO Publishing)
papers.abstract: The direct test of how long a nose flap needs to stay in. Beef calves wore flaps for either 7 or 21 days before separation; the two treatments differed only on day 1 of the post-separation observation period, so tripling the flap period bought nothing behaviourally. Read together with Haley's finding that 8 days gave no benefit over 4, and with Lippolis et al. 2016's finding that 21 days depressed vaccine titres and pre-weaning ADG, this closes the case for short flap periods: 4-7 days, never 21.

papers.title: Behaviour response to two-step weaning is diminished in beef calves previously submitted to temporary weaning
papers.authors: Hotzel, M.J.; Quintans, G.; Ungerfeld, R.
papers.licence: Subscription (Elsevier)
papers.abstract: Uruguayan work showing that the behavioural benefit of two-step weaning is smaller in calves that have already been through a temporary weaning (suckling restriction earlier in lactation for cow rebreeding). Relevant if a herd already uses nose plates or temporary calf removal mid-season, because it means the second intervention has less left to improve.

papers.title: Minimizing cows' stress when calves were early weaned using the two-step method with nose flaps
papers.authors: Ungerfeld, R.; Quintans, G.; Hotzel, M.J.
papers.licence: Open access per DOAJ, but no downloadable PDF could be verified
papers.abstract: One of the few studies to focus on the COW rather than the calf. Cows were weaned abruptly, weaned in two steps with nose flaps on their calves for 5 days, or left unweaned, with behaviour recorded at 10-minute intervals from day -3 to day 11. Abruptly weaned cows paced, walked and vocalised more and grazed and lay less; the two-step method reduced that response. Useful alongside Mac et al. 2024, which found the opposite sign on cow weight gain for fenceline weaning - the cow side of weaning method is not settled.

papers.title: Effects of weaning beef cattle in two stages or by abrupt separation on nasal abrasions, behaviour, and weight gain
papers.authors: Lambertz, C.; Farke-Rover, A.; Moors, E.; Gauly, M.
papers.licence: Subscription (CSIRO Publishing)
papers.abstract: The first study to score nose-flap injuries systematically, in 89 German Angus, Simmental and crossbred calves wearing plastic and metal flaps for 7 days. Nasal abrasions were present in over 95% of calves at flap removal: about 27% slight irritation, 58% slight or heavy bleeding, about 7% pus and 4% deep purulent wounds. Flap retention was 76.4%, i.e. about 24% loss, consistent with the two most recent North American studies and well below Haley's 95%. Cited by both Valente et al. 2022 and Kirk & Tucker 2023 as the baseline injury reference.

papers.title: Effects of alternate weaning methods on behavior, blood metabolites and performance of beef calves
papers.authors: Boland, H.T.; Scaglia, G.; Swecker, W.S. Jr.; Burke, N.C.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Registry of Professional Animal Scientists / Elsevier)
papers.abstract: The Virginia three-way comparison of conventional, fenceline and two-stage nose-flap weaning, summarised in NMSU Circular 648. Two-stage weaning reduced signs of behavioural stress relative to abrupt weaning, but fenceline weaning gave a similar reduction. Fenceline weaning produced over fivefold more vocalisations during the first week after remote physical separation yet still yielded improved weight gain, which the authors attributed to residual nose sensitivity reducing feed intake in flapped calves - an effect not seen in the Canadian or Montana studies. Weight gain was measured only for the first 7 days post-weaning, so no long-term fenceline-versus-flap comparison was possible.

papers.title: Influence of two-stage weaning with subsequent transport on body weight, plasma lipid peroxidation, plasma selenium, and on leukocyte glutathione peroxidase and glutathione reductase activity in beef calves
papers.authors: Burke, N.C.; Scaglia, G.; Boland, H.T.; Swecker, W.S. Jr.
papers.licence: Subscription (Elsevier)
papers.abstract: Two-stage weaning combined with transport, measuring oxidative-stress markers as well as body weight. Cited by Valente et al. 2022 as showing that the nose-flap ADG penalty has only a short-term effect, recovered by compensatory gain after flap removal - the main counterargument to the stage-1 weight loss other studies report. One of the few papers to put weaning method and transport in the same design.

papers.title: Effects of weaning management strategies on performance and health of calves during feedlot receiving
papers.authors: Boyles, S.L.; Loerch, S.C.; Lowe, G.D.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Registry of Professional Animal Scientists / Elsevier)
papers.abstract: The source of the most widely quoted health claim for fenceline weaning: fence-line weaned calves were treated about half as often as abruptly weaned calves during feedlot receiving, with improved gains. Cited by the Beef Cattle Research Council for exactly that figure. Treat with care - the effect size is only available second-hand, and three more recent trials (Taylor 2020, Bailey/Olson, Gubbels 2023) all failed to detect health differences because their calves were too healthy. This remains the single best-cited morbidity number for fenceline weaning, which is itself a statement about how thin the health evidence is.

papers.title: Effects of commingling beef calves from different sources and weaning protocols during a forty-two-day receiving period on performance and bovine respiratory disease
papers.authors: Step, D.L.; Krehbiel, C.R.; DePra, H.A.; Cranston, J.J.; Fulton, R.W.; Kirkpatrick, J.G.; Gill, D.R.; Payton, M.E.; Montelongo, M.A.; Confer, A.W.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Society of Animal Science / Oxford University Press)
papers.abstract: The study that quantifies where BRD risk actually comes from, and the strongest argument for keeping calves on the ranch. Ranch-origin calves commingled with auction-market calves over a 42-day receiving period: total morbidity was about 11% for ranch-origin calves, 42% for auction-market calves and 23% for commingled calves (reported elsewhere as 11.1, 41.9 and 22.6%). Calves held on the ranch for 45 days after weaning were less likely to require treatment than calves shipped at weaning. The practical reading is that single-sourcing and 45 days of ranch retention are the measured morbidity levers; no controlled trial has shown that the weaning method itself reduces BRD in a healthy herd. A later study (Mijar et al. 2023) found no commingling effect in its setting, so the effect is not universal.

papers.title: The effect of abrupt weaning of suckler calves on the plasma concentrations of cortisol, catecholamines, leukocytes, acute-phase proteins and in vitro interferon-gamma production
papers.authors: Hickey, M.C.; Drennan, M.; Earley, B.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Society of Animal Science / Oxford University Press)
papers.abstract: The reference physiological description of abrupt weaning: increases in plasma cortisol, catecholamines, leukocyte redistribution and acute-phase proteins with altered interferon-gamma production. Also the source, via the Enriquez et al. 2011 review, of a result directly relevant to how pairs are gathered and sorted: separating a group of cows and their calves from the main herd five days before weaning was by itself sufficient to raise calf blood cortisol. Social disruption is a stressor independent of maternal separation.

papers.title: The effects of alternative weaning methods on behaviour in beef calves
papers.authors: Enriquez, D.H.; Ungerfeld, R.; Quintans, G.; Guidoni, A.L.; Hotzel, M.J.
papers.licence: Subscription (Elsevier)
papers.abstract: The study that produced the strongest negative finding for long fenceline periods and the clearest statement that these methods may not work. Calves weaned after 14 days of fenceline separation GREW LESS than abruptly weaned calves and vocalised more frequently and over more days during the partial-separation period; calves spent more than half their time near the dividing fence in the first days. The authors concluded that the two alternative weaning methods did not appear to provide any clear benefit in reducing weaning distress compared with abrupt weaning. This is the evidence behind the rule that 14 days of fenceline contact is harmful rather than merely unnecessary.

papers.title: Behavioural responses of 6-month-old beef calves prevented from suckling: influence of dam's milk yield
papers.authors: Hotzel, M.J.; Ungerfeld, R.; Quintans, G.
papers.licence: Subscription (CSIRO Publishing)
papers.abstract: Isolates the nutritional component of weaning stress by preventing suckling with nose flaps while leaving the pair together. Six-month-old beef calves prevented from nursing showed increased vocalisation and walking and reduced playing, ruminating and grazing, indicating that cessation of nursing contributes to weaning distress at this age independently of separation. Weaning distress appeared greater in calves suckling higher-yielding cows, but not when live weight was controlled. Relevant to the question of what stage 1 of two-stage weaning actually costs the calf.

papers.title: Weaning and separation in two steps - A way to decrease stress in dairy calves suckled by foster cows
papers.authors: Loberg, J.M.; Hernandez, C.E.; Thierfelder, T.; Jensen, M.B.; Berg, C.; Lidfors, L.
papers.licence: Subscription (Elsevier)
papers.abstract: The Swedish dairy counterpart to Haley's work, and the paper whose sampling scheme Mac et al. 2024 adapted. Calves suckled by foster cows were weaned and separated in two steps rather than simultaneously; the two-step calves showed fewer behaviours indicative of distress such as vocalisation and locomotion. Useful as independent corroboration of the two-stage behavioural effect in a different production system and at a different age.

papers.title: Effects of remote and contact weaning on behaviour and weight gain of beef calves
