papers.authors: Stookey, J.M.; Schwartzkopf-Genswein, K.S.; Waltz, C.S.; Watts, J.M.
papers.licence: Subscription (abstract only)
papers.abstract: The early Canadian fenceline result, from the same University of Saskatchewan group that later produced the two-stage work. Reported effects on calf behaviour similar to Price et al. 2003, plus a short-term benefit on weight gain. Published only as a conference abstract, so there is no full paper to retrieve; it is cited in Haley's 2006 thesis as the precedent for fenceline contact in cattle. Included for provenance, not for numbers.

papers.title: Effect of a trainer cow on health, behavior, and performance of newly weaned beef calves
papers.authors: Gibb, D.J.; Schwartzkopf-Genswein, K.S.; Stookey, J.M.; McKinnon, J.J.; Godson, D.L.; Wiedmeier, R.D.; McAllister, T.A.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Society of Animal Science / Oxford University Press)
papers.abstract: A Canadian prairie trial on the one weaning-period intervention the Kansas State work identified as mattering most: teaching freshly weaned calves to eat from a bunk. Measured health, behaviour and performance effects of putting a trainer cow with newly weaned beef calves. Read alongside Loerch & Fluharty (2000) on trainer animals in feedlots and the Enriquez et al. 2011 review's caution that introducing unfamiliar animals may itself be a stressor and that the few trials found no health or growth benefit.

papers.title: Characterisation of physiological and immunological responses in beef cows to abrupt weaning and subsequent housing
papers.authors: Lynch, E.M.; Earley, B.; McGee, M.; Doyle, S.
papers.licence: CC BY 2.0
papers.abstract: Irish Teagasc work on the COW side of abrupt weaning, measuring physiological and immunological responses to weaning followed by housing. Part of the small set of studies that document what abrupt weaning does to the dam rather than the calf - worth having because the economic case for weaning is usually made on cow body condition, and because Mac et al. 2024 found fenceline weaning cost cows weight. Free full text and PDF.

papers.title: Effect of abrupt weaning at housing on leukocyte distribution, functional activity of neutrophils, and acute phase protein response of beef calves
papers.authors: Lynch, E.M.; Earley, B.; McGee, M.; Doyle, S.
papers.licence: CC BY 2.0
papers.abstract: The companion calf study to Lynch et al. 6:37, documenting leukocyte redistribution, neutrophil function and the acute-phase protein response when calves are abruptly weaned at housing. Useful as the mechanistic baseline against which to read the repeated failures of cortisol and haptoglobin to separate weaning methods in North American field trials (Mac 2024, Gubbels 2023, Freeman 2020, Landa 2011): the response exists and is measurable under a strong challenge, but it is not a reliable discriminator between methods in a healthy pasture herd. Free full text and PDF.

papers.title: Effect of pre-weaning concentrate supplementation on peripheral distribution of leukocytes, functional activity of neutrophils, acute phase protein and behavioural responses of abruptly weaned and housed beef calves
papers.authors: Lynch, E.M.; McGee, M.; Doyle, S.; Earley, B.
papers.licence: CC BY 2.0
papers.abstract: Tests the creep-feeding question with immune and behavioural endpoints: does supplementing calves with concentrate BEFORE weaning change how they respond to abrupt weaning and housing? Measures leukocyte distribution, neutrophil function, acute-phase proteins and behaviour. This is the mechanism the Kansas State work identified as the one that actually mattered - prior experience of concentrate - tested directly rather than inferred. Free full text and PDF.

papers.title: The effect of road and sea transport on inflammatory, adrenocortical, metabolic and behavioural responses of weanling heifers
papers.authors: Earley, B.; Murray, M.
papers.licence: CC BY 2.0
papers.abstract: Measures what transport does to freshly weaned heifers - inflammatory, adrenocortical, metabolic and behavioural responses to road and sea transport. Relevant to the truck-weaning question: Taylor et al. 2020 shows that shipping on the day of weaning or a week after costs 0.1-1.7 kg/d of gain, and this paper characterises the physiological side of why. Free full text and PDF.

papers.title: Evaluation of weaning stress in beef calves
papers.authors: Landa, C.E.
papers.source: MSc thesis, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (Biomedical and Veterinary Sciences)
papers.licence: Open access in Virginia Tech VTechWorks
papers.abstract: A careful null result that is rarely cited, and a useful corrective. Study 3 of this thesis compared fenceline (described by the author as two-stage) with abrupt weaning, measuring calf weights, immune cell function, antibody production, blood glucose, faecal cortisol and gene expression for FAS, IL-4, IL-10 and interferon-gamma before and after weaning. The ONLY difference detected was higher blood glucose in abruptly weaned calves on the day after weaning. Faecal cortisol and expression of FAS and IL-4 rose in both groups after weaning with no treatment difference; IL-10 and IFN-gamma did not change; no date, treatment or interaction effect was found for total weight gain or interferon-gamma production. The thesis also validates handheld glucometers for chute-side bovine blood glucose (Precision Xtra more accurate and precise than ReliOn), which is a cheap practical stress measure a ranch could actually use.

papers.title: Fence Line Weaning Reduces Stress During Weaning of Beef Calves (Animal Science Info Series AS-B 312)
papers.authors: Lane, C. Jr.
papers.licence: University of Tennessee Extension publication, freely distributed
papers.abstract: A two-page extension sheet whose value is that it REPRODUCES the Price et al. 2003 behaviour table in full, with letters for significance at P<0.05 - the only free source for those numbers found. Percentage of observations over the first three days by method: eating 41.1 (non-weaned), 37.3 (fenceline), 23.7 (separated on pasture), 28.9 (drylot, hay-preconditioned), 21.5 (drylot, no hay); walking 8.6, 10.1, 28.1, 9.6, 14.8; lying down 22.9, 23.3, 16.0, 21.9, 20.6; vocalisation 0.1, 216.7, 434.6, 371.2, 518.2 per 10-calf group. Its management guidance: move cows and calves into the weaning pen a few days beforehand so calves learn from their dams where feed and water are; at weaning remove the COWS and leave the calves in place; the fence must stop the calf reaching through to nurse; usually 7 to 14 days are required; complete dehorning, castration and vaccination before weaning; combine weaning with at least a 45-day preconditioning programme.

papers.title: Using Anti-suckling Devices to Wean Beef Calves (Circular 648)
papers.authors: Gifford, C. (revised); original authors Carter, B.; Mathis, C.; Loest, C.
papers.source: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension Service
papers.licence: NMSU Extension publication; may be freely reproduced with citation for educational purposes
papers.abstract: The most practical free summary of nose-flap practice, and notable for recommending fenceline over flaps. Reports that conventionally weaned calves vocalised 20 times more often than two-stage calves at the same point of separation; that flapped calves walked about 15% MORE during stage 1 but conventionally weaned calves then took roughly twice as many steps after separation; and that calves generally gain less weight while the device is in and remained lighter or equal at 50 days post-weaning, so the stage-1 loss may not be fully compensated. Practical specifications: place flaps 4 to 7 days before separation (stage 1 may run up to 14 days to fit vaccination protocols); retention is reported at about 95%, and calves weighing less than 425 lb are more likely to lose the device; flaps cost approximately about two dollars each and can be reused; check for ridges that could irritate the nose; flaps can be placed at the same visit as pre-weaning vaccines about 2 weeks before weaning, but consult a veterinarian because 28 days of wear reduced antibody responses to vaccination. Conclusion: flaps and fenceline give similar behavioural benefit, fenceline calves may have a performance advantage, so use flaps only where fenceline is impractical.

papers.title: Minimizing Weaning Stress on Calves (Bulletin B221)
papers.authors: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension Service
papers.source: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension Service
papers.licence: NMSU Extension publication; may be freely reproduced with citation for educational purposes
papers.abstract: Extension overview of weaning stress reduction, and one of the clearest free descriptions of the Price et al. 2003 design: a three-year study comparing calves not weaned, fenceline weaned, abruptly weaned on pasture, or abruptly weaned in a drylot with or without hay preconditioning. Reports that apart from vocalisation fenceline calves behaved like non-weaned controls and spent more time eating than calves weaned by other methods, that fenceline calves gained at least 50% more weight during the first two weeks and kept the advantage through at least 10 weeks, and that fenceline visits decrease over the first five days with weaning complete within a week. Useful for the practical description of putting cows and calves on opposite sides of a strong fence with the cows moved and the calves left in the original pasture.

papers.title: Preconditioning Beef Calves (Circular 637)
papers.authors: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension Service
papers.source: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension Service
papers.licence: NMSU Extension publication; may be freely reproduced with citation for educational purposes
papers.abstract: Extension treatment of preconditioning programmes: the vaccination, weaning interval, nutrition and marketing components, and the case for holding calves on the ranch rather than selling at weaning. Relevant as the free companion to the measured preconditioning evidence (Step et al. 2008 on single-source versus commingled morbidity, Taylor et al. 2020 on the cost of early shipping) and to the 45-day requirement of value-added marketing programmes.

papers.title: The bud box concept
papers.authors: Red Meat Producers Organisation (RPO) / Chemunique technical note
papers.licence: Industry technical note, freely distributed
papers.abstract: A short industry note included only because it records Bud Williams' own dimension recommendations in metric - between 3.7 and 4.2 m wide and between 6 and 9 m long - which bracket the imperial 12-14 ft by 20-30 ft range quoted in North American sources. Useful for reconciling the width disagreement between Kansas State (12 ft minimum), AgProud's quotation of Williams (14 x 20 ft, and not wider because the handler ends up too far out in the middle), Arkansas (12 ft on foot, 16 ft mounted) and Hi-Hog. No measured outcomes.

papers.title: Welfare of beef cattle (EFSA Scientific Opinion)
papers.authors: EFSA Panel on Animal Health and Welfare (AHAW)
papers.licence: CC BY-ND (PDF served as a forced download; could not be verified)
papers.abstract: The current European scientific position on beef cattle welfare, covering husbandry practices including weaning. Included as the most recent authoritative welfare synthesis against which the Canadian Code update can be read, and because it reviews the same weaning literature from a regulatory-science standpoint rather than a production one. Published 2025.

papers.title: Weaning as Stressor for Calf Welfare
papers.authors: Guasco, C.; Moriconi, M.; Vitale, N.; Fusi, F.; Schleicherova, D.; Razzuoli, E.; Vevey, M.; Bergagna, S.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: A recent open-access review framing weaning as a welfare stressor, useful for an up-to-date reference list and for the current state of the behavioural and physiological indicator literature. Use it to check whether anything published since 2023 has changed the picture established by Price 2003, Haley 2005, Enriquez 2011 and the North American null results; it does not supply new field data.

papers.title: Assessing Natural Weaning in Suckler Beef Cattle: A Single-Farm Retrospective Data Analysis of Calf-Raising Success and Colostrum Antibody Uptake in the Absence or Presence of a Yearling Calf
papers.authors: Albertsen, D.; Plate, P.; Held, S.D.E.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: A rare look at what happens when suckler beef cattle are NOT artificially weaned: retrospective single-farm data on calf-raising success and colostrum antibody uptake where a yearling calf is still present versus absent. Relevant as the practical counterpart to the textbook figure that natural weaning in domestic cattle occurs between 7 and 14 months (Reinhardt & Reinhardt 1981), and as a reference point for anyone asking what the welfare baseline actually is before any weaning method is applied. Recent, 2026.

papers.title: Impact of Two-Stage Weaning and Bovine-Appeasing Substance on Growth, Temperament, Pasture Behavior, and Immune System of Nellore Calves
papers.authors: Santos, M.; Oliveira, D.M.; de Souza, M.R.; Almeida, G.B.; Santos, A.R.D.; Belmonte, J.C.C.; Melo-Sterza, F.A.; Ferraz, A.L.J.; Vedovatto, M.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: A recent two-stage weaning trial that also tests a bovine-appeasing pheromone analogue, with growth, temperament, pasture behaviour and immune endpoints. Useful for two reasons: it is one of the newest two-stage datasets available free, and it represents the current research direction - pharmacological or pheromonal stress mitigation layered on or substituted for mechanical methods like flaps and fences. Nellore cattle in Brazil, so extrapolate to Red Angus with care.

papers.title: Impacts of Maternal Bovine Appeasing Substance Administered at Weaning on Behavioral and Physiological Adaptation of Beef Heifers to the Feedlot
papers.authors: Gellatly, D.; Lei, Y.; Neale, A.; Smith, L.; Edgar, E.; Bloomfield, B.; Elliot, B.; Wenger, I.; Thompson, S.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: An ALBERTA study - Technology Access Centre for Livestock Production, Olds College of Agriculture and Technology, Olds AB - which makes it one of the very few pieces of this literature done in the ranch's own province and climate. Tests maternal bovine appeasing substance applied at weaning on the behavioural and physiological adaptation of beef heifers entering the feedlot. Worth reading both for the result and as proof that the weaning-stress question is being worked on locally; the behavioural measurement approach is directly transferable to an Alberta cow-calf operation.

papers.title: Effect of temporary weaning and creep feeding on calf growth and the reproductive efficiency of their Hereford dams
papers.authors: Cruz, R.S.; Barbieri, I.; Olmos, V.M.; Montossi, F.; Vinoles, C.
papers.licence: CC BY-NC 4.0
papers.abstract: One of the few freely available papers that measures a weaning-type intervention against BOTH calf growth and dam reproductive efficiency, which is the real trade-off on a cow-calf operation. Temporary weaning (suckling interruption) and creep feeding in Hereford dams in Uruguay. Useful for the cow-condition-versus-weaning-weight question, where measured Canadian prairie data is essentially absent and the available evidence is US Great Plains early-weaning trials plus Alberta and Saskatchewan extension advice.

papers.title: Creep Feeding Beef Calves (NebGuide G2077)
papers.authors: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension
papers.licence: Nebraska Extension publication, freely distributed
papers.abstract: The numbers needed to decide whether creep feeding before weaning is worth it, updated September 2024. Feed conversion for high-energy creep is about 8 pounds of creep dry matter per pound of added gain, with a range of 6.8:1 to 15:1; added average daily gain from high-energy creep is 0.20 to 0.30 lb/d; limit-fed (intake-restricted) creep converts at about 4 pounds of feed per pound of gain. Includes a worked partial budget using an 8:1 conversion, and the warning that lighter calves have a price-per-pound advantage so added weight is sold into a price slide. Nutrient framework: a 220 lb calf gaining 2.0 lb/d must consume about 7 lb of total dry matter (milk, forage and creep), and the ration needs to supply 1.32 lb protein and 5.0 lb TDN per day. Also covers creep feeding replacement heifers and the risk of impairing later milk production if heifers are fed high-energy creep before three months of age. The practical reading for a weaning programme: creep-feed for bunk familiarity, not for weaning weight.

papers.title: Temperament and Performance of Beef Cattle (Beef Cattle Library BEEF021, publication 640)
papers.authors: Cooke, R.F.
papers.source: Oregon State University Beef Cattle Sciences
papers.licence: Oregon State University Extension publication, freely distributed
papers.abstract: The accessible version of the only measured evidence base for low-stress handling as applied to cattle, from the author of the 2014 Journal of Animal Science Kunkle symposium review (92:5325-5333). That review found that acclimating Bos indicus x Bos taurus or Bos taurus HEIFERS to human handling improved temperament (P<=0.02), reduced plasma cortisol (P<0.01) and hastened puberty (P<=0.02), but that NO benefit was observed when mature cows or feeder cattle were acclimated; a companion 2012 study found acclimation improved temperament without benefiting feedlot receiving performance. This is the honest boundary of the stockmanship evidence: temperament demonstrably affects production, reproduction and health independent of breed type, and acclimation demonstrably calms heifers, but the claim that handling acclimation improves weaning outcomes has not been tested. Enriquez et al. 2011 names it as an open question.

papers.title: Low-Stress Handling: How Bud Williams changed cattle handling
papers.authors: Hereford World / American Hereford Association
papers.licence: Breed-association magazine article, freely distributed
papers.abstract: Included deliberately as an EXAMPLE OF UNMEASURED ADVOCACY, so the ranch's software has a labelled specimen of the genre. A breed-magazine account of Bud Williams' influence on cattle handling. The behavioural principles it describes (cattle want to go back the way they came, cattle want to move past the handler, release pressure as soon as the animal responds) are sound and appear in university extension material. The outcome claims circulating in this literature are not: a family ranch saving a five-figure yearly saving on 500 yearlings from reduced shrink, Williams cutting a Canadian feedlot's doctoring from about 75 head a day to two or three, and an unsourced claim of 12% better weight gain and 15% better reproduction. These are case reports and assertions with no control group. Bud Williams' methods have never been tested in a controlled weaning trial. Treat all of it as advice, never as evidence.

papers.title: Weaning (topic page and 2023 Canadian Cow-Calf Survey adoption data)
papers.authors: Beef Cattle Research Council
papers.licence: Beef Cattle Research Council web resource, freely accessible (no PDF)
papers.abstract: The Canadian industry's own synthesis, and the source of the adoption data and of the two Stookey videos that document the pair-sorting method. Reports the Haley et al. 2005 headline figures (two-stage calves vocalised 97% less, spent 23% more time eating and walked 5.8 km/day less over the four days after separation; their dams vocalised 84% less), recommends 4-5 days of nose paddle and at least 3-4 days of fenceline contact with sturdy fencing, and cites Boyles et al. 2007 for fence-line calves being treated about half as often as abruptly weaned calves. Also reports a Saskatchewan veterinarian's producer-level figures of 5-10% treatment rates for low-stress weaned calves versus 25-30% for abruptly weaned calves - practitioner experience, not a study. Adoption, 2023 Canadian Cow-Calf Survey: over 32% of respondents used fence-line weaning and almost 12% used two-stage weaning, with fence-line use up more than 10 percentage points and two-stage use nearly doubled since the 2014 calf-crop survey; the main reason given for continuing abrupt weaning was that calves are marketed at weaning. Canadian weaning ages averaged 215 days (calves from cows) and 212 days (from heifers). Hosts Stookey's 5-minute two-stage weaning video and 1.5-minute efficient cow-calf pair sorting video.

papers.title: Sorting cow-calf pairs (Stookey method) and the Biggs calf-stripping technique
papers.authors: Stookey, J.M. (University of Saskatchewan); Biggs, D. (Alberta); as documented by Canadian Cattlemen, Hi-Hog, Grainews and Progressive Cattle
papers.source: Canadian Cattlemen / Hi-Hog Farm and Ranch Equipment / Progressive Cattle (trade press and manufacturer documentation)
papers.licence: Trade press and manufacturer web resources, freely accessible (no PDF; no peer-reviewed publication exists)
papers.abstract: The only named, documented method for the ranch's actual problem - separating pairs with the fewest people and the least pushing - and it is UNMEASURED. Developed by Dylan Biggs, an Alberta rancher, and popularised by Joseph Stookey of the University of Saskatchewan, who credits Biggs. Method: precondition the herd to all the pens; bring the mixed herd into a cow-calf pen; as the herd passes, open and secure a cow sorting gate hung at an angle across the alley; at the group pen open the lower half of a split (Dutch-door) calf sorting gate whose upper section is set at the calves' shoulder height; the sorter stands at the main alley exit with at most one helper walking the exit fence line; cows walk past the handler and out while calves, which respond to the handler sooner than cows do, duck under the rail into the adjacent calf pen, so both keep walking and nothing balls up at the gate; let strays go, because a second pass is designed in - at the end, close both sorting gates and open the gate between the cow pen and the calf pen. The stripper gate should sit where the cows are going out; the operator works mostly on the far or hinge side of the gate; rail height must be reset for each year's calf size, and operations with creep feeders can add a vertical bar at creep-gate width. UNMEASURED CLAIMS to flag: that Biggs and Stookey both cut sorting time nearly in half, and that it needs very few boots on the ground. Stookey's own caveat is the honest part: it works very well for gentle cattle but may not work for wild cattle with big flight zones. No peer-reviewed study of this or any other pair-sorting method exists.

papers.title: Calf gate and creep gate opening dimensions that pass a calf and stop a cow (extension consensus)
papers.authors: University of Florida IFAS (AG193); University of Georgia Extension (B 1315); Hi-Hog; Tarter
papers.source: University extension publications and manufacturer specifications, compiled
papers.licence: Extension publications and manufacturer specifications, freely accessible (compiled; no single PDF)
papers.abstract: The dimensional answer to the ranch's calf-gate question, drawn from creep-feeder design because that is the same cow-exclusion geometry problem. WIDTH is consistent across sources at 16-18 inches (41-46 cm): University of Florida gives 17-18 in wide by 36-48 in high; University of Georgia gives 18 in entrance slots; a general extension guide gives 16-18 in wide by 36-40 in tall; Hi-Hog's calf creep feeder panel has openings approximately 17.25 in wide; Tarter's panel has six 17 in openings. For a wire rather than a gate, UGA states that a single strand 36-42 in above ground lets calves pass under while keeping cows out. For growing calves, a non-university source suggests starting at 18 in of opening height and raising it to 20-22 in once calves average 300-400 lb - treat as advice. HEIGHT FOR WEANING-WEIGHT CALVES IS NOT PUBLISHED ANYWHERE: Hi-Hog's commercial Calf Sorting Gate (item 382) is a 12 ft wide, 8 ft high split gate, about 297 lb, with seven height settings, and the instruction is simply to set the bottom of the upper section at the calves' shoulder height and readjust as they grow. No study has measured any calf-gate dimension against pass rate or cow exclusion. A ranch must measure its own calves' shoulder height; software must not assert a number here.

papers.title: One-way gates, crowd pen and single-file chute placement guidance
papers.authors: Grandin, T.
papers.source: grandin.com cattle handling facility design pages
papers.licence: Author's freely accessible web resource (HTML, no PDF)
papers.abstract: The standard free reference for one-way (ratchet) gate placement, which matters for any sorting system that uses them. A one-way gate at the junction between the single-file chute and the crowd pen should be located at least one body length up the single-file chute, and gates placed too close to the crowd pen can stop movement, so at least two body lengths up the race is preferable; equipping the gate with a remote control rope operable from the crowd pen facilitates cattle entry; most gates can be tied open when cattle are calm, except the one nearest the squeeze chute, which keeps the leader from backing out. Engineering and behavioural guidance, not a measured comparison - no trial has tested one-way gate placement against flow rate or stress. Note also that Hibbard and Locatelli published a point-by-point critique of Grandin's facility designs in the Stockmanship Journal; that is a position paper, not evidence either way.

papers.title: Low-Stress Weaning (extension summary of SDSU weaning research)
papers.authors: DeHaan, E. (updated); originally Harty, A. and Olson, K.C.
papers.licence: SDSU Extension web resource, freely accessible (no PDF)
papers.abstract: The Northern Plains extension summary of the SDSU low-stress weaning work, updated July 2025, and the free source for several figures the peer-reviewed papers bury in figures rather than tables. Reports that fenceline-weaned calves gained similarly to unseparated calves during nutritional separation and maintained weight for the first 7 days after physical separation while abruptly weaned calves lost about 2.4 lb per day, and that nose-tag calves gained almost 1.5 lb more per day than calves without them during stage 1. Note that this stage-1 nose-flap result has the OPPOSITE SIGN to Taylor et al. 2020 and Haley et al. 2005, which both found reduced gain while the flap was in - a real unresolved inconsistency in the literature. Practical guidance given: low-stress weaning means nutritional separation then physical separation at least 3 days later; fenceline nutritional separation takes about 3 to 7 days; nose tags are worn 4 to 7 days; example fence is 5-strand barbed wire or electric. Also cites Utah work (fenceline advantage lasting 10 weeks post-weaning) and Michigan work (advantage lasting 14 days, with lower serum haptoglobin at day 5).

papers.title: Effects of Low-Stress Weaning on Calf Growth Performance and Carcass Characteristics (SDSU Beef Day 2020 and Meat and Muscle Biology)
papers.authors: Gubbels, E.R.; Salverson, R.R.; Cammack, K.M.; Grubbs, J.K.; Underwood, K.R.; Olson, K.C.; Blair, A.D.
papers.source: South Dakota State University Beef Day 2020 Summary Publication, pp. 117-124; also Meat and Muscle Biology
papers.licence: Open access (Open PRAIRIE / Meat and Muscle Biology), but no PDF download could be verified
papers.abstract: The earlier report of the South Dakota State low-stress weaning work that was later published in full as Gubbels et al. 2023 in Translational Animal Science. Angus x Simmental crossbred steers (n=90 in the Meat and Muscle Biology version, 89 in the 2023 paper), comparing two low-stress weaning methods with conventional weaning. Conclusion as stated in the proceedings: low-stress weaning methods do not significantly improve post-weaning growth performance or carcass merit compared with calves weaned using conventional methods. Use the 2023 Translational Animal Science paper for the full statistics; this entry is for provenance.

papers.title: Weaning management of beef calves with implications for animal health and welfare
papers.authors: Lynch, E.M.; McGee, M.; Earley, B.
papers.licence: Open access per DOAJ, but no downloadable PDF could be verified
papers.abstract: The Teagasc review of weaning management with health and welfare implications, from the group that produced the Irish physiological and immunological weaning studies. Covers the methods, the stress markers and the health consequences, and is the most recent full review before the 2025 Animals review. Listed in DOAJ as open access; the publisher's PDF could not be retrieved for verification.

papers.title: The effect of early weaning on feedlot performance and measures of stress in beef calves
papers.authors: Arthington, J.D.; Spears, J.W.; Miller, D.C.
papers.licence: Subscription (American Society of Animal Science / Oxford University Press)
papers.abstract: One of the reference studies on early weaning, measuring feedlot performance and stress markers in early-weaned beef calves. Relevant to the timing question on the prairies: early weaning (calves 1-5 months, or around 70-90 days of lactation in range systems) is the standard drought and thin-cow response, and the measured cow-side benefits come from US Great Plains work showing early-weaned cows end heavier and in better condition. Cited repeatedly in the acute-phase-protein weaning literature as the source of the early-weaning stress profile.

papers.title: Effects of castration and weaning conducted concurrently or consecutively on behaviour, blood traits and performance in beef calves
papers.authors: Marti, S.; Velarde, A.; de la Torre, J.L.; Bach, A.; Aris, A.; Serrano, A.; Manteca, X.; Devant, M.
papers.licence: Open access per DOAJ, but no downloadable PDF could be verified
papers.abstract: Directly relevant to the handling-count question a two-stage programme raises: is it better to stack procedures into one handling event or spread them out? Compares castration and weaning conducted concurrently versus consecutively, with behaviour, blood traits and performance endpoints. This is the closest the literature comes to measuring the cost of extra handling events around weaning - a cost that nose-flap weaning adds two of (insert and remove) and that no nose-flap study has measured. A companion paper by the same group appears in Applied Animal Behaviour Science (10.1016/j.applanim.2014.09.003).

papers.title: Fatalities Caused by Cattle — Four States, 2003–2008
papers.authors: Kraemer MU, Leinenkugel K, Myers JR (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
papers.licence: public domain (US government)
papers.abstract: Surveillance review of 21 occupational cattle-caused deaths in Iowa, Kansas, Missouri and Nebraska, 2003-2008, drawn from Iowa FACE and the Great Plains Center for Agricultural Health. Gives the only published fatal task/location breakdown: 33% while tending or treating cattle in enclosed areas such as pens and chutes, 24% while herding/moving/sorting toward pens, 14% while loading onto trucks or trailers, 14% feeding, 14% in open pasture. Bulls caused 10 of 21 deaths, cows with calves 3, cows without calves 3, multiple cattle 5; 16 deaths were purposeful strikes and 5 were crushing against a stationary object or being struck by a gate. 67% of decedents were 60 or older (median age 65), 95% male, one third working alone, and all but one death was blunt force trauma to chest and/or head.

papers.title: Cattle-Related Injuries and Farm Management Practices on Kentucky Beef Cattle Farms
papers.authors: Browning SR, Westneat SC, Sanderson WT, Reed DB
papers.source: Journal of Agricultural Safety and Health 19(1):37-49 (ASABE)
papers.licence: NIOSH-deposited author manuscript, free to read
papers.abstract: Mail survey of 2,500 Kentucky Cattlemen's Association members yielding 1,149 complete responses from active beef cattle operators. 157 farms (13.7%, 95% CI 11.7-15.8) reported at least one cattle-related injury to the operator or a family member in the previous 12 months. Reports crude injury rates per 100 farms for each piece of handling equipment present: crowding pen OR 1.80 (1.27-2.55), palpation cage OR 1.65 (1.16-2.35), manual squeeze chute with head gate OR 1.55 (1.10-2.18), working chute or alley OR 1.32, loading chute OR 1.25; ATV/Gator herding was protective (adjusted OR 0.51, 0.30-0.86). Also records the Oklahoma location breakdown (pens 40%, alleyways 17%, squeeze chutes 16% of 150 injuries on 100 cow-calf operations) and injury detail: 33.6% needed medical care or caused over 4 hours lost work, leg/hip/knee 30.2%, cows 36% of injuries, calves 16.8%, bulls and steers 13.4%.

papers.title: More Than Time and Money: A Mixed-Methods Study of the Barriers to Safer Cattle Handling Practices
papers.authors: Scott-Harp D, Peek-Asa C, Rohlman DS, Janssen B
papers.licence: NIH/NIOSH author manuscript, free to read
papers.abstract: Iowa survey (N=66) plus four beef-operation site visits documenting which handling-facility components farms actually have and why they do not change them. Over 50% of farms had an alley, manual head gate, sorting/diverter gate and manual squeeze chute; hydraulic head gates 24.5% and hydraulic chutes 10.2%. Of farmers naming desired changes, 40% wanted to redesign one element or the whole facility and 10% wanted designed worker escape routes. Its introduction assembles the key denominators: US farmer/rancher fatality rate 24 per 100,000 FTE, livestock-production nonfatal incidence 6.9 per 100 full-time workers versus 5.7 for crops, and the Hubert/Huhnke finding that pens, alleyways and squeeze chutes are the commonest injury locations with about 25% of cattle-handling injuries attributable to equipment used and working-facility design.

papers.title: Agriculture-related Fatalities in Canada, 1990–2020
papers.authors: Canadian Agricultural Injury Reporting (CAIR) / Canadian Agricultural Safety Association
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (© Canadian Agricultural Safety Association)
papers.abstract: National Canadian agricultural fatality surveillance covering 2,814 deaths from 1990 to 2020, with an overall rate of 10.7 per 100,000 farm population and an age-specific rate of 45.2 per 100,000 for farmers aged 80 and over. For 2011-2020 animal-related events caused 33 fatalities (5% of the decade's deaths), tied with traffic collisions and falls from height; of the 32 animal-related deaths with animal type recorded, 53% (17) involved a horse and 47% (15) involved a cow or cattle. 66% of all agricultural fatalities were machine-related, leaving animals among the leading non-machine causes.

papers.title: Agricultural Injuries in Canada for 1990–2000 (National Report: fatalities and hospitalizations)
papers.authors: Canadian Agricultural Injury Surveillance Program / CAIR, Canadian Agricultural Safety Association
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (© Canadian Agricultural Safety Association)
papers.abstract: The richest Canadian source because it reports fatalities and hospitalizations side by side. 77 animal-related agricultural deaths (6.1% of all agricultural fatalities) in 1990-2000, of which 37.7% involved horses, 32.5% bulls and 19.5% cows; by task, 29.9% were working with a bull or with other animals near a bull and 9.1% were calving. Separately, 2,800 hospitalized non-machine agricultural injuries involved animals (April 1990-March 2000) against a farm population denominator of 842,595: cattle 1,136, horses 1,111, bulls 186, calves 143, with cattle and horses causing 92% of the total and 67.2% of animal hospitalizations in adults 60+ caused by cattle. Cattle injuries peaked March-May (calving) and bull injuries peaked in August. 18 of 20 (90%) corral/animal-pen fatalities occurred at the scene, the highest at-scene proportion of any farm location.

papers.title: Agricultural-related Fatalities in Canada, 2003–2012
papers.authors: Canadian Agricultural Injury Reporting (CAIR) / Canadian Agricultural Safety Association
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (© Canadian Agricultural Safety Association)
papers.abstract: National Canadian fatality surveillance for 2003-2012 covering 843 agriculture-related deaths. Animal-related events caused 65 fatalities, 8% of the total: 54% (35) involved horses and 45% (29) involved cows, bulls, steers or calves. Of the 35 horse deaths only 22 (59%) were work-related and 14 (38%) were recreational riding, so the apparent horse dominance in Canadian animal-fatality data is partly a recreation artefact while the cattle share is essentially all occupational.

papers.title: Seniors (60+) Agriculture-Related Fatalities in Canada, 2006–2015
papers.authors: Canadian Agricultural Injury Reporting (CAIR) / Canadian Agricultural Safety Association
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (© Canadian Agricultural Safety Association)
papers.abstract: 358 agriculture-related fatalities of Canadian farmers aged 60 and over in 2006-2015, 96% male, at an age-specific rate of 30.4 per 100,000 farm population; farmers aged 60-69 had both the most deaths (160) and the highest rate (52.1 per 100,000). Animal-related events were the third leading mechanism among seniors with 35 deaths (10%), behind rollovers (65, 18%) and runovers (58, 16%). Of those 35 animal deaths, 51% (18) involved a horse and 49% (17) a cow or cattle; farmers aged 70-79 had the highest number of animal-related deaths of any senior age band.

papers.title: Agricultural-Related Injuries in Alberta, 1990–2009
papers.authors: Canadian Agricultural Injury Surveillance Program (CAISP/CAIR) / Alberta Agriculture and Rural Development
papers.source: Government of Alberta / Canadian Agricultural Injury Reporting
papers.licence: Crown copyright (Government of Alberta), free to read
papers.abstract: The Alberta-specific CAIR analysis: 355 Albertans killed in agricultural injury events 1990-2009 at a rate of 10.0 per 100,000 farm population, with animal-related events the fourth leading cause at 9% of fatalities. Of 31 Alberta animal-related deaths, 68% (21) involved horses and 32% (10) involved cows, steers or calves (7 male, 3 female victims). Among Albertans aged 60 and over, animal-related events caused 17 deaths, 13% of senior agricultural fatalities. The report also establishes the Alberta severity ratio: for every agricultural injury death there were 25 hospital admissions, 11 of them major trauma.

papers.title: Fatal Farm Injuries in Saskatchewan 1990 to 2019 (30 years)
papers.authors: Karunanayake C, Ulmer K, Hagel L, Koehncke N (Canadian Centre for Health and Safety in Agriculture, University of Saskatchewan)
papers.source: Canadian Centre for Health and Safety in Agriculture, University of Saskatchewan
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (University of Saskatchewan)
papers.abstract: Thirty-year Saskatchewan farm fatality surveillance. Among 109 work-related non-machine fatalities, animal-related injury was the single most common mechanism at 20.0% (n=19), and beef cattle accounted for 68% of those animal-related cases — the most cattle-specific and most prairie-relevant Canadian figure available. Males were 89% of non-machine fatality victims and the oldest age group made up the majority. Being struck by an object was the next most common non-machine mechanism (n=19), most often by a heavy non-machine object such as a gate or door.

papers.title: Agricultural Fatalities and Hospitalizations in Ontario 1990–2004
papers.authors: Canadian Agricultural Injury Surveillance Program (CAISP) / Canadian Agricultural Safety Association
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (© Canadian Agricultural Safety Association)
papers.abstract: Provincial surveillance reporting fatalities and hospitalizations on the same population, which exposes how much fatality counts understate animal injury. Animal-related events caused 5.7% of Ontario agricultural fatalities (fourth-ranked) but 13.8% of hospitalized agricultural injuries, the second leading cause after machine entanglements. By age, animal events caused 12.0% of hospitalizations in children under 16, 14.2% in adults 16-64 and 14.0% in adults 65 and over. Among fatalities in adults 65+, being struck by an animal was the third leading cause at 10.1%.

papers.title: Livestock-related injuries in the Midland region of New Zealand
papers.authors: Tosswill M, Roskruge M, Smith A, Christey G
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (NZMA)
papers.abstract: Midland Trauma System Registry study of 168 livestock injury admissions 2012-2015, of which 127 (75.6%) were cattle-related. Gives the clearest published location and task split for cattle handling: moving and loading stock caused 38% of injuries (moving 27%, loading 11%) and at least 29% of cattle-related injuries occurred near gates, poles or fences. Mechanisms: cattle caused 89.7% of all crush injuries (trapped between two animals or between animal and structure), 91.9% of kicks, 72.3% of hits and 100% of tramplings. Cattle were the only animal responsible for any head/neck, chest or abdominal injury in the series; body regions were upper/lower extremity 40% and external 34%. Cattle injuries peaked in September-October (calving) with daily peaks at 9-10am and 3-5pm, and age peaks at 20-29 and 50-59.

papers.title: Cattle-related trauma: a 10-year retrospective cohort study from a Swiss level 1 trauma centre
papers.authors: Ehrhard S, et al. (Inselspital, University Hospital Bern)
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (open access)
papers.abstract: Ten-year cohort of 94 cattle-related trauma patients at a Swiss level 1 trauma centre (101 of roughly 470,000 presentations, 0.02%). Median age 52, 75% male, 73% farmers; cows caused 86% of injuries, bulls 10% and calves 2%. Mechanisms were head-butt 36%, kick 35%, body contact 20% and trampling 12%, with all 10 penetrating injuries caused by head-butts. Injuries were contusions 82%, lacerations 46%, face fractures 28%, closed head trauma 19% and chest injuries 17%; head AIS 3 or more in 12%, chest in 9%, abdomen in 3%; 12% had an ISS of 16 or more and in-hospital mortality was 3%. Bull injuries required surgery in 90% of cases versus 49% for cow injuries (p = 0.023), quantifying the severity gap between bulls and cows.

papers.title: Horse and Cattle-Related Trauma: A Retrospective Review of Injuries and Outcomes at a Regional Australian Hospital
papers.authors: Savage G, Liesegang A, Campbell J, et al.
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: Review of 1,002 emergency presentations for horse or cattle trauma at Rockhampton Base Hospital in Queensland's largest cattle region, January 2018 to April 2021. Cattle accounted for 19.3% of presentations and horses 80.7%. Cattle injuries were most often caused by trampling (39.4%) or crushing (22.3%), were 79.3% male, and produced soft tissue injury 56.5%, rib fracture 14.5% and upper limb fracture 14.5%; mean ISS was 2.3 for cattle versus 1.9 for horses, and cattle cases were more likely to be admitted and to need an operation. Rib fracture appears as a cattle-specific signature absent from the horse and paediatric groups.

papers.title: Are Animals Occupational Hazards? (US Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 1992–1997)
papers.authors: Drudi D (Bureau of Labor Statistics)
papers.source: Compensation and Working Conditions, US Bureau of Labor Statistics (Fall 2000)
papers.licence: public domain (US government)
papers.abstract: BLS analysis of 375 US animal-related work fatalities and the matching SOII nonfatal cases over 1992-1997. Cattle caused 141 deaths (38%), more than any other animal, but only 7% of nonfatal animal injuries (5,300 cases), so cattle are injury-light and death-heavy relative to other animals. Bulls, about 2% of the cattle population, caused about half the cattle-related fatalities (68 of 141); 5 deaths arose from birthing or maternal defensiveness by cows. Animal attacks accounted for 114 of the 141 cattle deaths, 14 were vehicle collisions, and 6 were cases of cattle knocking a gate or panel into the worker — the only published count of the swinging-gate mechanism. Agriculture accounted for three-quarters of cattle-related fatalities, over 9 in 10 cattle cases involved men, and fractures were one-sixth of nonfatal cattle cases versus under one-tenth of all nonfatal cases. Note: this PDF returns 403 to a curl HEAD request but downloads and parses correctly via a normal GET.

papers.title: Cattle Handling Safety in Working Facilities (OSU Extension Fact Sheet BAE-1738)
papers.authors: Hubert DJ, Huhnke RL, Harp SL
papers.source: Oklahoma Cooperative Extension Service, Oklahoma State University
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (OSU Extension)
papers.abstract: The single most useful extension document for a design-flagging tool. Gives numeric flight-zone radii (five to over 25 feet for feedlot cattle, as far as 300 feet for range cattle), the 45 to 60 degree working angle behind the shoulder, and the statement that cattle see in all directions except directly behind. Carries explicit facility-safety rules: do not enter a crowding area with animals if they become bunched; add a 14-inch wide pass-through for worker escape in pen corners; position the catwalk about 36 inches below the top of the fence so workers can move animals while avoiding direct animal contact; smallest pen dimension no less than 16 feet; at least 20 sq ft per mature animal; alley width 12 to 14 feet with a 10-foot minimum. Also reports a 1997 Oklahoma State study of 150 cattle-handling injury cases on 100 Oklahoma cow-calf operations in which more than 50 percent of injuries were due to human error and about 25 percent to equipment and facilities.

papers.title: Non-intentional farm-related incidents in Australia, January–December 2024
papers.authors: AgHealth Australia, University of Sydney (for AgriFutures Australia)
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (AgriFutures Australia)
papers.abstract: Annual media-surveillance report on Australian on-farm deaths and injuries. 72 on-farm deaths in calendar 2024 against 32 in the equivalent 2023 window, and 1,815 non-intentional on-farm deaths since 2001, of which 53% (n=971) were aged 50 or over, 88% (n=1,601) were male, and 14% (n=248) involved children under 15. Cattle and, separately, cattle yards appear as agents of fatal injury in the 2024 agent table. Of 133 non-fatal on-farm injury events reported in media in 2024, cattle accounted for 12, behind quads (46) and horses (14). Because the method is media monitoring, all counts are undercounts.

papers.title: Fatal Animal Related Incidents on Australian Farms — a 20-Year Review
papers.authors: Peachey K-L, Lower T, Rolfe M
papers.licence: unknown (paywalled; abstract free via Europe PMC)
papers.abstract: Descriptive study of National Coronial Information System records for people fatally injured by an animal on an Australian farm, 2001-2020. The mean was 6.5 animal-related deaths per year, a 35% reduction on the 1989-92 mean of 10. Horses and cattle together accounted for 81% of incidents (horses n=75, cattle n=31); 46% of decedents were aged 60 or over, more than half of cases occurred during work, 85% of decedents fell from or were struck by an animal, and 40% sustained a head injury. The abstract's male count (86, 66%) does not reconcile with the horse-plus-cattle totals, an inconsistency in the source. Full text is paywalled (publisher site returns 403); no free PDF found.

papers.title: The Stockman's Scorecard: quantitative evaluation of beef cattle stockmanship
papers.authors: John K. Yost, Jarred W. Yates, Matt P. Davis, Matthew E. Wilson
papers.source: Translational Animal Science (Oxford University Press / American Society of Animal Science)
papers.licence: CC BY 4.0
papers.abstract: A validated observation instrument (the Stockman's Scorecard) was used to score 84 stockmen at 39 Texas beef feedlots between March 2018 and April 2019; mean score 84.5 (SD 14.73, range 20-100). The most frequent handler errors were filling the crowd pen or tub more than half full (n=39), slow to remove pressure (n=29), unnecessary noise (n=25), standing in front and tapping the rear (n=24) and failing to regulate flow through a pinch point (n=22). Scorecard score was strongly negatively associated with the number of cattle touched with an electric prod on the BQA feedyard assessment (rho = -0.51, P < 0.0001) and moderately with cattle vocalising in the chute (rho = -0.31). Cattle disposition had little effect on handler score (Kappa = 0.17), so poor scores were not explained by wild cattle. NOTE: the pdf_url is a CDN mirror of the PMC PDF; PMC's own /pdf/ path is reCAPTCHA-gated and returns HTML.

papers.title: Developing measures to audit welfare of cattle and pigs at slaughter
papers.authors: Temple Grandin
papers.source: Animal Welfare (Universities Federation for Animal Welfare / Cambridge University Press)
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (Creative Commons, per the paper's own re-use notice)
papers.abstract: Reports a decade of restaurant-chain welfare audit data from 30-49 beef and 22-28 pork plants against five numerically scored criteria: percentage falling, percentage moved with an electric prod, percentage vocalising, stunning efficacy and insensibility. Thresholds are stated: prod use 25% or less to pass with 5% 'excellent', falling 1% or less, cattle vocalisation 3% or less. Measured results include beef plants achieving 5% or less prod use rising from 25% (1996) to 81% (2010), 0% falls in 30 of 32 plants in 2010, and mean prod use by line speed of 12.5-27%. Grandin also notes that after auditing began in 1999 most plants banned electric prods in the lairage and crowd pen.

papers.title: Wolf presence in the ranch of origin: impacts on temperament and physiological responses of beef cattle following a simulated wolf encounter
papers.authors: R. F. Cooke, D. W. Bohnert, M. M. Reis, B. I. Cappellozza
papers.source: Journal of Animal Science (American Society of Animal Science)
papers.licence: author copy on an Oregon State University (EOARC) server, free to read
papers.abstract: One hundred multiparous pregnant Angus-cross cows, 50 wolf-naive (Burns, Oregon) and 50 from a wolf-depredated Idaho herd, were commingled for 50 days then exposed for 20 minutes to a simulated predator encounter consisting of wolf-urine-soaked plugs on the fence, continuous wolf howls and three leashed dogs walked along the pen perimeter, followed by 20 seconds of dog exposure while restrained in a squeeze chute. Chute score, temperament score and plasma cortisol all increased (P <= 0.01) in the wolf-experienced cows but did not change in the naive cows (P >= 0.19); vaginal temperature rose more in the wolf-experienced group (P = 0.03). This is the only controlled cattle study I could verify that measures the effect of dogs on crush score and cortisol, and the effect was conditional on prior predator experience.

papers.title: An evaluation of cattle handling categories in the beef quality assurance feedyard assessment, compliance of large feedyards with these guidelines, and influence of handling practices on behavior and performance of feedlot cattle
papers.authors: Ruth Woiwode (advisor Temple Grandin)
papers.source: PhD dissertation, Animal Sciences, Colorado State University
papers.licence: institutional repository, free to read
papers.abstract: Part one surveyed 28 large feedyards (1,000+ head) in Colorado, Kansas and Nebraska against Beef Quality Assurance cattle-handling limits: electric prod use 3.8% (limit 10%), falls 0.6% (limit 2%), stumbles 5.7% (limit 10%), vocalisation 1.4% (limit 5%), jumping or running on exit 52% (limit 25%) and improperly caught cattle not readjusted 1.2% (limit 0%). Part two used 496 Hereford steers at a Kansas feedlot to test how handling before processing and on release from the squeeze chute affected behaviour and average daily gain: vocalising during restraint was associated with lower ADG, and faster exit speed correlated with both more vocalisation and lower ADG. Note that magazine summaries of the same survey report prod use as 5.5% and falls as 0.8%.

papers.title: Low Stress Livestock Handling
papers.authors: Manitoba Agriculture (Manitoba Agriculture, Food and Rural Initiatives)
papers.licence: Government of Manitoba publication, free to read
papers.abstract: A prairie-province extension guide built around a hazard table from the Institute of Agricultural Rural and Environmental Health in Saskatchewan. States that a cow sees nearly 90 percent of the area around her and that the only dead spot is directly behind her between the hips, and that the most common handler mistake is inadvertent entry into that blind spot, which makes cattle stop and 'hook'. Warns that aggression in cattle can be triggered by yelling, whistling, erratic movements and waving arms, and never to turn your back on an aggressive or anxious animal. Recommends filling a crowd pen only one-third to one-half full so cattle can find the exit, and lists seven causes of handling problems including too many animals in the crowding pen and handlers frightening the animals.

papers.title: Low Stress Cattle Handling (APSC-167)
papers.authors: Jennifer Ligon, John Benner, Rachel Grosse, Laura Siegle
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (US land-grant extension)
papers.abstract: An extension review of low-stress handling built on pressure-and-release learning, the flight zone and the point of balance. Explicitly names improved safety for both handler and cattle as the first of two benefits, citing Grandin 1998, but gives no injury measurements, which makes it a clean example of the expert-advice-without-measurement category. Also summarises the measured production literature that low-stress handling draws on (immunity and vaccine response, clinical sign detection, weaning response, weight gain, milk yield and quality, feedlot performance and carcass quality) with citations, and notes that docility EPD selection gradually produces calmer temperaments.

papers.title: Alabama Beef Quality Assurance: Using Handling Facilities Correctly (ANR-1283)
papers.authors: Alabama Cooperative Extension System (Auburn University / Alabama A&M)
papers.licence: publisher PDF, free to read (US land-grant extension)
papers.abstract: A state Beef Quality Assurance facility-use guide that contains the clearest BQA-side statement of the design rule a corral-design tool needs: a catwalk built along the cattle-working chutes or loading chutes is a much better place from which to work cattle than standing behind them. Also advises staying out of kicking range rather than working close, warns that cattle become nervous or aggressive when alone, tells handlers to avoid electric prods wherever possible and to apply them only to the side or back, notes that cattle move forward when approached behind the shoulder and backward when approached ahead of it, and covers sweep tubs and the Bud Box as the two funnel options.

papers.title: Low-Stress Cattle Handling and Cattle Handling Facilities
papers.authors: Canadian Angus Association
papers.licence: industry association publication, free to read
papers.abstract: A short Canadian producer-facing guide that frames poor cattle handling as increasing stress and risk of injury for both cattle and people, and names Bud Williams and Temple Grandin as the two sources of low-stress method. Its handling checklist includes the rule most relevant to flagging a design that puts a person behind animals: do not chase cattle from the rear of the group as you will then be in their blind spot. Also advises working with another person where possible, avoiding quick movements and loud noises, not overcrowding alleys, and avoiding electric prods and physical force. No measurements of its own; cites 2009 and 2011 cortisol and weight-gain work and a 2020 reproduction review.

papers.title: Safe and Low Stress Cattle Handling
papers.authors: Farm Safety Manitoba (Manitoba Farm Safety Program)
papers.licence: industry/agency publication, free to read
papers.abstract: A prairie farm-safety agency presentation that packages low-stress handling explicitly as an occupational-safety intervention rather than a welfare one, which is the framing a design-flagging tool is making. Useful as evidence that a Canadian safety association endorses the flight zone, point of balance and blind spot rules as injury-prevention measures, and as a plain-language source for operator-facing wording. Contains no original measurement.

papers.title: The response of beef cattle to noise during handling
papers.authors: J. L. Waynert, J. M. Stookey, K. S. Schwartzkopf-Genswein, J. M. Watts, C. S. Waltz
papers.licence: unknown (publisher paywall; University of Saskatchewan authors)
papers.abstract: The study behind the widely repeated claim that human shouting is more stressful to cattle than equipment noise. Trial 1 assigned 29 treatment-naive heifers to pre-recorded handling noise consisting of humans shouting plus metal clanging (n=14) or to silence (n=15). Trial 2 split the noise into pre-recorded human shouting (n=15) or metal-on-metal clanging (n=15). Heart rate was recorded by remote telemetry. The reported conclusion is that the sound of humans shouting was more alarming than the sound of metal striking metal, judged by heart rate and movement. I could not obtain the full text, so no cortisol values or p-values are confirmed, and this study did not test an electric prod. Saskatchewan-authored, so directly relevant to a prairie operation.

papers.title: Aversion learning techniques to evaluate dairy cattle handling practices
papers.authors: Edmond A. Pajor, Jeffrey Rushen, Anne Marie B. de Passille
papers.licence: unknown (publisher paywall)
papers.abstract: Used a Y-maze choice test to rank how aversive cattle find common handling practices. In a second experiment 24 cows chose between paired treatments thought to be aversive: shout versus hit, shout versus cattle prod, and control versus tail twist. The reported conclusions are that shouting and the use of cattle prods are both aversive and that tail twisting is not aversive if done gently. A 2013 secondary review places the ordering as electric prod most aversive, shouting second, then tail twist and hitting. This is the primary source behind the extension claim that yelling is 'as stressful as an electric prod', and it actually ranks the prod above shouting, so the claim should be stated carefully.

papers.title: Occupational Health and Safety Code, Alberta Regulation 191/2021 (office consolidation current as of March 31, 2025)
papers.authors: Government of Alberta / Alberta King's Printer
papers.licence: Crown copyright (Alberta King's Printer; reproduction permitted with acknowledgement)
papers.abstract: The complete Alberta OHS Code, containing every technical occupational safety standard in the province. Section 1.1(1) states the Code does not apply to farming and ranching operations including 'the raising and maintenance of animals or birds', with only Part 13 (joint health and safety committees and representatives, ss.196-204) applying per s.1.1(4) and s.201 training limited to co-chairs and representatives per s.1.1(5). It therefore specifies no dimensions, man gates, escape routes, race widths or pen allowances for livestock handling facilities, and contains no provision about working with animals at all. Part 2 (ss.7-9 hazard assessment and the eliminate/engineer/administer/PPE control hierarchy) and Part 28 (ss.393-394 working alone, where s.393(2) declares working alone a hazard) are exempt for ranches but are the best available Alberta standard-of-care benchmarks.

papers.title: Occupational Health and Safety Act, SA 2020 c O-2.2
papers.authors: Government of Alberta / Alberta King's Printer
papers.licence: Crown copyright (Alberta King's Printer; reproduction permitted with acknowledgement)
papers.abstract: The only Alberta occupational safety instrument that binds a farm or ranch employing waged non-family workers. Section 1(cc)(i) excludes from 'occupation' those farming and ranching operations paying wages only to listed family members, and s.1(tt)(ii) correspondingly excludes those persons from 'worker', so one waged non-family hire brings the whole Act into force. Section 3(1)(a) imposes the general duty to ensure worker health, safety and welfare 'as far as it is reasonably practicable', with s.3(2)-(4) covering adequate training, competent performance of endangering work and keeping hazard information available; ss.13-14 set the 20+/5-19 worker thresholds for committees and representatives. Section 33(1)-(2) requires reporting worker deaths and hospital admissions to a Director as soon as possible and s.33(5)-(6) requires investigation of potentially serious incidents, but only where the injured person is a 'worker', so owner and family injuries are not reportable.

papers.title: VBP+ Standards (Verified Beef Production Plus), updated June 2026
papers.authors: Verified Beef Production Plus (Canadian Cattle Association)
papers.licence: free to download
papers.abstract: The current publicly available standards document for Canada's on-farm food safety, animal care and environmental stewardship certification, enforced contractually through Corrective Action Requests and Critical Control Points. Its Animal Care and Welfare handling expectation states methods should minimise stress 'through the use of appropriate equipment, minimal physical contact, trained personnel and appropriate footing and lighting', with the rationale noting handling affects animal welfare, meat quality and human safety and that the intent is to ensure 'the safety of people and animals'. It names human safety more explicitly than the NFACC Code but attaches no design criterion, specifies no dimensions, and does not mention electric prods at all. Deeper handling detail sits in the VBP+ Animal Care Manual (Section 05), which is published only as an issuu embed and not as a downloadable PDF.

papers.title: Handling and housing cattle (Agriculture Information Sheet No 35, Revision 1)
papers.authors: Health and Safety Executive
papers.licence: Crown copyright (UK, OGL)
papers.abstract: The UK safety regulator's core guidance on handling adult cattle, stock bulls and bull beef, formally advisory but evidentially weighty: following it means 'you will normally be doing enough to comply with the law' and inspectors may refer to it. It contains the clearest regulator statement of the separation principle a corral-design tool enforces: arrange race, crush and loading areas 'so that no one ever needs to be in them with the animals', keeping fixed handling system or lorry tailboard gates between handler and animal at all times. It requires an adequate escape route where a downer or loose-box animal cannot be secured, forbids working on animals held by gates alone, forbids working on a crushed animal with an unsecured animal waiting behind, requires race doors operated from the working side, and forbids entering a bull-beef pen or letting a lone person handle bull beef. Concrete dimensions: bull pen walls of 215 mm reinforced concrete block; railings and bars minimum 48 mm outside diameter; bull pen outer walls, fences and gates at least 1.5 m high; vertical bar spacings no more than 100 mm; bull-beef pen divisions around 1.5 m above floor with the lower 1 m meshed or sheeted; group size no more than 15-20; and crush flooring of bolted hardwood, chequer-plate or rubber mat.

papers.title: Code of Practice for Preventing Injury and Occupational Ill Health in Agriculture (For Farms with Three or Less Employees)
papers.authors: Health and Safety Authority (Ireland)
papers.licence: © Health and Safety Authority (Ireland); free to download
papers.abstract: Ireland's farm safety code, issued by the HSA under section 60 of the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 after consultation with the Farm Safety Partnership and with ministerial consent, which makes failure to observe it admissible in evidence in criminal proceedings; this is the most nearly mandatory document in this collection. Section 7.0 'Safety with Livestock' and s.7.3 'Design and use of handling facilities' (p.32-33) list the elements to examine (collecting pen, race or chute, forcing pen, catwalk, crush gate, dispersal pen) and set work practices including 'Never enter a crush with livestock' and standing aside while closing the restraining gate when enclosing a herd in a collecting pen, to prevent crushing if an animal charges. Section 7.3 delegates all dimensions to the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine standard S137 for cattle crush, race and enclosures. Section 7.4 reports that bulls cause 27% of farm livestock deaths, restricts bull handling to trained, fit handlers aged 18-65, requires two handlers every time, and illustrates the rule 'Have an escape route'.

papers.title: Cattle Handling in Marts and Lairages: Information Sheet
papers.authors: Health and Safety Authority (Ireland)
papers.licence: © Health and Safety Authority (Ireland); free to download
papers.abstract: A four-page summary of the HSA's Guidance on Safe Operation of Marts and Lairages, and the live equivalent of HSE's apparently withdrawn livestock-markets publication; it credits New Zealand ACC for its cattle-arousal diagrams. Advisory. Its handler-protection content is unusually explicit for a welfare-adjacent document: there must be no chance of livestock escaping by slipping between vehicle and side railings; step aside behind the gate or to a refuge point when opening the rear door or ramp and do not walk down the pen in front of the cattle; always plan your escape route; work from above off a raised catwalk and never place arms or hands through the rails; use overhead walkways wherever possible; do not overload sorting pens because cattle must have somewhere to move; the ringman must not enter the weighing box and must have effective shelter and be able to open the exit gate without leaving it. It also covers cattle arousal signs, penning incompatible cattle separately, never mixing mature bulls, and excluding children from all cattle work.

papers.title: Safe Cattle Handling (Information Sheet WSNZ_2284_JUN 16)
papers.authors: WorkSafe New Zealand
papers.licence: Crown copyright (New Zealand); free to download
papers.abstract: WorkSafe New Zealand's surviving cattle-handling guidance; the fuller 'Safe cattle handling - good practice guidelines' PDF (dmsdocument 194) has been WITHDRAWN and now redirects to a no-longer-available notice, with readers pointed to saferfarms.org.nz/guides. Advisory but formally accepted: 'WorkSafe NZ accepts these recommendations as current industry good practice' in support of the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 PCBU duty to ensure health and safety so far as reasonably practicable, a close analogue of Alberta OHS Act s.3(1). It contains no dimensions but several directly codable design and procedure rules: plan an escape route in advance when working cattle in the yards; never get in the race with large cattle and do not put arms, head or legs through the race walls; make sure cattle have room to move in the forcing pen; pack the race firmly; use a safe and well-maintained catwalk if there is one; install kick rails and stay behind them; never stand in front of a slip rail or hock bar; never dehorn large cattle alone in the race; work from above the head when ear-tagging; and if cornered by a bull with no escape route, step sideways out of his best vision.

papers.title: Cattle Handling Safety: A Practical Guide
papers.authors: L Fragar and J Temperley, Australian Centre for Agricultural Health and Safety
papers.source: Australian Centre for Agricultural Health and Safety, University of Sydney (RIRDC pub 16/024)
papers.licence: © Australian Centre for Agricultural Health and Safety; free to download
papers.abstract: A 32-page hazard-and-control guide that treats absence of handler escape routes as a named hazard and preserves dimensional figures from New Zealand ACC's withdrawn Better Yard Design (1999) and Stafford's Cattle handling skills (1997). Advisory. Its Access and Escape Ways entry states that serious injury and deaths have occurred where there has been no escape for the handler from cattle in the drafting pound and forcing pen, controlled by escapeways built into both. Dimensions: minimum 1.5 square metres per adult animal in yards; top rail 1,600 mm adequate with 1,800 mm in forcing yards, pens and the drafting pound; forcing pen maximum width 3 m so cattle can be worked from the catwalk; forcing-to-race angle at least 30-35 degrees off a straight wall; race clear width 660-710 mm and about 1,600 mm of length per adult beast; loading ramp incline about 20 degrees maximum and width about 800-900 mm; catwalks at buckle height on forcing pens, race and loading ramp with non-slip surfacing, steps and handrails. Its crush-selection checklists include a Handler Safety column covering adequate escape routes, slam latches, break-away levers and kick-shut rear gate latches.

papers.title: Cattle yards: design, materials and construction, Third Edition (Information series QE94009)
papers.authors: Evan Powell and John Lapworth, Queensland Department of Primary Industries and Fisheries
papers.source: Queensland Department of Primary Industries and Fisheries (hosted by FutureBeef)
papers.licence: Crown copyright (Queensland); free to download
papers.abstract: A 71-page government engineering manual and the richest dimensional source found, including the only explicit man-gate specification: manways preferably 400 mm wide with the opening not exceeding 500 mm, covered by a spring-loaded blank plate-steel door that opens into the working yard and butts the post so it cannot swing through, with a latch where stock are held in an adjoining yard. Advisory. Its safety section calls for easy operator escape avenues such as manways, foot holes and open rail construction, gates positioned to reduce the chance of workers getting stuck, strong positive self-latching gates, a walkway beside loading ramps, and in high-throughput yards plans that enable stock to be worked from outside forcing areas. Further dimensions cover top rail heights (1.7 m quiet to 2 m fractious), rail spacings (300 mm ground to bottom rail, then 250 and 250-280 mm), post diameters and embedment depths, race widths (680 mm vertical, up to 700 mm for large European breeds; V-race 450 mm at ground spreading to 690-700 mm at 1 m), race length by herd size from 3 m to 12 m, catwalks (1.1 m below top rail; loading-ramp catwalk minimum 500 mm wide), forcing pens (30-35 degree approach, rear gate 1.8-2.2 m, no wider than 3.5 m and 4-6 m long), yard space allowances (2, 1.8 and 2.5 square metres per head for holding, drafting and cooling yards) and loading ramps (1 in 4 slope, 1170 mm width, 400-500 mm tread with 100 mm rise, 5 m curve radius, 15 degree offset).

papers.title: Recommendations for the design of new, safe and efficient cattle handling systems (Technical Note TN565)
papers.authors: Scottish Agricultural College (SAC) / SRUC
papers.licence: © SRUC; free to download
papers.abstract: A six-page Scottish technical note written explicitly around maximising human and animal safety alongside movement efficiency, drawing on a survey of Scottish producers plus US and Australian research. Advisory. Its handler-protection rules include designating a cattle-free safe working area around the crush, enabling a handler to operate the head yoke while standing at the rear of the crush, fitting the forcing gate with an automatically catching non-return latch so it cannot be pressed back against the handler, controlling the sorting gate by a lever on a universal joint so the handler need not stand in front of the animal, and placing the raised walkway on the inside radius of a curved race. Dimensions: collecting pens of about 30 cows, roughly 15 m long by 3.5-4.0 m wide; forcing pens handling 8-10 cattle with a 3 m forcing gate and one wall converging at 30 degrees; race curve radius not below 5 m with a minimum 5 m section; race side height 1.52 m for British and 1.67-1.83 m for continental breeds; race width 40 mm wider than the largest animal, giving 660-710 mm for adult cows and 510 mm for calves, with 150 mm inserts for calves; at least 6 m of unobstructed space visible beyond the crush; sorting gates about 3 m long; and loading ramps limited by a 22 degree slip angle, remedied by a 0.5 m raised platform giving a maximum 15 degree (1 in 3.54) ramp, with 400 mm minimum stair tread width and a 1.5 m docking area.

papers.title: Livestock handling guidelines
papers.authors: SafeWork SA (Government of South Australia)
papers.licence: Crown copyright (South Australia); free to download
papers.abstract: A South Australian work-health-and-safety guidance sheet that treats yard design itself as the hazard, listing poor design that hinders animal flow or causes bottlenecks and blockages, ramps without suitable walkways, gates and access points, uneven surfaces, and poor maintenance of yards, ramps, fences and gates. Advisory. Its key control states the correct hierarchy for a design tool: install escape gates, bottom rails no less than 300 mm above the ground, and safety barriers if the separation of people and animals cannot be achieved. Further controls forbid loading cattle from inside the ramp, require that a ramp not allow limbs to be placed through the bars, ask whether gates can be opened externally, specify positive bolt slam-shut spring-loaded latches especially in forcing yards, and require a safety gate at the interface between transport vehicle and loading ramp. It cites AS 5340:2020 Livestock loading/unloading ramps and forcing pens, the authoritative but paywalled Australian dimensional standard. NOTE: verified via a third-party mirror because the safework.sa.gov.au copy returns HTTP 403.

papers.title: FarmSafe Plan Manual (AgSafe Alberta)
papers.authors: AgSafe Alberta
papers.licence: free to download
papers.abstract: The August 2023 edition of Alberta's industry farm safety management system, licensed by AgSafe Alberta from the Government of Alberta in 2019 and built around eight planning elements with hazard assessment as the first substantive module. It supplies the hazard-assessment machinery that OHS Code Part 2 would otherwise mandate but does not, because of the Code s.1.1 ranching exemption, and so is the practical route by which an Alberta ranch discharges the OHS Act s.3(1) general duty. Accompanying free downloads include Hazard Assessment Forms 1 and 2, a Hazard Identification Checklist and Hazard ID Cards, plus an Inspection Form and Report specifically for a Cattle Handling Facility (Word format, May 2025), which is the closest thing to an Alberta-sanctioned corral inspection template in existence. The manual specifies no dimensions and no facility design criteria.

papers.title: Toolbox Talk: Safer Animal Handling for People and Livestock (2022-ALL-0018)
papers.authors: AgSafe Alberta
papers.licence: free to download
papers.abstract: A two-page Alberta crew-briefing sheet, the most directly local advisory document on handling-facility condition. Advisory. Its facility content: non-slip flooring in holding and handling facilities keeps everyone on their feet, with grooved patterns in concrete preferred to rough broom finishes because broom finishes wear smooth over time; gates, fences and chutes should be checked for sharp edges, weaknesses and damage, since a protruding nail injures worker or animal and a gate that cannot close when needed can have severe consequences. It also covers the 20-30 minutes an excited animal needs to settle, restricting work to trained handlers familiar with livestock behaviour, staying out of the blind spot, not chasing escaped cattle, scheduling handling around heat and cold stress, and lighting and noise effects on movement including shadows causing refusal. It specifies no dimensions.

papers.title: Toolbox Talk: Loading and Unloading Livestock
papers.authors: AgSafe Alberta
papers.licence: free to download
papers.abstract: An Alberta crew-briefing sheet covering the loading and unloading task, which every national source identifies as among the most dangerous activities in a yard. Advisory, with no dimensions. It is the Alberta-local counterpart to the ramp and loading-area guidance in HSE AIS35, the Irish HSA marts and lairages sheet and SafeWork SA, and is useful as the locally recognised reference when a corral-design tool flags a loading area that requires a person to stand between animal and vehicle.

papers.title: Handling Livestock Safely (Agdex 086-4)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Forestry
papers.source: Canadian Agricultural Safety Association (CASA) SafetyShop library
papers.licence: free to download
papers.abstract: CASA's livestock-handling factsheet, authored by Alberta Agriculture and Forestry in March 2004 and the national safety association's only livestock-handling resource. Advisory and behaviour-based rather than facility-based, it supplies the quantified animal-behaviour parameters a corral-design tool needs for its flow model: the flight zone of a range cow may be as large as 90 metres (300 ft) against 1.5 to 7.5 metres (5 to 25 ft) for a feedlot animal; the point of balance sits at the shoulder; there is a blind spot directly behind where animals will usually kick; and a stressed animal takes 20 to 30 minutes to calm. Its facility-relevant notes are that solid sides on handling facilities prevent animals seeing distractions, that animals balk at changes in flooring surface or texture, and that shadows and bright spots should be minimised. It reports that on average half of all farm-related injuries in Alberta involve large animals. It specifies no dimensions and no handler escape provision.

papers.title: MP239 Cattle Working Facilities
papers.authors: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, Cooperative Extension Service (adapted in part from R. Gill and R. Machen, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)
papers.source: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, publication MP239-PD-7-2015-RV
papers.licence: free-to-read publisher PDF (US land-grant extension publication; no explicit open licence)
papers.abstract: The most complete single extension document for ranch-scale corral dimensions, in the imperial units the ranch thinks in, and the only one giving a full Bud Box dimension table alongside the classic working-facility table. Table 2 gives holding area 14/18/20 sq ft per head, crowding pen 6/10/12 sq ft per head, straight-sided working chute 18/22/26 inches at a minimum 20 ft length, sloping-sided chute bottom 15/15/16 inches and 20/24/28 inches at 4 ft height, chute and corral fence heights split by gentle versus wild cattle up to 72 inches, and loading chute width, length and rise plus ramp heights by vehicle type. The footnote gives the bull answer: add 4 inches to chute widths for bulls over 2,000-2,200 lb and cows over 1,300-1,400 lb. Table 1 gives Bud Box width and depth by handler mode (12 ft and minimum 20 ft on foot; 14 ft and 20-30 ft afoot and horseback; 16 ft and maximum 30 ft horseback).
