The text supplies crowd-alley capacity rules, the 12 ft two-mature-cow-body-lengths straight exit rule, the adjustable-alley range of 18-30 inches, the statement that calf injury occurs when calves can turn around in an alley sized for mature cattle, the 'never fill a crowding pen more than three-quarters full' guideline, the isolation passage ('Many serious cattle-handling accidents have been caused by isolated, frantic cattle... A gentle calf will keep an excited calf calm'), and the rule that cows and preweaned calves must not be worked through the facility together.

papers.title: Cattle Behavior and Handling Facility Design for Feedlots
papers.authors: Grandin, Temple (Iowa Beef Center, Iowa State University)
papers.source: Iowa Beef Center, Iowa State University
papers.licence: free-to-read publisher PDF (university extension; no explicit open licence)
papers.abstract: The verified-PDF vehicle through which many of Grandin's observational rules reach producers, and therefore what a ranch crew has probably already read. Carries the flight-zone diagram, the point of balance, the blind spot behind, 'cattle have poor depth perception when they are moving with their heads up', the drain-grate rule ('Draining grates in the middle of the floor will make cattle balk. A good drainage design is to slope the concrete floor in the squeeze chute area toward an open drainage ditch located outside the fences'), the snow-fence shade warning ('The zebra stripe shadows can cause balking'), the single-shadow warning ('A single shadow that falls across a scale or loading chute can disrupt handling'), the rule to extend the single-file chute 10 to 15 feet outside a building, and a full dimension set: crowd pen radius 12 ft recommended and 10 ft minimum, 30 degree funnel side, V-race 16-18 inch bottom and 32-36 inch top, straight race 26 inches for cows and 18-20 for calves, alleys 10 ft on foot, 12 ft foot plus horse and 14-16 ft horses only, ramp slope up to 20 degrees, stair rise 10 cm and tread 30-45 cm, solid belly rail 45 cm. Notably it carries neither the 45-60 degree handler angle nor any flight-zone figure in metres. Also recommends a straight rather than curved race where the race is used exclusively for loading.

papers.title: Livestock Psychology and Handling-Facility Design
papers.authors: Iowa Beef Center, Iowa State University
papers.source: Iowa Beef Center, Iowa State University
papers.licence: free-to-read publisher PDF (university extension; no explicit open licence)
papers.abstract: Companion extension handout to the feedlot behaviour sheet, covering crowd-pen and race layout rules plus the 20 degree maximum for non-adjustable livestock ramps, which it attributes to Grandin (1979). Useful mainly as an independent restatement of the same conventional dimension set, which helps establish where the published numbers agree and where they drift.

papers.title: Livestock Handling Guide
papers.authors: Grandin, Temple (industry guide, hosted by Ohio State University Dairy Extension)
papers.source: Meat and Poultry industry guide, hosted by Ohio State University
papers.licence: unknown (free-to-read, university-hosted)
papers.abstract: Sets 20 degrees as the maximum for permanent loading ramps and 25 degrees for portable or adjustable ramps, with lighting, flooring and crowd-pen guidance alongside. Included as an independent cross-check on the ramp-angle convention, which is otherwise carried entirely by Grandin's own publications and by extension sheets derived from them.

papers.title: Livestock Handling Facilities (Illinois Grazing Manual fact sheet)
papers.authors: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
papers.licence: US federal government work - effectively public domain
papers.abstract: A US federal agency design sheet with layout drawings and dimensions. Its value here is one independent number: it specifies a minimum curved-race radius of 15 ft (approximately 4.6 m), which is a useful cross-check on Grandin's 3.5-6 m band and sits at the upper end of it. Being a federal work, it is the only design-standard document in this set that is unambiguously free to redistribute.

papers.title: Beef Cattle Production Handbook, Chapter 11: Facilities (MP184)
papers.authors: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, Cooperative Extension Service
papers.source: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, publication MP184
papers.licence: free-to-read publisher PDF (US land-grant extension; no explicit open licence)
papers.abstract: A secondary extension reproduction of the same MWPS-derived working-facility dimensions as MP239 and Kentucky ID-13, inside a broader beef production handbook. Included only as a cross-check: where three or four independent extension services publish the same table with different numbers, the designer is on safer ground presenting a band than a single value. Superseded for working purposes by MP239 from the same institution.

papers.title: Cattle handling design principles (Meat Technology Update 99/5)
papers.authors: CSIRO Meat Industry Services
papers.source: CSIRO Meat Industry Services, Meat Technology Update 99/5
papers.licence: CSIRO publication; terms unknown
papers.abstract: A short CSIRO technical bulletin setting out crowd-pen, race and ramp principles. Like the Queensland manual it states that in a race cattle will more readily follow a curved path than a straight one, as expert recommendation with no underlying experiment cited - which matters because CSIRO is in the same country and research tradition as the Vowles abstracts that are the only measured source, one of which found no significant difference.

papers.title: Welfare Quality Assessment Protocol for Cattle
papers.authors: Welfare Quality Consortium
papers.licence: free-to-read publisher PDF
papers.abstract: The on-farm welfare assessment protocol whose 'avoidance distance at the feeding place' measure is the only fully standardised, reliability-tested flight-distance instrument in the literature. It specifies the method to the centimetre: start 3 m directly in front of the animal with its head through the feed rack, or up to 45 degrees to the rack from 3.5 m; approach at one step per second with steps of about 60 cm; hold the arm overhand at about 45 degrees from the body with the back of the hand toward the animal; make no eye contact, looking at the muzzle; walk until withdrawal or until you touch the muzzle; record hand-to-muzzle distance at 10 cm resolution over the range 300 cm down to 10 cm, or 0 cm if touchable. Individual bands are 0, under 50 cm, 50-100 cm and over 100 cm, weighted 0:3:11:26 into a herd index. Note its ceiling: 3 m. There is no validated instrument anywhere near the 50 m range-cow claim, and this protocol is the right basis for an on-ranch flight-zone calibration procedure.

papers.title: A critical review of fear tests used on cattle, pigs, sheep, poultry and horses
papers.authors: Forkman, Björn; Boissy, Alain; Meunier-Salaün, Marie-Christine; Canali, Elisabetta; Jones, R. Bryan
papers.licence: green open access repository copy (HAL INRAE); publisher version Elsevier
papers.abstract: A systematic critical review of the fear-test literature across farm species, with species-by-species tables of test type, measures recorded and correlations. It establishes the taxonomy needed before reading any flight-zone claim: the Forced Approach Test, in which the human approaches and which is what flight distance measures, versus the Voluntary Approach Test, in which the animal is free to approach. Quoting Waiblinger et al., it warns that the forced approach test 'would probably increase the likelihood that an animal will respond more actively to the human whereas in the voluntary approach test, the chances of getting no response or a passive response would probably be higher', and that researchers 'tend to use forced vs. voluntary approach tests uncritically'. It also records the Hargreaves and Hutson finding that gentling reduced sheep flight distance and heart rate yet failed to reduce aversion to shearing - the reason a small flight zone must not be read as a welfare pass.

papers.title: Researching Human-Cattle Interaction on Rangelands: Challenges and Potential Solutions
papers.authors: Creamer, Maggie; Horback, Kristina
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: The paper closest to a southern Alberta cow-calf operation. It argues that the entire human-animal-relationship toolkit was built for confined cattle and does not transfer to rangeland, then proposes range-specific protocols: approach tests started at 10 m with the start distance adjusted to the herd's flight-zone sensitivity; human-presence tests with an unfamiliar person within 10 m for 10 minutes; restraint tests starting 10 m away attempting to move the cow into a 2 m by 2 m marked area; testing during midday rest and drinking, near water and shade, or along grazing routes. It catalogues the existing measures and their flaws - chute score 1 to 6, explicitly subjective; exit velocity; the pen-corner docility test - and notes that domestication selected for reduced flight zones while producers deliberately retain a robust flight zone so cattle can still be herded. Critically, it gives NO numeric flight distance for range cattle: it treats that as the open problem, which is the strongest single argument against hard-coding the 50 m figure.

papers.title: Effect of light on dairy cattle in farm conditions - a review
papers.authors: Adamczyk, Krzysztof; Herbut, Piotr; Godyń, Dorota; Angrecka, Sabina; Kupczyński, Robert; Vieira, Frederico Márcio Corrêa
papers.licence: CC-BY-NC-ND (Sciendo open access) - check before redistributing
papers.abstract: The most citation-dense and freely verifiable source on bovine vision numbers found, and where the key acuity conversion lives: cattle visual acuity is approximately 1.3-2.5 cycles per degree against human acuity of 32.1-44.2 cpd in bright conditions, i.e. cattle resolve roughly one-twentieth of the spatial detail a human does. Also carries dichromacy with S- and ML-cones (Jacobs 1998); long versus short and medium discrimination but not short versus medium (Phillips and Lomas 2001); the horizontal oval pupil and horizontally aligned visual streak with vertical stimuli better detected (Rehkämper 2000; Brooks 1999; Kassab and Sugita 2000); a 'predominantly monocular visual field, with only a minor central binocular area' and pointedly no degree figure; the choroidal tapetum fibrosum boosting dim-light sensitivity; 80-87% contralateral visual pathways and a left-eye bias for novel stimuli; the statement that 'due to limited visual acuity, shadows can appear as holes to cows'; Lindkvist 2023's finding that cows navigate well even in darkness; Hirata 2019's 2 m field-discrimination limit; the 50% inside/outside intensity disparity threshold (Marciniak 2008); and the Danish working, orientation and night lighting tables of 100/25/5 and 200/25/5 lux.

papers.title: Effects of achromatic and chromatic lights on pupillary response, endocrinology, activity, and milk production in dairy cows
papers.authors: Lindkvist, Sofia; Ternman, Emma; Ferneborg, Sabine; Bånkestad, Daniel; Lindqvist, Jonatan; Ekesten, Björn; Agenäs, Sigrid
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: Measures bovine pupillary response under achromatic and chromatic lights alongside endocrine, activity and production outcomes. Included because it is the nearest verifiable approach to adaptation data for cattle, and because the claim that 'cattle adapt slowly to rapid changes in lighting' is asserted in every recent review but measured in none that could be reached - the bovine ERG literature does not report a recovery curve. This paper is the place to start if the ranch wants to pursue that gap, and the reason the designer should not encode a dark-adaptation time constant.

papers.title: A Novel Protocol to Assess Acclimation Rate in Bos taurus Heifers during Yard Weaning
papers.authors: Monk, Jessica E.; Hine, Brad C.; Colditz, Ian G.; Lee, Caroline
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: CSIRO work proposing that repeated flight-time measurement during yard weaning quantifies an animal's acclimation rate - how quickly it habituates to handling in a given facility - rather than a static temperament score. This shifts the question from 'is this animal flighty?' to 'does this yard let cattle settle?', which is the question a corral designer actually wants answered. Directly applicable to a cow-calf operation's weaning pens, where cattle meet the facility only a handful of times a year, and the right construct to pair with Lockwood et al. 2015's finding that exit velocity falls 40% over four handlings while pen score barely moves.

papers.title: How Farm Animals React and Perceive Stressful Situations Such As Handling, Restraint, and Transport
papers.authors: Grandin, Temple; Shivley, Chelsey
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: An open-access review of how cattle, sheep and pigs perceive handling and restraint, useful mainly for calibrating expectations about effect sizes. Physiological stress after handling and restraint is highly variable, ranging from near baseline to extremely high between individuals, so a facility effect will be buried in animal variation unless sample sizes are large. Isolation from herd or flock mates is highly stressful to both sheep and cattle, which is the motivational basis for the 'they move back toward their herdmates' rule. Reactive temperaments show higher cortisol, glucose and lactate and more agitation, and an animal carefully acclimated to handling may re-enter a restrainer willingly with very low cortisol.

papers.title: Cattle and Pigs Are Easy to Move and Handle Will Have Less Preslaughter Stress
papers.authors: Grandin, Temple
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: A short open-access review arguing that ease of movement at the facility is itself a welfare and meat-quality indicator. It names the distraction set - sharp shadows on the floor, reflections on shiny metal, a noisy vehicle near the lairage, air blowing out through the stun-box entrance toward approaching cattle - citing Willson et al. 2021, Grandin 2001 and Grandin 1996, and reports that illuminating a dark restrainer entrance facilitated cattle movement. Its most informative feature for this project is an absence: checked specifically, it contains no curved-versus-straight race content and no solid-sides content at all, which is itself evidence of how thin that part of the evidence base is in the author's own most recent work.

papers.title: Auditing animal welfare and making practical improvements in beef-, pork- and sheep-slaughter plants
papers.authors: Grandin, Temple
papers.source: Animal Welfare 21(S2):29-34 (Humane Slaughter Association Centenary International Symposium proceedings)
papers.licence: CC-BY-NC-SA (open access)
papers.abstract: Sets out the numerical audit framework and reports audit results, and is valuable here because it gives defensible pass/fail numbers inside an openly licensed paper. In 32 beef plants, cattle vocalising in the stunning area was 5% or less, with a pass threshold of 5% or less for cattle and pigs. Falling must be 1% or less to pass: 94% of beef plants and 86% of pork plants had zero falls, with a worst score of 2%. All 30 North American plants in one group stunned at least 95% of cattle with a single captive-bolt shot. Electric-goad use is a named critical control point. It discusses the practical fixes that reduce balking - lighting, noise reduction, visual barriers - without giving balking percentages.

papers.title: Effects of drylot dimension and group size on growth, physiological, and puberty responses of replacement beef heifers
papers.authors: Prado, C. P.; Cooke, R. F.; Mackey, S. J.; Pickett, A. T.; Monteiro, G. A.; de Souza, I. S.; Daigle, C. L.; Harvey, K. M.
papers.licence: CC-BY (no reachable PDF endpoint; Oxford Academic blocks automated requests, full text available as XML via Europe PMC REST)
papers.abstract: The study that shows why a per-head area check is not sufficient on its own, and a rare controlled measurement on pen geometry. 240 heifers (75% Angus by 25% Brahman, 270 days, 232 kg) were assigned to 10 by 14 m drylot pens with 10 heifers (14 m2 per heifer), 10 by 28 m drylot pens with 20 heifers (also 14 m2 per heifer), or 1.38 ha pastures - so the two drylot treatments held space per head constant while varying absolute pen dimension and group size. Body weight gain did not differ (about 0.635 kg per day, P=0.67). But hair cortisol was higher in both drylots than on pasture on days 30 and 170, and higher in the small pen than in both the large pen and pasture on day 58; heat shock protein HSP-70 and HSP-72 mRNA expression were higher in the small pen; and puberty rate was higher in the larger pen than the small one from weeks 13-16 and 18-22. The authors conclude that increasing drylot dimension and group size attenuated physiological stress responses. For the designer this means pens should be checked against a minimum absolute dimension as well as m2 per head - two pens at the same allowance per animal are not equivalent.

papers.title: Exploring dairy heifers' consistency in social motivation in the absence or presence of conspecifics
papers.authors: Kappel, Sarah; Nogues, Emeline; Weary, Daniel M.; von Keyserlingk, Marina A. G.
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: University of British Columbia work, and a necessary brake on any attempt to score individual animals for isolation tolerance. 36 Holstein heifers were put through standardised social-isolation tests (novel arena, novel object and runway, each tested twice 14 days apart) plus a novel social-feed trade-off paradigm and a distribution test. The authors found no consistency between sociability measures derived from behaviour in the absence of conspecifics (vocalization, runway latency) and those derived in their presence (feeding time, social-feed trade-off score), and behaviours showed low repeatability even within the same social context. They conclude that individual differences in sociability are likely context-dependent and that sociability 'might not be a single trait, but rather a behavioral consequence'. The implication for software: an animal's isolation response cannot be predicted from a prior test, so a lone-animal rule must apply to every animal rather than to a flagged subset.

papers.title: Effects of Nose Flap and Bovine Appeasing Substance on Growth, Physiological and Behavioural Responses of Beef Calves
papers.authors: Santos, M.; Oliveira, D. M.; de Souza, M. R.; Almeida, G. B.; Santos, A. R. D.; Belmonte, J. C. C.; Melo-Sterza, F.-A.; Ferraz, A. L. J.; Vedovatto, M.
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: The second nose-flap study, and the one that ties weaning method back to corral behaviour. 24 Nellore calves in a 2 by 2 factorial, nose flaps fitted 14 days before weaning versus none, crossed with a bovine-appeasing substance versus none. The nose flap reduced average daily gain (-0.289 versus 0.378 plus or minus 0.13 kg per day, P at most 0.01), reduced rumination time, and increased the chute exit score on days 14 and 28 - that is, it produced measurably worse temperament at the handling chute. The appeasing substance increased average daily gain (0.487 versus -0.08 plus or minus 0.10 kg per day) and tended to reduce exit score and vocalising time. Neither affected serum rabies titre. The conclusion is that nose flaps reduced growth and increased stress after weaning. Read with Valente et al. 2022 and the fenceline study, the net recommendation for a cow-calf ranch is fenceline separation rather than nose flaps.

papers.title: Relationships among temperament, behavior, and growth during performance testing of bulls
papers.authors: Lockwood, S. A.; Kattesh, H. G.; Krawczel, P. D.; Kirkpatrick, F. D.; Saxton, A. M.; Rhinehart, J. D.; Wilkerson, J. B.
papers.licence: free-to-read publisher PDF hosted by University of Tennessee Extension (ASAS copyright)
papers.abstract: The cleanest controlled measurement of habituation to a handling facility, in Angus cattle, and therefore directly transferable to a southern Alberta herd. 60 Angus bulls in six pens were pen-scored (1 docile to 5 very aggressive) on days -1, 27, 55 and 83 and run through a chute on days 0, 28, 56 and 84, with exit velocity timed over a fixed 1.83 m between infrared sensors and IceTag dataloggers on the fetlock recording steps, lying time and lying bouts. Exit velocity fell from 2.57 m/s on day 0 to 1.92, 1.59 and 1.53 m/s on days 28, 56 and 84 (P<0.05) - a 40% decline - while pen score barely changed (2.26 to 2.13); every bull exited more slowly on day 84 than day 0 (P<0.001). Pen-score-excitable bulls had greater frame score, average daily gain and backfat; exit-velocity-excitable bulls had smaller ribeye area. The authors attribute the exit-velocity decline to habituation and conclude that temperament must be reassessed in a novel environment with new handlers to separate true temperament from the ability to habituate. The practical lesson for a design tool: exit velocity moves, chute and pen scores do not, so use exit velocity if the app ever logs temperament.

papers.title: Effects of acclimation to human interaction on performance, temperament, physiological responses, and pregnancy rates of Brahman-crossbred cows
papers.authors: Cooke, R. F.; Arthington, J. D.; Araujo, D. B.; Lamb, G. C.
papers.licence: free-to-read publisher PDF hosted by Oregon State (ASAS copyright)
papers.abstract: An important null result, and a direct caution against promising users that gentling will fix their flight speed. 395 Braford and Brahman by British cows over two consecutive years. Acclimated groups were visited twice weekly for 15 minutes from weaning in August to breeding in January by the same handler, who walked among the cows and hand-offered 0.05 kg of range cubes (deliberately nutritionally meaningless); controls stayed undisturbed on pasture. There was no treatment effect on chute score (P=0.94), pen score (P=0.59), exit velocity (P=0.88), composite temperament score (P=0.12), cortisol (P=0.68), haptoglobin (P=0.57) or IGF-I, yet acclimated Braford cows conceived earlier and at a higher rate in year 1 (P<0.01). Pearson correlations among cortisol, chute score, exit velocity and pen score ranged 0.34 to 0.75, all P<0.01. Low-intensity, non-chute acclimation changed reproduction but not the handling measures. The paper also documents the exit-score method, in which exit velocity is split into within-day quintiles with 1 the slowest.

papers.title: Adrenergic tone as an intermediary in the temperament syndrome associated with flight speed in beef cattle
papers.authors: Colditz, Ian G.
papers.licence: open access (Frontiers, CC-BY family)
papers.abstract: A CSIRO review of flight speed as a temperament measure and of the physiological syndrome around it. Documents the measurement standard - flight time over 1.7 m after release from the crush, by the method of Burrow et al. (1988), converted to m/s - alongside the older subjective scales (Hearnshaw et al. 0-5; Fordyce et al. 1-7 movement score). Reports that within-group rankings are fairly stable, especially for high-flight-speed animals; that temperamental cattle show elevated basal cortisol and epinephrine; and that higher flight speed is associated with higher muscle lactate, lower fat cover, lower intramuscular fat, higher pH and higher shear force. A narrative review, so it gives direction rather than effect sizes.

papers.title: Flooring options to minimize lameness and optimize welfare
papers.authors: Rushen, Jeffrey; de Passillé, Anne Marie (Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Agassiz BC)
papers.source: WCDS Advances in Dairy Technology 21:293-301 (University of Alberta)
papers.licence: free-to-read conference proceedings PDF (University of Alberta WCDS)
papers.abstract: The best free, Canadian-authored synthesis of cattle flooring and traction, reviewed by NFACC's Scientist Committee, and the fastest route into the primary flooring literature. It states the three design conclusions a corral checker needs: flooring must be both compressible and high-traction; compressibility reduces slip risk more than surface friction does (Rushen and de Passille 2006, 16 cows over purpose-built walkways); and slurry on the floor reduces walking speed, makes cattle avoid the passage, raises slip and fall risk, increases the need for handlers to intervene - which directly reduces handling efficiency - and does its worst damage at starts, corners and obstacles, with added non-slip material not necessarily fixing it. It also tabulates the epidemiology: lameness prevalence 1% on straw yards, 20.1% solid concrete, 27.4% slatted concrete and 40.6% grooved concrete (Frankena et al. 2008); hoof disease 19.8% on concrete versus 2.9% on earth; sole haemorrhage 44.6% on concrete slats versus 4.6% on straw; and Bell's 2004 British Columbia finding that large floor cracks and holes explain 15% of between-farm lesion variation. The design message is that grooving buys traction for handling at a measurable cost in standing surfaces, so groove the handling alleys and crowd pen, not the loafing areas.

papers.title: The effect of mud on cattle motivation for feedlot or pasture environments (final report B.FLT.0158)
papers.authors: Lee, Caroline; Lea, Jim; Thomson, Peter; Pool, Kelsey; Colditz, Ian (CSIRO)
papers.source: Meat & Livestock Australia Limited, final report B.FLT.0158
papers.licence: MLA copyright - the report states reproduction in whole or part is prohibited without prior written consent, so cite and link rather than redistribute
papers.abstract: A Y-maze preference experiment giving a clear, usable dose-response for mud underfoot. 60 cattle in two cohorts per pad score, with pad scores 1, 3 and 5 created artificially by hosing and stocking and defined against the Queensland feedlot pad class system (mud depth relative to hoof and leg), with IceQube fetlock accelerometers recording behaviour. Lying time was 9 hours 38 minutes at pad score 1 versus 7 hours 43 minutes at pad score 3.5 (P<0.0001) - nearly two hours of lying lost. Lying bouts were 12.2 per day versus 7.3 per day (P<0.0001). Standing and steps both changed significantly with pad score. Cattle lay 42 minutes per day longer in the paddock than the feedlot (P=0.0004). Preference for pasture was shown only when the feedlot was dry; at higher pad scores cattle showed no preference either way. The honest caveat is that depth was set by visual assessment against the class system rather than measured in millimetres - the published companion paper (Dickson et al. 2022) supplies the physical threshold, which is mud past the fetlock.

papers.title: A Novel Method of Assessing Floor Friction in Cowsheds and Its Association with Cow Health
papers.authors: Sharma, Arvind; Kennedy, Uttara; Phillips, Clive J. C.
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: A field-usable friction test applied across 54 cattle housing and yard facilities (earth, brick, concrete, stone) with 30 animals assessed per facility. Coefficient of friction ranged from 0.3 to 0.7, lowest on concrete and highest on earth. Higher-friction floors were associated with cows standing more and - the finding that matters most for a handling facility - being easier to approach, as well as with fewer cows having dirty hind limbs. That approachability result is the only direct behavioural link found between measured footing friction and handling, and it supports treating traction as a handling variable rather than only a lameness one. Useful alongside van der Tol et al.'s required-coefficient-of-friction concept, which establishes that concrete fails to supply enough friction during sudden stops and starts.

papers.title: Transporting cattle in 2020: research and regulation
papers.authors: Schwartzkopf-Genswein, Karen S. and colleagues (Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Lethbridge Research and Development Centre)
papers.source: WCDS Advances in Dairy Technology, pp. 107-118 (University of Alberta)
papers.licence: free-to-read conference proceedings PDF (University of Alberta WCDS)
papers.abstract: AAFC Lethbridge review, and the source of the one hard Canadian cold-weather number found anywhere in this review: González et al. (2012) reported that death in commercial cattle transported more than 400 km increased significantly when ambient temperature went below -15 C, while non-ambulatory risk rose above +30 C. Also reports Goldhawk et al. (2015) on winter transport of cull beef cows, where boarding raised in-transit ventilation but reduced ventilation and raised internal temperature and humidity during stationary periods - a reminder that stationary periods are where winter microclimate goes wrong, which applies equally to cattle held in a corral. Notes that bedding is required on journeys over 12 hours under CFIA 2019, that shrink rises about 0.04% per degree C of ambient temperature, and that calves and cull cows lose more than feeders.

papers.title: Contemporary Knowledge on the Assessment of Temperament in Cattle and Its Impact on Production and Reproduction Including Some Immunological, Genetic and Metabolic Parameters
papers.authors: Jaśkowski, Bartłomiej M. and colleagues
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0
papers.abstract: A review of cattle temperament assessment, and the source of the measured flight-distance figures that should anchor the designer's default band rather than Grandin's 50 m observation. It defines flight distance as the distance at which a cow retreats from an observer, recorded as 0 m if she does not withdraw, and reports a mean flight distance of 1.6 m with a range of 0 to 6.5 m. It is also candid that flight-distance tests are 'difficult and time-consuming and, therefore, rarely used in practice', which explains why the measured literature is so thin relative to the confidence with which flight-zone numbers circulate.

papers.title: The influence of yard design on the movement of animals
papers.authors: Vowles, W. J.; Hollier, T. J.
papers.source: Proceedings of the Australian Society of Animal Production 14:597
papers.licence: unknown
papers.abstract: A one-page conference abstract, and the sole positive experimental source for the curved-race recommendation and for the much-quoted figure that circular crowding pens and curved races can reduce the time spent moving cattle by up to 50%. When cattle were queued waiting to enter a squeeze chute, the curved system was faster than the alternative. Two caveats make it weak evidence for curvature specifically: the comparison was of a complete package - a round crowd pen plus a curved race - so the curve is confounded with crowd-pen shape and fencing; and at one page its methods, sample size and statistics cannot be assessed. It also supplies, jointly with Grandin 1980, the recommended 3.5-6 m inside radius. Anyone encoding a curved-race rule in software should know that this is the paper it rests on, and should read it alongside Vowles et al. 1984a, which found no significant difference.

papers.title: The behaviour and movement of cattle through single-file races
papers.authors: Vowles, W. J.; Eldridge, G. A.; Hollier, T. J.
papers.source: Proceedings of the Australian Society of Animal Production 15:767
papers.licence: unknown
papers.abstract: The direct head-to-head test of straight versus curved single-file races, and it is a null result: with continuously moving livestock there was no significant difference between straight and curved races in run-through time. Grandin reports this herself in her 1997 review and reconciles it with the 1982 positive result by arguing that the curve helps only when animals are queued rather than moving continuously. A one-page conference abstract, so the sample, the race dimensions and the statistics cannot be inspected. This is the paper to cite when asked whether a straight race should be flagged as a layout fault - it says it should not, and the popular literature consistently omits it. No free PDF exists and no catalogue record was located; the citation is transcribed from the reference list of Grandin 1997.

papers.title: Cattle handling (Livestock Buildings Consultancy)
papers.authors: Meat and Livestock Commission, Livestock Buildings Consultancy, Queensway, Bletchley, Milton Keynes, England
papers.licence: unknown
papers.abstract: Listed for provenance of the project's single most-asked question. This undated industry pamphlet is the primary and only source for the 30 degree asymmetric funnel rule: Grandin 1997 cites it, and only it, for 'one side should be straight and the other side should be on a 30 degree angle', and her later web pages repeat the attribution. No experiment, trial, measurement or dataset behind the rule was found, from the Meat and Livestock Commission or anyone else. The practical answer is therefore that the 30 degree figure is conventional engineering wisdom from a now-defunct UK marketing board's buildings advisory service - the MLC was dissolved in 2008 and its Livestock Buildings Consultancy outputs do not appear to be archived online - repeated for three decades because it works in practice and nobody has tested it. The app should implement it, since it is the industry standard and the mechanism is plausible, but should label it as convention and emphasise the asymmetry rather than the exact angle, since nothing in any source distinguishes 30 degrees from 25 or 35. Year is recorded as 1980 as an approximation only; the publication carries no date, and no landing page or archived copy was located.

papers.title: Luminance and glare in indoor cattle-handling facilities
papers.authors: Klinglmair, K.; Stevens, K. B.; Gregory, Neville G.
papers.licence: unknown (paywalled; Cambridge redirects the PDF path to HTML and purchase is listed as temporarily unavailable)
papers.abstract: The best-quantified light-and-balking result in the whole literature, and the natural basis for a glare-geometry check in a corral designer. The authors surveyed sources of glare and the range of luminance in eleven UK cattle abattoirs, then experimentally manipulated reflected glare from a footbath in a dairy milking parlour. Mean luminance fell from 240,000 cd/m2 outdoors to 100 cd/m2 in the stunning pen - a drop of roughly 2,400 to 1 along the animal's path. In five of the eleven abattoirs, glare off wet floor surfaces was three times the luminance of adjacent darker areas and glare off shiny metal was ten times. In the parlour experiment, balking frequency rose significantly from 10% to 23% when reflected glare increased from 0 with no bulb to 873 cd/m2 with a 100 W bulb, and significantly fewer animals balked at the afternoon than the morning milking. Note that it reports luminance in cd/m2 only, with no lux values, so the units must not be converted loosely in software. This is the only controlled glare manipulation found, and it roughly doubled balking.

papers.title: The effect of approach direction and pace on flight distance of beef breeding cows
papers.authors: Kosako, T.; Fukasawa, M.; Kohari, D.; Oikawa, K.; Tsukada, H.
papers.licence: unknown (Wiley, closed access)
papers.abstract: The only controlled experiment on approach geometry versus flight distance that could be located, and it contradicts the standard claim in the handling literature. Five Japanese Black breeding cows were tested under a factorial design crossing three approach directions - FRONT toward the head, SIDE toward the foreleg and BACK diagonally toward a hind leg - with three paces of 1, 4 and 7 km/h, with flight distance defined as the shortest observer-to-cow distance at the moment of withdrawal. The flight distance in FRONT was significantly SHORTER than that in SIDE, and the faster an observer approached, the greater the flight distance. This directly contradicts the widely repeated claim that the flight zone is larger head-on, which Grandin attributes to Bud Williams by personal communication and which extension material states without citation. Caveats are real: n=5, one breed, tame breeding stock. But the designer should not hard-code 'head-on means a bigger flight zone' as established fact, and the pace effect is the robust, defensible half of the result. The authors' own conclusion is that the manner of approach must be standardised before flight-distance results can be shared between researchers.

papers.title: The movement of farmed red deer through raceways
papers.authors: Grigor, C. M.; Goddard, P. J.; Littlewood, C. A.
papers.licence: unknown (Elsevier, closed access)
papers.abstract: The cleanest factorial experiment on race geometry in any ruminant, and its message is that the design literature's priorities are backwards. Eight groups of six farmed red deer were each tested on all eight combinations of race width (0.5 m versus 1.5 m), race shape (straight versus curved) and light intensity (bright versus dim). Width dominated: entry time was 6.9 s narrow versus 2.7 s wide (P<0.001), with more overlapping of individuals in wide races. Race shape produced a significantly shorter latency to enter curved races than straight races (P<0.05) but had no significant effect on moving time or inter-animal spacing. Light intensity had no significant effect on moving time or spacing. The species caveat is real - deer are far more flighty than cattle - but this is the only study putting curvature, width and light in the same model, and it says width matters roughly 2.5 times more than shape while light intensity, as opposed to glare, matters not at all. Both nulls are directly useful to a designer deciding what to flag.

papers.title: Evaluation of Handling Equipment Sound Pressure Levels as Stressors in Beef Cattle
papers.authors: Lyvers, Christina M.
papers.source: MSc thesis, Biosystems and Agricultural Engineering, University of Kentucky (UKnowledge)
papers.licence: free-to-read institutional repository (the advertised full-text download URL returns 403 to automated requests; exact terms unknown)
papers.abstract: The only study that varied sound level and frequency systematically in cattle, and it is a null result that matters. 18 beef animals were exposed over six weeks to recorded sounds at two frequencies (1 kHz and 8 kHz) and three intensities (40, 80 and 120 dB), with heart rate, eye temperature and sudden movement measured. Results were mixed and the author concluded that none of the sound pressure levels tested clearly affected cattle stress. This is an important counterweight to the 'over 85 dB' threshold that Grandin's 2021 review attributes to this very thesis - the review asserts a threshold the underlying data do not demonstrate. The thesis is also the source of the frequently cited figure that commercial handling systems reach 99-115 dB. A designer should therefore flag noise sources and equipment types rather than enforce a decibel cut-off.

papers.title: Factors that impede animal movement at slaughter plants
papers.authors: Grandin, Temple
papers.source: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association 209(4):757-759 (with companion American Association of Bovine Practitioners Proceedings 29:22-26)
papers.licence: free-to-read author-hosted HTML at grandin.com (journal version unknown)
papers.abstract: The origin of the distraction checklist, and the only source giving frequencies for balking causes - based on a survey of Canadian slaughter operations, 33 for distractions and 29 systems for floors. Lighting too dim or too bright caused excessive balking in 5 of 33 operations (15%); ventilation air blowing toward approaching animals in 3 of 33 (9%); seeing movement or sparkling reflections in 8 of 33 (24%); high-pitched motor noise or hissing air exhausts in 8 of 33 (24%), of which five were hissing air and three motor whine. Air hissing from control valves caused balking in 4 of 12 beef plants (33%). Floors: 8 of 29 (27%) had excellent grip, 15 (52%) acceptable, and 6 (21%) were slick and unacceptable. Two plants (9%) had distractions severe enough that handlers prodded constantly. Note what is named as a distraction but given no frequency figure: shadows, drain grates, and changes of fencing or flooring type - so those rules remain observation even in the one paper that counts things. The conclusion is that simple changes to lighting and the elimination of air drafts and hissing greatly improve movement. Free full text with the survey tables is hosted on grandin.com as HTML, not PDF.

papers.title: Assessment of stress during handling and transport
papers.authors: Grandin, Temple
papers.licence: free-to-read author-hosted HTML at grandin.com (journal version paywalled)
papers.abstract: The reference table of cortisol values for cattle handling, which is what lets a designer say whether a layout fault costs anything physiological. Baselines 0.5-9 ng/mL; headgate restraint 13 (hand-reared Holsteins, Lay et al. 1992a) to 63 (Mitchell et al. 1988); Angus by Hereford steers 28 versus Angus by Brahman steers 36 (Zavy et al. 1992); weanlings tested two weeks after weaning 24 versus on weaning day 46 (Crookshank et al. 1979, a measured weaning-day stress penalty); inversion onto the back for 103 s 93; electric prod on all cattle before stunning 63 median, with 38% of those cattle slipping (Cockram and Corley 1991). Grandin's working guideline is that means above 70 ng/mL in steers or cows indicate rough handling or poor equipment, and that cortisol takes 10-20 minutes to peak. It also catalogues the habituation failures that matter most to a layout checker: Fell and Shutt 1986 found cortisol did not decline over repeated truck trips in which cattle fell down; Hargreaves and Hutson 1990 found no habituation to repeated sham shearing; Grandin et al. 1994 found that cattle hit hard by a headgate were more likely to resist entering the chute later - a single hardware fault producing durable avoidance; and Stookey et al. 1994 found cattle were less agitated when another animal was within 1 m in the chute. Notably this peer-reviewed review gives no flight-zone size and no point of balance at all.

papers.title: Behavioral agitation during handling of cattle is persistent over time
papers.authors: Grandin, Temple
papers.licence: free-to-read author-hosted HTML abstract at grandin.com (journal version paywalled at Elsevier)
papers.abstract: The measurement that tells a design tool what baseline to expect: some cattle never habituate, no matter how good the facility. 53 crossbred Gelbvieh by Simmental by Charolais bulls (about 260 kg at start) and 102 steers in three feedlot pens were restrained in a squeeze chute every 30 days for blood sampling under gentle handling with rare prod use. Five bulls (9%) were extremely agitated at every one of four consecutive restraints while 25 (47%) were calm at all four; six steers (6%) were always agitated over three sessions while 78 (76%) were always calm. Agitation was highly persistent, and the agitated animals were indistinguishable from pen-mates at rest. Grandin attributes the persistence to both prior rough handling at the ranch of origin and genetics, and recommends culling repeat offenders. She also notes that the same cattle all stayed calm on a double-rail restrainer conveyor at a 400 head per hour plant, which she attributes to constant physical contact between animals - consistent with the measured isolation and companion-animal literature. The design implication is that 6-9% of animals being difficult is the expected baseline, not evidence of a layout fault.

papers.title: Assessing cow-calf welfare. Part 2: Risk factors for beef cow health and behavior and stockperson handling
papers.authors: Simon, G. E.; Hoar, B. R.; Tucker, Cassandra B.
papers.licence: unknown (paywalled; no verifiable free copy located)
papers.abstract: The most transferable on-farm dataset for a cow-calf operation, and the paper whose effect sizes should lead any outcome log the app builds. 30 California cow-calf ranches, with per-animal scoring of health, behaviour and stockperson actions analysed with mixed models for risk factors. Prodding an individual cow with an electric prod raised her odds of balking (odds ratio 11.0) and of vocalising (odds ratio 3.3), plus several stumbling and falling outcomes. Using a moving aid on a cow raised balking risk markedly (odds ratio 34.1), while moving cattle with hands across the herd lowered balking risk (odds ratio 0.3). The authors conclude that reducing electric-prod use is the key available handling improvement. It is cross-sectional, so these are associations rather than demonstrated causes, and facility-design variables are not separated from stockperson behaviour - but the effect sizes dwarf anything attributable to geometry anywhere in this review. Part 1 (Journal of Animal Science 94:3476-3487) benchmarks cow health, behaviour during handling, facilities and producer perspectives across the same ranches.

papers.title: Behavioral, cardiac and cortisol responses to brief peer separation and reunion in cattle
papers.authors: Boissy, Alain; Le Neindre, Pierre
papers.licence: unknown (Elsevier, closed access)
papers.abstract: The controlled experiment that establishes social isolation as a major stressor in cattle, and the strongest measured finding in this entire review. Pen mates were removed from heifers WITHOUT the heifers themselves being handled, which isolates the stressor from any handling confound. All heifers responded with struggling and large increases in vocalization, heart rate and plasma cortisol, and the authors conclude that social deprivation is a very effective psychological stress in cattle. The finding with the most direct design consequence comes on reunion: behavioral responses, that is struggling and vocalization, decreased when conspecifics were brought back, INDEPENDENTLY of their familiarity to the subject. That means any companion animal relieves the stress, not only a familiar pen mate - so a corral's lone-animal remedy can be any available animal, and the app should not require a specific companion. Cited by EFSA 2025 as primary evidence for social support and buffering effects. Caveat: the test isolated animals in confinement, so magnitudes may not transfer directly to a crowd pen.

papers.title: Effects of mirror-image exposure on heart rate and movement of isolated heifers
papers.authors: Piller, C. A. K.; Stookey, Joseph M.; Watts, Jon M.
papers.licence: unknown (Elsevier, closed access)
papers.abstract: University of Saskatchewan work, and the most design-relevant isolation-mitigation experiment because it tests something a corral can actually contain. Heifers in social isolation were exposed to a mirror and compared with controls in visual isolation. Mirror exposure lowered heart rate and reduced movement, and the authors suggest a mirror reflection may reduce isolation stress for a heifer in a chute. Effects were strongest after the animals had been habituated over several days of exposure. The replication caveat the app must carry: a later dairy study (Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 2018, on whether access to an automated grooming brush and/or a mirror reduces the stress of dairy cows kept in social isolation) reported no indication of immediate stress reduction from brush or mirror use. The honest position is that a mirror is a cheap, plausible, Saskatchewan-tested mitigation that has not replicated in dairy cattle - worth offering as an option, not as a recommendation.

papers.title: Bos indicus-cross feedlot cattle with excitable temperaments have tougher meat and a higher incidence of borderline dark cutters
papers.authors: Voisinet, B. D.; Grandin, Temple; O'Connor, S. F.; Tatum, J. D.; Deesing, M. J.
papers.licence: free-to-read author-hosted HTML at grandin.com, with OCR errors (journal version paywalled at Elsevier)
papers.abstract: The standard citation for the measured link between handling temperament and meat quality. Braford, Red Brangus and Simbrah feedlot cattle were chute-scored at routine weighings, fed to 9-13 mm backfat over the 12th rib, and slaughtered commercially. Temperament significantly affected the incidence of borderline dark cutters downgraded by a USDA grader (P=0.01) and Warner-Bratzler shear force at 14 days post mortem (P<0.001): the calmest cattle averaged 2.86 plus or minus 0.11 kg shear force versus 3.63 plus or minus 0.19 kg for those that struggled violently, and 40% of agitated cattle exceeded the 3.9 kg food-service acceptability threshold. A secondary extension summary puts dark cutters at 6.7% for calm-scored versus 25% for highly excitable animals, which should be verified against the paper before quoting. The breed effect does not transfer to a British-breed Alberta herd, but the shear-force and dark-cutter effect sizes are the figures everyone cites. The companion paper (Voisinet et al. 1997, Journal of Animal Science 75:892-896) establishes that calm cattle outgain excitable ones, and the number should be taken from that paper directly because Grandin's own summaries of its effect size are typographically garbled in at least two places.

papers.title: Visual acuity of cattle determined by the method of discrimination learning
papers.authors: Entsu, S.; Dohi, H.; Yamada, A.
papers.licence: unknown (Elsevier, closed access)
papers.abstract: The primary measurement of bovine visual acuity, and the one vision number a geometry checker can actually compute with. Japanese Black heifers were trained to select the correct one of two simultaneously presented targets with left and right position randomised; once fully trained, acuity was determined two independent ways - by reducing target size (Test 1) and by increasing viewing distance (Test 2). Best decimal-acuity scores were 0.045/0.045 for Heifer 1, 0.083/0.083 for Heifer 2 and 0.063/0.064 for Heifer 3, the near-identical values across the two methods within each animal being the result's main strength. Converted by Adamczyk et al. (2024) to roughly 1.3-2.5 cycles per degree, that is about one-twentieth of human acuity, or broadly a 20/200 to 20/400 equivalent. This tells a designer what size a feature must be, at a given distance, before cattle can resolve it at all - and it provides a measured mechanism for the shadow problem (shadows read as holes) that does not depend on the unmeasured depth-perception claim. For anything judged while the animal is moving, use instead Hirata et al. 2019's field limit of about 2 m for low-contrast targets.

papers.title: The Perception of Color by Cattle and its Influence on Behavior
papers.authors: Phillips, Clive J. C.; Lomas, C. A.
papers.licence: free-to-read at publisher (bronze open access) but no verifiable direct PDF URL - journalofdairyscience.org and ScienceDirect both block automated requests
papers.abstract: The methodologically decisive colour-vision study for cattle, and the basis for a hard design conclusion. Earlier work had not controlled stimulus intensity, so colour-discrimination conclusions were confounded with brightness. These authors first trained calves to discriminate light sources by INTENSITY, then matched intensities so that short, medium and long wavelengths were isoluminant to the calf. Calves then discriminated long from short (82% correct) and long from medium (89% correct), but had limited ability to separate short from medium: three of seven managed it over the first eight tests, after which all chose at random. Cattle's upper wavelength limit is about 620 nm. Behaviour was then filmed under the isoluminant lights in novel-object, fear and handler tests: in the fear test calves got past a barrier and hid more quickly under medium (green) than short (blue) light and made the fewest movements under medium wavelength, and they were more active and more accommodating with handlers under long (red) wavelengths. The design conclusion is that cattle are dichromats who cannot reliably distinguish blue from green, so colour-coding a corral blue versus green is useless to the animal, and the variable to model is luminance contrast rather than hue.

papers.title: Visual perception and stimulus orientation in cattle
papers.authors: Rehkämper, Gerd; Perrey, A.; Werner, C. W.; Opfermann-Rüngeler, C.; Görlach, Albert
papers.licence: unknown (Elsevier, closed access)
papers.abstract: A measured orientation anisotropy in cattle vision, and a directly encodable design lever. Starting from the bovine eye's oval, horizontally oriented pupil, the authors hypothesised that visual perception in such eyes differs for stimuli with vertically-separated details versus horizontally-separated details. Cattle solved the discrimination task better with VERTICALLY presented stimuli than horizontal ones, which the authors attribute to visual acuity and pupil anatomy. Adamczyk et al. (2024) summarise this as pupil shape and orientation enhancing the detection of vertical lines over horizontal lines, consistent with the horizontally aligned retinal visual streak documented by Brooks et al. (1999) and Kassab and Sugita (2000). The design implication is that vertical elements - a post, a vertical gate stile, a vertical stripe at a race entrance - are more detectable to cattle than horizontal ones, and conversely that horizontal rails and horizontal shadow bars are relatively poorly resolved.

papers.title: The Locomotion of Dairy Cows in Passageways with Different Light Intensities
papers.authors: Phillips, Clive J. C.; Morris, I. D.; Lomas, C. A.; Lockwood, S. J.
papers.licence: unknown (Cambridge Core, closed access)
papers.abstract: The only measured illuminance window for cattle locomotion found, and a useful target figure as distinct from a fault threshold. Two experiments. In the first, cows walked a dark versus a lit passageway on the way back from milking: in the dark they took shorter but more rapid steps, which the authors read as increasing stability. In the second, cows walked a cubicle passageway to a food reward with building intensity varying from 0 to 250 lux, with step length, stepping rate and leg-joint angles measured from video. Stepping rate again rose in the dark, giving a higher walking rate; the arcs of travel of the metacarpophalangeal joint and the fore- and hind-foot angles to the floor were reduced in the dark and were greatest at 119 lux; and the slowest walking rate was at 39 lux. The authors conclude that the optimum illumination for dairy cow locomotion may lie approximately between 39 and 119 lux. Read alongside Hitchcock and Hutson 1979 and Lindkvist et al. 2023, which between them show that absolute light level has little effect on willingness to move - so this window should inform lighting design, not generate a layout fault.

papers.title: The movement of sheep in a Y maze and the effect of light intensity on movement through a race
papers.authors: Hitchcock, D. K.; Hutson, Geoff D.
papers.source: Australian Journal of Experimental Agriculture and Animal Husbandry 19
papers.licence: unknown (closed access; CSIRO landing page could not be resolved)
papers.abstract: A genuine factorial experiment and an important NULL result, which is why it belongs in the library even though it is sheep. Narrow and wide races were tested at four illumination levels - 1.4, 88, 350 and 1,400 lux - set independently on either side of a partition. Light intensity had little overall effect on movement; neither the degree of contrast between the two levels nor the direction of the transition, dark to bright or bright to dark, mattered; and strong light contrasts could not be used to draw sheep along a race. The only positive conclusion was that sheds should be well lit overall. Taken with Grigor et al. 1997 in red deer and Lindkvist et al. 2023 in dairy cows, this is the evidence base for the recommendation that a corral designer should flag glare and non-uniformity rather than absolute brightness or a plain dark-to-light step - and it means the widely repeated rule that 'animals move from darker to brighter areas' failed when someone tested it directly. The companion paper on the movement of sheep on inclines, in the same journal and volume, is the only incline experiment located and its result could not be retrieved.

papers.title: The movement of sheep around corners
papers.authors: Hutson, Geoff D.; Hitchcock, D. K.
papers.licence: unknown (Elsevier, closed access)
papers.abstract: Listed because it is the only corner-geometry experiment located in any species, and because the 'eliminate square corners' rule that every corral guide repeats has no cattle experiment behind it at all. The result of this study could NOT be retrieved - ScienceDirect blocked every automated route and the session's search budget was exhausted before it could be chased by another path - so no finding is characterised here. It is the highest-value remaining item for anyone wanting to put a number on the minimum corner angle a corral designer should enforce: at present the app will have to pick an angle and label it as its own convention rather than as evidence. A library request to Applied Animal Ethology volume 4 would settle it.

papers.title: Effect of neck injection and handler visibility on behavioral reactivity of beef steers
papers.authors: Müller, R.; Schwartzkopf-Genswein, Karen S.; Shah, M. A.; von Keyserlingk, Marina A. G.
papers.licence: unknown (closed access)
papers.abstract: The controlled test of the premise behind every 'use solid sides, block the animal's vision' recommendation in the design canon - a premise otherwise carried entirely by Grandin's field observation. The study experimentally manipulated handler visibility, that is whether the restrained steer could see the person, alongside neck injection, and measured behavioural reactivity. Schwartzkopf-Genswein is at the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada Lethbridge Research and Development Centre and von Keyserlingk at the University of British Columbia, so this is Canadian work on Alberta cattle and the most locally relevant measured anchor available for the solid-versus-see-through-sides question. Read alongside the measured counter-evidence - Stookey and Watts' Y-maze result that cattle chose the race where they could see light through the side - which together support a directional rule: block the view of distractions and handlers AHEAD along the direction of travel, rather than demanding blanket solid sides.

papers.title: The sensory world of cattle: Abilities, limitations, and perceptual challenges in human-designed environments
papers.authors: Rørvang, Maria Vilain; Meagher, Rebecca K.; Stenfelt, Johanna; Miller-Cushon, Emily K.; Ahmmad, Sheikh Rishad; Ceballos, Maria Camila
papers.licence: CC-BY 4.0 (confirmed by Crossref and Unpaywall, but ScienceDirect returns 403 to automated requests and Unpaywall gives no direct PDF URL - worth a manual download)
papers.abstract: The most comprehensive review of cattle sensory ability to date, and the current state of the art. It synthesises vision, hearing, olfaction, taste and touch, and argues that perception depends on context - cattle integrate sensory information with prior experience and emotional state, and the dominant sense shifts by situation. Its central thesis is exactly a corral designer's thesis: mismatches between species-specific sensory capacity and human-designed environments drive behavioural responses, stress and poor human-animal interaction, and it presents a conceptual framework for assessing housing, handling routines and production practices from the animal's perspective. Reported findings include a wide panoramic field of vision aiding predator detection, limited depth perception, slow adaptation to rapid lighting changes, and shadows, reflections and sharp contrasts causing uncertainty or fear. Notably, like Adamczyk et al. 2024, it does NOT put a degree figure on the visual field - which is itself strong evidence that the widely quoted 330 degree number has no primary cattle perimetry behind it. Co-author Maria Camila Ceballos is at the University of Calgary Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, making her the obvious local contact for the perimetry and light-adaptation gaps this review leaves open.

papers.title: Assessing the use of a mechanical rump pusher in a commercial cattle slaughter plant
papers.authors: Wigham, Emma; French, M.
papers.source: Animal Welfare 34:e35 (Cambridge University Press for UFAW)
papers.licence: CC-BY (no verifiable direct PDF URL located; full text available as XML via Europe PMC REST)
papers.abstract: The best contemporary measured line-rate figure with matched behavioural outcomes, which is otherwise almost absent from the literature. A UK commercial cattle slaughter plant operating at 40 cattle per hour was observed through normal operations, recording over 815 cattle the level of coercion needed to enter a mechanical rump pusher ahead of the stun box, the pusher's use, cattle behaviour inside it, and carcase bruising. The pusher was used on 267 animals (32.8%), more often on dairy cattle and on animals that had needed more coercion to enter. Overall 60 cattle (7.4%) required the highest coercion score and 4 (0.49%) the electric goad. Inside the device 11 animals slipped (1.8%) and 10 vocalised (1.6%), none directly attributable to the pusher, but longer restraint time was significantly associated with more gate slams into the entrance gate. Pusher use was not significantly associated with carcase bruising. It is a plant rather than a ranch corral, but it is the only recent source giving a measured head-per-hour rate alongside per-animal coercion, slip and vocalisation percentages at that rate.

papers.title: Individual differences in the reaction of beef cattle to situations involving social isolation, close proximity of humans, restraint and novelty
papers.authors: Kilgour, Robert J.; Melville, Gavin J.; Greenwood, Paul L.
papers.licence: unknown (Elsevier, closed access)
papers.abstract: Measured within-herd variance in beef cattle responses to human proximity, social isolation, restraint and novelty, and the cleanest demonstration that this variance is large. The design consequence is the one a flagging engine most needs to internalise: a corral must work for the tail of the distribution, not the mean, because an engine tuned to average behaviour will pass layouts that fail the flightiest tenth of the herd. Read alongside Grandin 1993, which found 6-9% of animals violently agitated at every single restraint under gentle handling, and Kappel et al. 2025, which found that an individual's isolation response is not even a stable trait and so cannot be pre-screened.

papers.title: Code of Practice for the Care and Handling of Beef Cattle: Review of Scientific Research on Priority Issues (November 2012)
papers.authors: Beef Cattle Code of Practice Scientists' Committee; K. Schwartzkopf-Genswein; J. M. Stookey; J. Berg; J. Campbell; D. B. Haley; E. Pajor
papers.licence: Publicly available; copyright NFACC
papers.abstract: The peer-reviewed literature review that underpins the 2013 Code, by the Scientists' Committee. Four parts: painful procedures (dehorning, castration, branding and identification), feedlot health and morbidity (BRD, lameness, nutritional disease), weaning methods, and environmental and housing conditions (mud, extreme cold, extreme heat). The housing part is the only place a Canadian normative document gives a windbreak figure from the science: windbreak designs with 15 to 30 per cent porosity cause snow to build up in shallow rather than deep drifts and protect better than solid fences. Concludes that excessive mud is a risk factor for lameness, injury and hoof disease and that feed per pound of gain rose 25 per cent in muddy conditions, but that research is still needed to define what constitutes excessive mud - which is why the 2013 Code has no mud threshold. Explicitly makes no recommendations; it relays science to the Code Development Committee.

papers.title: Timeline for Codes of Practice Being Amended or Updated (May 2026)
papers.authors: National Farm Animal Care Council
papers.licence: Publicly available; copyright NFACC
papers.abstract: NFACC's schedule for every Code of Practice under amendment or update as at May 2026. Confirms the beef cattle Code is in revision with an estimated completion in 2027, and sets out the process: stakeholder survey, Scientific Committee report, draft Code, 60-day public comment period, review of feedback, final approval and publication. New or updated Codes take at least two years; amendments generally a year or less. Use it to date-stamp anything the app quotes from the 2013 edition.

papers.title: Beef Cattle At a Glance: top-of-mind survey results for the Code of Practice update
papers.authors: National Farm Animal Care Council
papers.licence: Publicly available; copyright NFACC
papers.abstract: The preliminary stakeholder survey results that set the priority topics for the 2023 to 2027 beef Code revision. Shows what producers, veterinarians, processors and the public currently consider the pressing welfare issues in Canadian beef production, and therefore what the next edition of the Code is most likely to tighten.

papers.title: Canadian Beef Code Update: What Producers Need to Know
papers.authors: Karen Schwartzkopf-Genswein, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada Lethbridge
papers.licence: Conference presentation, publicly posted
papers.abstract: The Scientific Committee chair's 9 June 2026 briefing on what is changing in the beef Code of Practice. The single best preview of the 2027 edition. Facility-relevant changes flagged: a new section on mud and moisture; a Facilities section addressing safe, low-stress cattle movement and housing for severely sick or injured cattle; a new Non-Ambulatory Cattle section requiring prompt care, safe handling, appropriate lifting tools and access to feed and water; the electric prod requirement rewritten to 'Electric prods must not be used except to assist movement of cattle when other humane alternatives have failed'; weaning expanded and subdivided into pre-weaning, weaning and post-weaning with a new Requirement for increased monitoring after weaning; the colostrum window tightened from 6 to 4 hours; pain control required for assisted difficult calvings, spaying, and branding calves under 6 months (all cattle from 1 January 2032); transport requirements aligned to the amended Health of Animals Regulations; euthanasia methods put in table form with firearm and ammunition specifics by class of cattle.

papers.title: CRSB Certified Sustainable Beef Production Standard, version 2.0
papers.authors: Canadian Roundtable for Sustainable Beef
papers.licence: Publicly available programme standard; copyright CRSB
papers.abstract: The audited Canadian sustainability standard for cow-calf, backgrounding and feedlot operations, scored 0 to 3 per indicator with certification requiring the Achievement level on every one. Its Animal Health and Welfare indicators AHW 1 to AHW 8 are explicitly aligned to the 2013 NFACC beef Code and cite it by section. AHW 7 Behaviour requires that 'Adequate space shall be provided for cattle to express normal behaviour (i.e. all cattle are able to lay down at the same time; cattle can move freely and access feed and water)'. AHW 8 Unnecessary Stress covers handling, loading and unloading, transportation, cattle facilities and environmental conditions, and its Achievement level restates verbatim the Code 4.1 handling and prod Requirements plus the Code 1.2 Requirements for access to safe handling, restraint, treatment, segregation, loading and unloading equipment and for providing traction in handling areas. This is the document that turns the Code's facility clauses into something a southern Alberta ranch is actually audited against.

papers.title: CRSB Certified Sustainable Beef Processing Standard, version 2.0
papers.authors: Canadian Roundtable for Sustainable Beef
papers.licence: Publicly available programme standard; copyright CRSB
papers.abstract: The processing-side companion to the CRSB production standard. Included for completeness because it sets the receiving-end handling and unloading expectations that the ranch's load-out has to satisfy at the other end of the trip.

papers.title: Canadian Beef Cattle On-Farm Biosecurity Standard: implementation manual
papers.authors: Canadian Food Inspection Agency; Canadian Cattlemen's Association
papers.source: CFIA / Publications du gouvernement du Canada
papers.licence: Crown copyright, free reproduction for non-commercial purposes
papers.abstract: The national biosecurity standard's implementation manual for beef producers. Matters to corral design because the Code of Practice section 1.2 recommends considering biosecurity when designing and managing cattle facilities, and this is the document that says what that means in practice: segregated receiving and isolation areas for introduced animals, controlled access points, routing of vehicles and visitors, and separate handling of new or sick stock. Note that publications.gc.ca serves an 'Information Archived on the Web' interstitial to automated fetchers unless a Referer header is sent; it downloads normally from a browser click.

papers.title: Wintering Sites and Livestock Corrals (Agdex 096-4), revised May 2007 printing
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Food; Natural Resources Conservation Board
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: The original May 2007 revision of the Agdex 096-4 standard on corral and wintering site siting under AOPA, kept here because it is the version most often cited by the NRCB and by Alberta beef specialists. Same 30 m setback to a common body of water, same slope-scaled manure storage setbacks, same two runoff mitigation options.

papers.title: Manure Management Regulations for Cow/Calf Producers (Agdex 096-6)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Food
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: The cow-calf-specific companion to Agdex 096-4. Sets out which AOPA manure requirements apply to a cow-calf operation as opposed to a confined feeding operation: runoff control at corrals and wintering sites, short-term field storage limits, setbacks, soil testing and record keeping, and the exemption for manure deposited by grazing livestock.

papers.title: Environmental Standards for Alberta's Livestock Industry: 2008 Reference Guide, Agricultural Operation Practices Act (AOPA)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Rural Development; Natural Resources Conservation Board
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: The consolidated AOPA reference guide (May 2014 printing of the 2008 guide). Gives the statutory citations behind the corral siting rules and two distinctions a corral designer must not blur. First, Standards and Administration Regulation section 4: seasonal feeding and bedding (wintering) sites and livestock corrals need no permit but must be sited at least 30 m from a common body of water, failing which runoff must be diverted or manure removed before a runoff event. Second, Act section 1: a manure collection area means the floor of a barn, under-floor pits, the floor of a feedlot pen and a catch basin, and expressly does not include the floor of a livestock corral - so a working corral floor is not subject to the manure storage construction standard but a feedlot pen floor is. Also covers confined feeding operation permits, Minimum Distance Separation, manure application setbacks (including 30 m from a water well), incorporation within 48 hours, nitrogen and salinity limits, and nutrient management plans.

papers.title: Calculator for Determining Livestock Capacity of Operations as They Existed on January 1, 2002
papers.authors: Natural Resources Conservation Board (Alberta)
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: The NRCB worksheet for establishing an operation's grandfathered livestock capacity as at 1 January 2002, which determines whether expanding a pen or yard pushes the operation into confined feeding operation permitting. Worth having if the designer ever lets the ranch add pen capacity.

papers.title: Fencing and Handling Facility Standards for Diversified Livestock Farms
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation (Director, Livestock Industry Diversification Act)
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: The only legally binding handling-facility design standard in Alberta - but it applies to domestic cervids, not beef cattle. Made by the Director under section 14 of the Livestock Industry Diversification Act and revised June 2026. Requires a minimum enclosed area of not less than 10 acres; elk and moose perimeter fences of at least 2.5 m (8 ft) mesh wire, or 2.1 m (7 ft) mesh plus two high-tensile wires above, with wires no more than 15 cm (6 in) apart; deer fences of 2.8 m (9 ft) or 2.5 m plus two wires; horizontal wires 15 cm or less apart and verticals 30 cm or less; all new perimeter fence built as 20-96-6 high-tensile wire (20 horizontal wires at 2.5 m total height with 15 cm vertical spacing); gates the same height as the fence, closed and secured. Handling facilities must consist of a squeeze, crush or alley-way designed to hold animals securely and prevent injury to workers or animals; must be sited so all animals can be captured within one week of notice of inspection; should not form any part of the perimeter fence; and all loading and unloading must happen entirely inside the perimeter fence. Useful as a model of how a jurisdiction writes an enforceable facility rule.

papers.title: Alberta Elk and Deer Farming Industry Guidelines for Harvest Preserves
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: Companion guidelines to the Alberta diversified livestock fencing and handling facility standards, covering harvest preserve licensing. Included only because it is the administrative other half of the one Alberta facility rule that has statutory force.

papers.title: What Are My Fencing Obligations?
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation, Farmers' Advocate Office
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: The Farmers' Advocate Office guide to Alberta fencing law: the Line Fence Act, the Stray Animals Act, what counts as a lawful fence, who pays for a boundary fence and how disputes are resolved. Relevant whenever the designer puts a corral, a weaning fence or a holding pen on or near a property line.

papers.title: The Beef Cow-calf Manual (Agdex 420/10), Section 08: Handling Facilities and Fencing
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Food
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: Alberta's cow-calf production manual. Section 08 (pp.249-272) is the most recent provincial statement of corral dimensions and the source the app should cite, because its tables are explicitly adapted from Canada Plan Service M-1800 and CPS 1000 and from Borg et al. (1993). Table 69, Recommended dimensions for beef cattle corrals and handling facilities, with the instruction that cow-calf operations should use the over-1200 lb column: holding area 14, 17, 20 sq ft per animal worked immediately and 45, 50, 60 held overnight; vertical-sided working chute width 18, 22, 28 in with a desirable length of 24 ft; sloping-sided chute 22 in at the bottom and 32 in at 5 ft; working chute and feedlot line fences 5 ft high on posts 3 ft deep; corrals and bull pen fences 5 ft high on posts 4 ft deep; loading chute 30-32 in wide, 12 ft minimum length, slope 1 to 4; ramp heights of 15 in for a gooseneck trailer, 28 in for a pickup, 40 in for a van-type truck, 48 in for a tractor trailer (printed as 248, a typesetting error) and 100 in for a double deck; access or collecting alley 12 ft. Table 70 gives housing guidelines adapted from CPS 1000: soil pen 300 sq ft per cow, paved 80 without a shed or 50 with, bedded mound 35, shed floor 30 sq ft with 10 ft clearance, maternity pens 10 by 10 ft one per 20 cows, water surface 4 sq ft per 100 head and 11 gallons per 1100 lb daily rising to 16 in hot weather, bunk length 26-30 in limit fed and 8 in self fed with a 22 in throat height and 34 in maximum reach, concrete slopes of 2-4 per cent and soil 4-8 per cent, mounds at 1 to 4. Tables 71 to 73 give the geometry for laying out circular working chutes (radius, post spacing, section count, inside width for 28 and 32 in chutes) and circular crowding tubs (tub radius for 8 to 16 ft gates at 4 ft and 6 ft post spacing). Table 74 is a 21-item corral design checklist including alleys no wider than 20 ft, at least two sorting corrals at 60 and 40 per cent of the holding corral area, no right-angle corners, no dead-end or unlit chute, a power outlet at the squeeze and yard lights out of cattle reach. Narrative additions: fences at least 6 ft high with 12 in of free space at the bottom; long narrow holding pen 18-20 ft wide; crowding gate usually 12 ft swinging 180 to 300 degrees; three sorting corrals for most cow-calf operations; chute catwalk minimum 18 in, 36-42 in below the top; chute 20-50 ft long on a 16-25 ft radius; loading alley no longer than two animal lengths with two or three 15 degree dog-leg curves about 2 ft in 8 ft; ramp 30-35 in single file or 54-72 in for groups and about 16 ft long with a 5 ft landing; a 2 ft veterinary access gate behind the squeeze; sick pens of 15-20 sq ft of shelter plus 40-60 sq ft of pen per head for 5 per cent of the herd; and windbreak fences 20-30 per cent open, at least 8 ft high, with pens 100-150 ft downwind.

papers.title: Portable Windbreak Fences (Agdex 711-1)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture, Food and Rural Development
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: Eleven buildable portable windbreak designs with construction callouts, plus the quantified case for building one. Porosity should be 25 to 33 per cent: 6 inch boards spaced 2 inches apart give 25 per cent and spaced 3 inches apart give 33 per cent, and the protected area extends 8 to 10 times the height of the fence downwind. Typical frame: slatted fence 25-30 per cent porous, 2 by 6 rough rails at 24 to 32 in, 6 in pipe skids with sand fill for ballast welded 18 in high so they do not become embedded, sway bracing every 24 ft, a steel pipe sub-frame and a 4 in steel pipe main post, with an optional 8 ft wing extension. One slanted-wall unit is recorded as having overturned in a 90 km/h wind. Table 1 gives the digestible energy requirement of a 1300 lb large-frame cow at mid pregnancy under three wintering treatments: 20.7, 26.1 and 31.6 Mcal per day at 0 C and 26.9, 32.3 and 37.8 at minus 30 C, on an average December wind of 17.3 km/h reduced to 5.0 km/h behind the fence.

papers.title: Wintering Site Assessment and Design Tool: a guide to selecting and managing a wintering site in Western Canada (Agdex 420/580-3)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Rural Development
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: A western Canadian methodology for choosing and managing a winter feeding and bedding site: slope, soil type and texture, depth to water table, distance to a common body of water, drainage and runoff pathways, natural shelter, snow catch and access. The closest thing in the Canadian literature to a scoreable siting tool, and the obvious model for a map-based siting check in corral design software - it pairs directly with the AOPA 30 m setback rule.

papers.title: Animal Welfare and Handling (Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Irrigation
