papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: The current provincial statement on animal welfare and handling: how Alberta's Animal Protection Act works, the role of the NFACC Codes of Practice as the reference for generally accepted practice, and who enforces what. This is the document that explains why a voluntary national Code has practical legal weight in Alberta.

papers.title: Review of Provincial Involvement in Livestock Welfare Protection in Alberta
papers.authors: Government of Alberta
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: A provincial review of how livestock welfare is protected and enforced in Alberta, and where the national Codes of Practice sit within that machinery. Background for anyone deciding how hard the software should assert a Code clause.

papers.title: Horse Handling Facilities (Agdex 460/722-1)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Rural Development
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: Alberta's handling facility design sheet for horses, written in the same idiom and by the same engineering group as the cattle corral material: alleys, pens, chutes, gates and loading. Useful as a cross-check on the cattle dimensions and if the designer is ever extended to horse corrals.

papers.title: Managing Feedlot Pen Dust
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Forestry
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: Pen surface moisture and dust management in Alberta feedlots: stocking density, manure pack depth, watering and cleaning schedules. The dry-season counterpart to the mud problem the 2027 Code draft is adding a section on, and directly relevant to pen surface specification in a designer.

papers.title: Creep Feeding Calves (Agdex 400/50-4)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture, Food and Rural Development
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: Alberta's creep feeding sheet: when it pays, what to feed and how to build and site a creep so calves can use it and cows cannot. Relevant because the 2025 NFACC Scientific Committee concludes that creep feeding and other pre-weaning supplementation buffer weaning stress - which makes the creep pen a layout element the designer should support.

papers.title: Traceability in Alberta: Best Practices for RFID Ear Tag Application (Agdex 420/26-1)
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture and Forestry
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: What has to happen at the chute for mandatory traceability: correct RFID tag placement, retention, readers, and the restraint needed to tag safely. Directly informs the equipment and working-room allowance at a squeeze station, and connects to Code of Practice section 4.3 Identification.

papers.title: Development of Physiological Procedures to Objectively Measure Stress in Cattle
papers.authors: Alberta agricultural research report
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: Alberta-funded research on objectively measuring handling stress in cattle. Background to the measurable handling outcomes the Code of Practice section 4.1 Recommended Practice d asks producers to score - falling, stumbling, prod use, running or jumping from the chute, and vocalisation under restraint - and to the idea that those scores should drive changes in lighting, noise, equipment or environment.

papers.title: Electric Fencing Manual for Alberta
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: Alberta's full electric fence design manual: energizers, grounding, wire spacing, post spacing, bracing, gates and maintenance. Useful for the temporary and weaning fences around a corral system, where the 2008 cow-calf manual gives only summary spacings.

papers.title: High-tensile Smooth Wire Fencing Manual for Alberta
papers.authors: Alberta Agriculture
papers.licence: Open Government Licence - Alberta
papers.abstract: The companion manual for high-tensile smooth wire fencing in Alberta: 12.5 gauge minimum, breaking load and tensile strength specifications, wire spacing tables by use, post and stay spacing, bracing, in-line strainers and tension springs. The full version of the summary tables in the Beef Cow-calf Manual, and the fence type most likely to be drawn around a weaning paddock.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan index (all series)
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service; hosted by the Canadian Society for Bioengineering (CSBE/SCGAB)
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The master index of every Canada Plan Service plan and leaflet, hosted by CSBE now that the CPS website is gone. Lists the beef cattle handling set - M(I) 1800 Cattle Handling Facilities, 1811 Corral and Feedlot Fencing, 1812 Crowding Gate, 1813 Working Chute (with 1813a Option Two), 1814 Blocking Gates, 1816 Stationary Adjustable Loading Chute, 1817 Adjustable Loading Chute, 1818 Pregnancy Testing and A.I. Chute, 1819 Herringbone A.I. Breeding Chute, 1831 Minimum Working Corral, 1832 Small Working Corral, 1833 Cattle Handling Corral, 1834 Corral for Cow-Calf Operations, 1835 Large Working Corral and 1836 Cattle Working Corral - together with the 1000-series beef housing, feeder and calf shelter plans. M means metric, I imperial and M(I) both. Start here when hunting a specific plan number.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan M-1800: Cattle Handling Facilities (planning guide)
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The parent Canada Plan Service planning guide for cattle handling facilities (revised 86-01), and the origin of the dimension set every Canadian source repeats - Alberta's Table 69 is explicitly adapted from it. Its behaviour section is based on work by Dr Temple Grandin. TABLE 1, with the note that cow-calf operations use the over 540 kg (1200 lb) column: holding area 1.3, 1.6 and 1.9 sq m (14, 17, 20 sq ft) per animal worked immediately and 4.2, 4.6 and 5.6 sq m (45, 50, 60 sq ft) held overnight; working chute with vertical sides 450, 550 and 700 mm (18, 22, 28 in) wide with a desirable minimum length of 7.2 m (24 ft); working chute with sloping sides 550 mm (22 in) at the bottom and 800 mm (32 in) at 1.5 m (5 ft) height; working chute and feedlot line fences 1.5 m (5 ft) high on posts 1.0 m (3 ft) deep; corral and bull pen fences 1.8 m (6 ft) high on posts 1.2 m (4 ft) deep; loading chute 650 mm (26 in) wide under 270 kg and 750-800 mm (30-32 in) above, minimum 3.4 m (12 ft) long, rise to run 1 to 4; ramp heights of 375, 700, 1000, 1200 and 2500 mm (15, 28, 40, 48 and 100 in) for a gooseneck trailer, pickup, van-type truck, tractor trailer and double deck; access or collecting alley 3.6 m (12 ft). It is the tiebreaker where the Alberta reprints disagree - it confirms 6 ft corral fences on 4 ft posts (Alberta's table mis-sets both rows as 5 ft) and a 48 in tractor trailer ramp (Alberta prints 248 in). The narrative adds rules the reprints drop: choose a well-drained site with a slope of about 1 in 50 away from the headgate and squeeze; merge concrete paving into unpaved areas rather than ending it in a step; stake out a full-scale layout before digging postholes; plan so cattle can reach the facility from every pen; single-file chute at least 6 m (20 ft), 9-15 m (30-50 ft) in larger facilities, 6-15 m (20-50 ft) overall; run one wall of the crowd pen straight into the funnel and do not make the funnel entrance symmetrical; make blocking and sorting gates inside the chute from spaced planks, not solid panels; keep illumination uniform, use solid rather than slotted sunshades, and face loading and squeeze chutes north or south to minimise shadows; extend a single-file chute 3-5 m (10-16 ft) outside a building and never put the building wall where the crowd pen meets the chute; keep dogs out of the crowd pen and chute; flight zone up to 90 m (300 ft) for range cattle and 1.5-8 m (5-26 ft) for feedlot cattle; posts 2.5 m (8 ft) long for feedlot fences and 3 m (10 ft) for corral fences at no more than 2.4 m (8 ft) spacing, four rails at 1.5 m and five rails at 1.8 m, with curved fences to stop cattle bunching in corners; collection alley about 3.6 m (12 ft); at least one holding pen sized for the herd, two better; crowding gate on a 3 in galvanised pipe pivot in concrete with adjustable height and multiple latch stops; catwalk about 1 m (3 ft) below the top of the chute fence, outside the chute on the inner curve, never overhead; loading chute curved with solid sides on a 3.6-5.1 m (12-17 ft) radius, the larger the better, 750-875 mm (30-35 in) single file, 650 mm (26 in) for calves only, 1350-1800 mm (54-72 in) double width, and a straight 1.8-3 m (6-10 ft) chute where it is used only for unloading; level landing about 1.5 m (5 ft); fixed ramp no more than 20 degrees and adjustable no more than 25; height adjustment 650-1125 mm (26-45 in); cleats 19 by 38 mm at 200 mm apart edge to edge; concrete stepped ramps strongly recommended with 90-100 mm rise and 300 mm tread run; self-aligning dock bumpers and telescopic side panels to close the gap to the truck; V-squeeze bottom widths of 150, 200, 300 and 350-400 mm by class; a small access gate behind the squeeze; A.I. dark box with 325 mm (13 in) man openings and a cross rail at three positions; and a scale offset from the chute whose cage, floor and gates form one weighed unit touching nothing.

papers.title: Service de plans canadiens plan M-1800 (French): Installations de manutention des bovins
papers.authors: Service de plans canadiens / Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The French edition of Canada Plan Service plan M-1800, Cattle Handling Facilities - a second verified copy of the single most important dimension sheet in this collection, carrying the same Table 1 of recommended dimensions for beef cattle corrals and handling facilities.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1812: Crowding Gate
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The Canadian crowding gate plan (revised 83:12) - the 12 ft gate used in the crowding tub of plans 1831 and 1835. Pivot post is 3 and a half inch by 12 ft long pipe set in concrete backfill 4 ft deep, with the note that in soft soils the post hole diameter and concrete should be increased. The hinge is a 4 inch pipe by 3 inch long sleeve that rotates on the post and is greased as necessary, with a three-eighths by 3 by 1 ft 4 in hinge strap welded to the sleeve and bolted to the gate members; a 4 inch pipe by 3 inch collar is drilled with the post for a three-eighths bolt, and additional holes are drilled in the post for vertical adjustment - which is how the gate is raised to clear snow, ice and manure build-up. The gate itself is 1 by 6 in uprights, 2 by 6 in rails, 1 by 6 in cross bracing, three-eighths sheathing plywood with the face grain vertical so cattle cannot see through, 1 by 6 in spacer blocking, and a 2 by 6 in latch board with a U-bolt handle.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1814: Blocking Gates
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The blocking gate plan (rev. 84:01) for controlling cattle moving through a working chute such as Plan 1813, used wherever cattle must be stopped or prevented from backing up. Two interchangeable designs are drawn: a plywood-covered gate running on rollers and an inclined sliding-door track, which is self-closing, and a plank gate running on greased pipe. Callouts include a gate stop with rubber bumpers, a 2 by 6 by 8 ft track board with slide-door track and roller hardware, a control rope through a pulley and screw eye on a spacer block tied with a loop and bowline knot, 2 by 6 in members, three-quarter inch plywood, a 4 by 6 by 12 ft CCA pressure-treated post, a 6 in diameter by 9 ft CCA post, 2 in galvanised pipe 7 ft 6 in long, 2 by 4 in stop blocks, three-eighths carriage bolts with nuts and washers, one-eighth by one and a half inch strap iron, and concrete backfill. Plan M-1800 notes the design choice: an open gate where the cattle at the gate should see ahead, a solid one where they must be shut off, as in an A.I. chute.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1818: Pregnancy Testing and A.I. Chute
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The dark box pregnancy testing and artificial insemination chute (revised 84:04), designed for beef cow herds. Three cows are brought into position at once by closing the blocking gates and placing a cross rail behind each animal; after servicing the gates open and the rails are removed, giving an even flow of cattle. The cross rails fit at three different places behind the solid blocking gate to suit animal size, and only the solid gate from Plan 1814 should be used. Dimensions stated: working chute 28 in clear width with optional catwalk per leaflet 1813; blocking gate sliding on greased one and a half inch pipe or sliding barn-door hardware; a 13 inch man opening that lets a handler enter safely behind the cow; 2 by 4 in cleats and a 2 by 4 in cross rail; a plywood-covered area over the head, top and sides, with a canvas or burlap curtain hanging at the back of the top to keep cows calm. The catwalk must be built on the side opposite the man openings. Any number of man openings and cow positions can be built in. Plan M-1800 adds the warning never to use the A.I. chute for branding, dehorning or injections, or the animals will associate it with pain.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1831: Minimum Working Corral
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The smallest complete Canada Plan Service corral, described as a minimum handling facility for the cattleman with a few head who handles cattle infrequently during a year, or for a separate pasture facility remote from the central facilities of a cow-calf operation - which makes it the right starting point for a satellite corral on a southern Alberta ranch. It consists of a holding pen, a crowding area and a small working chute, with a semi-circular crowding pen and crowding gate per leaflet 1812 that helps squeeze animals into the chute with minimum effort; the same crowding unit can move animals into a loading chute placed adjacent to the working chute. The leaflet is candid that this corral has a short working chute and that longer is preferred, and notes that as the herd or the operator's needs increase the layout can be readily expanded. It may be equipped with a home-made pipeframe headgate or a commercial squeeze with attached headgate. Dimensions stated: 10 ft gate per leaflet 1811; posts 6 ft on centre; optional man gate the same width as the chute. Reproduced as Corral Layout 1 in Alberta's Corrals for Handling Beef Cattle, where it is the cost baseline at about 1200 to 1400 dollars of materials in January 1993.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1836: Cattle Working Corral
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The Canada Plan Service cattle working corral, sitting between the minimum corral 1831 and the large working corral 1835 in the series and listed next to 1835 in both the CPS index and the 2004 Saskatchewan catalogue. Note that this leaflet is image-only - there is no extractable text, so its dimensions have to be read off the drawing itself rather than from a callout list. Built to the same conventions as the rest of the 1800 series: fencing and gates per 1811, crowding gate per 1812, working chute per 1813, blocking gate per 1814 and loading chute per 1816 or 1817.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1811: Corral and Feedlot Fencing
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The Canadian corral and feedlot fence plan, with gate and latch details. Specifies a 4-rail fence and gate for a 5 ft 0 in feedlot fence and a 5-rail fence and gate for a 6 ft 0 in corral fence; minimum 6 in top diameter wood posts; 2 by 6 in horizontals with 1 by 6 in both sides and 1 by 6 in spacer blocking both sides; 2 in blocking between upright and brace boards; a brace dimension of 3 ft 0 in for a 12 ft 0 in gate and 4 ft 0 in for a 16 ft 0 in gate; gate hardware of quarter by 2 in iron strap both sides with seven-sixteenths machine bolts through the gate members, a five-eighths galvanised bolt hook with two nuts and two washers, half inch pipe welded to the strap, keepers of half inch plywood both sides and a 2 by 6 in latch board; and gate posts of minimum 8 in top diameter by 14 ft 0 in pressure-treated wood set with concrete backfill. Referenced by CPS 1835 and 1819 as the fencing standard for the whole corral.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1813: Working Chute
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The Canadian single-file working chute plan, revised July 1984, showing a straight chute section and an alternate tapered section. States that the chute dimensions are recommended for feeder cattle up to 1000 lb and that heavier cattle and some exotic breeds may need a wider chute. Components: commercial pipe-frame headgate and cattle squeeze; an access gate to close across the chute; 5 in top diameter or 4 by 6 by 12 ft 0 in CCA pressure-treated sawn poles; a blocking gate per leaflet 1814; a catwalk of three 2 by 6 in on 2 by 6 in each side of the pole with a 2 by 6 by 2 ft 0 in brace to the pole; three 2 by 8 in bottom rails and three 2 by 6 in top rails; 2 by 6 in cross-ties and 8 in carriage bolts; an optional filler for handling young cattle of 2 by 6 in at 2 ft 0 in on centre with 4 ft 0 in high plywood suspended from the top rails; three-eighths inch exterior select sheathing plywood with the face grain vertical; an optional rough-textured concrete base on compacted granular fill; and temporary cross-bracing to the pole pairs while locating and tamping them into position.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1816: Stationary Adjustable Loading Chute
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The newest Canada Plan Service loading chute plan (new May 2006). The chute is 2 ft 9 in wide and consists of a 12 ft ramp section with an adjustable extension at the upper end, in plank construction on a pressure-treated post framework, with cleats for traction and a catwalk along the ramp. Details: 6 by 6 in pressure-treated posts; 2 by 6 in sidewalls and cross-ties; catwalk of 2 by 6 in with 1 by 2 in hardwood cleats at 6 in on centre, 2 by 4 in struts and brace and half inch plywood; ramp floor of two 2 by 6 in stringers bolted to the posts with 2 in cross planking and 1 by 2 in hardwood cleats at 6 in on centre; an alternate ramp floor of compacted earth with gravel topping behind a treated plank retaining wall; an adjustable deck pivoting on the 6 by 6 in support posts on a one and a half inch diameter pipe pivot shaft; a one and a half inch pipe support with two and a quarter by 9 by 1 ft 8 in adjustment plates bolted to the posts and slotted like a gun rack; and an optional three-quarter by 2 ft 0 in by 2 ft 8 in plywood extension on heavy-duty tee hinges. The plan that satisfies the Code of Practice section 5.3 requirement for no unprotected gap between the ramp and the vehicle.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1817: Adjustable (portable) Loading Chute
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The portable, skid-mounted adjustable loading chute, revised July 1984, with a full cut list. Six 4 by 4 in posts - two at 4 ft 10 and a half in, two at 6 ft 2 and a half in and two at 7 ft 6 in; ten 2 by 8 by 12 ft 0 in planks; two 2 by 4 by 3 ft 7 in slip guards nailed to cleats; sixteen 1 by 2 by 3 ft 2 in cleats; sixteen 2 by 8 by 3 ft 2 in ramp planks, giving a nominal 3 ft 2 in ramp width; two 4 by 4 by 4 ft 2 in hinged ramp supports on quarter by 4 by 3 ft 0 in strap hinges; a 4 by 4 by 7 ft 2 in ramp support; 4 by 4 by 11 ft 0 in skids with both ends bevelled 45 degrees; 3 by 3 by five-sixteenths angle-iron adjustable ramp brackets 1 ft 0 in long; a half inch diameter pipe 4 ft 0 in long with one and a half inch washers welded on as stops; a 2 by 4 by 3 ft 2 in adjustable ramp stop; cross braces; and thirty three-eighths by 6 in and twenty three-eighths by 9 in bolts. The design to reach for where the ranch wants a load-out that can be towed to a different pen.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1819: Herringbone A.I. Breeding Chute
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: A herringbone artificial insemination breeding chute for larger beef herds or for synchronised estrus, based on University of California leaflet 21029 and designed so one person can handle the cows. Cows are gathered in a holding pen, crowded quietly into a curved chute and fill the farthest stalls first; a short chain behind each cow stops her backing out; stall fronts, tops and front sides are solid plywood with a burlap flap over the back to isolate her; a rope control releases each stall exit door and a spring opens it. Stall width is adjusted by changing the angle of the side gates, which pivot on their rear posts, and the number of stalls can be changed without affecting the design. Dimensions stated: holding pen 27 sq ft per head; 6 by 6 in by 8 ft pressure-treated posts set 4 ft 0 in deep; 2 ft 8 in man gate. References corral and feedlot fencing 1811, crowding gate 1812, working chute 1813, loading chute 1816 or 1817 and blocking gate 1814.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1835: Large Working Corral
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The Canada Plan Service large working corral, revised July 1985 - a compact, practical corral that easily holds a breeding herd of 100 cows and their calves plus young cattle, built around a very popular semicircular working alley whose inner radius is at least 10 ft, with the explicit recommendation to increase that radius if space allows. Numbered components: cattle alley with access from feedlot or pasture; 12 ft 0 in gate with open corral fencing per leaflet 1811; 12 ft 0 in crowding gate with closed fencing per leaflet 1812; crowding pen of approximately 80 head; working chute with catwalk per leaflet 1813; optional scale, subtract 8 ft 0 in from the overall length if it is not used; blocking gate per leaflet 1814; loading chute per leaflet 1816; man gate; cattle squeeze with headgate; 5 ft 0 in sorting gate; holding pens of approximately 70, 60 and 30 head; a waterer if animals are held more than a day; post spacing of 8 ft 0 in maximum; an optional scale layout and bypass gates for the scale. The plan advises placing the scale near the service alley but not in line with it, to limit wear and maintenance. Reproduced as Corral Layout 9 in Alberta's Corrals for Handling Beef Cattle, with a relative material cost index of 2.1 against the minimum working corral.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1835 leaflet (French): Grand corral de manutention
papers.authors: Service de plans canadiens / Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The French edition of Canada Plan Service plan 1835, Large Working Corral, hosted by Agri-Reseau in Quebec. A second working free host for the plan, useful because the English copy is only available through the Internet Archive. Same content: a corral for a 100-cow breeding herd with calves plus young cattle, a semicircular service alley of at least 10 ft inner radius that should be enlarged where space permits, a crowding pen of about 80 head, holding pens of about 70, 60 and 30 head, 12 ft gates, a 5 ft sorting gate, maximum 8 ft post spacing, an optional 8 ft scale section and a waterer where animals are held more than a day.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan M-1000: Beef Cattle Housing and Equipment
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The parent sheet for beef cattle pens, yards and housing, and the source of Alberta's Table 70 housing guidelines (84:07). Opens with the principle that governs a prairie yard: cattle suffer more from mud, wet weather and cold winter winds than from low temperatures alone. Siting: build on a well-drained site, ideally a south-facing slope on well-drained soil, near an adequate water supply but away from streams and population centres, with natural tree shelter. Drainage: where existing slopes give less than 1 in 25, move fill to increase effective slope and build earth mounds; shape pens so drainage runs away from resting, feeding and watering areas; slope barn roofs away from pens or fit eave troughs; pave around feeders and waterers, and pave the whole pen where annual rainfall exceeds 500 mm. Shelter: porous windbreak fences at 20 per cent open give the best protection, and in heavy snow country a snow fence should be erected about 45 m upwind of the windbreak with space between for a snow trap; open-front sheds should have a roof sloping away from the opening and the opening should face south in most areas. Ventilation by eave and ridge openings, with hinged panels or retractable curtains if the building doubles as a summer sunshade. Feeding: feeders high enough that lot drainage runs away from the feeding area, with concrete aprons at least as wide as the scraper and tractor wheels sloped 1 in 10 away from the bunk, or a step 100 to 150 mm high and 300 to 400 mm wide next to the bunk where the apron slope is less; run bunks north-south to reduce frozen manure build-up. Runoff control: runoff from cattle lots and manure storage must not enter any watercourse, so diversion dykes or ditches keep clean runoff out of the lots and settling and retention basins hold lot runoff through spring thaw and heavy rain - the engineering form of the AOPA interceptor requirement. An imperial companion is archived at the same path as 1000L.pdf.

papers.title: Canada Plan Service plan 1820: Loading System for Large Trucks
papers.authors: Canada Plan Service; D. Darby (designed and drawn)
papers.licence: Free distribution; Canada Plan Service co-operative
papers.abstract: The newest sheet in the Canada Plan Service beef handling set (new June 1999, designed and drawn by D. Darby of Alberta Agriculture Engineering Services), and the one most relevant to a modern ranch shipping on a liner. A corral system for efficient and orderly loading of large cattle liners, which typically hold about 50 finished steers in compartments, so an efficient loading system pre-sorts batches of animals for each section of the load. Worked example of one load of fat cattle: 8 head in the front compartment, 14 for the belly section, 18 head to the upper deck and 10 to finish the rear. The sheet states that assembling those batches by pre-sorting in a pen ahead of the chute is less stressful and preferred over crowding and cutting as cattle go up the chute. The holding pen should hold a truck load, typically up to 55 finished animals; the crowding tub conveniently holds over a dozen head, and a second crowding gate at the start of the loading alley helps handle larger batches and sort. Numbered components: handling alley, cutting gate, 12 ft crowding gate, tub with catwalk, holding and sorting pen, loading alley, loading chute with off-set sight lines, a second holding pen to aid multiple loadings, and a rugged man gate. Pen dimensions on the drawing run 32 to 40 ft, 24 to 32 ft, 18 to 24 ft and 12 to 14 ft. Its basic loading-chute rules: have a rugged chute, offset the truck from the chute entrance so cattle turn a corner before they see the truck, provide good access for the truck driver, and use solid sides to reduce spooking.
